texts.title: Picatrix
texts.description: The Latin Picatrix is the principal medieval Latin witness to the Arabic Ghayat al-hakim and a central source for astral image magic.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Picatrix is the most sophisticated and influential astrological magic text of the medieval and early modern periods. Originally composed in Arabic as the Ghāyat al-ḥakīm (Goal of the Wise), probably in Andalusia around 1000 CE and attributed to the Pseudo-Majriti (the mathematician Maslama al-Majriti was sometimes named), it was translated into Castilian in 1256 under Alfonso X of Castile and from Castilian into Latin around 1300. The Latin translation circulated widely through the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and portions of it were used by Marsilio Ficino, copied into miscellanies alongside the Clavicula Salomonis, and drawn on by Cornelius Agrippa in De occulta philosophia.

Contents

The Picatrix is organized in four books covering: the principles of astrological magic and celestial influence (Book I); the practical construction of talismans and images keyed to the planets and fixed stars (Book II); more advanced planetary magic, fumigations, suffumigations, and the manipulation of planetary spirits (Book III); and a theoretical treatment of the soul, the world-spirit (pneuma), and the philosophical principles underlying magical efficacy (Book IV). The text draws on Arabic astrology, Neoplatonic philosophy, Hermetic cosmology, and practical ritual traditions to produce a comprehensive system of astral magic that is both theoretically sophisticated and practically detailed.

The talismanic procedures are keyed to the twenty-eight lunar mansions as well as the seven planets, providing a very fine temporal and astrological grid for magical operations. The text specifies the materials (metals, plants, stones, fumigations) appropriate to each celestial power, the images to be inscribed or cast, and the invocations to be used. Its treatment of planetary spirits — as intermediary agents between the celestial bodies and terrestrial matter — is the most elaborate in medieval Latin magical literature.

Scholarship

The critical edition of the Latin text is by David Pingree (2 vols., Warburg Institute, 1986); Pingree's introduction is the essential guide to the text's sources and manuscript tradition. An English translation by John Michael Greer and Christopher Warnock appeared in 2010 (Adocentyn Press) and a more recent scholarly translation with apparatus has been produced by Attrell and Porreca (Penn State, 2019). The Arabic text has been edited by Hellmut Ritter (Leipzig, 1933). For the relationship of the Picatrix to Latin natural philosophy and to Ficino, see Brian Copenhaver's articles and the relevant sections of Weill-Parot's work on addressative magic.

texts.title: Ars Notoria
texts.description: The Ars Notoria is a ritual art of memory and learning transmitted in medieval Latin manuscripts.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Ars Notoria (Notory Art) is a Latin magical text, probably compiled in the twelfth or thirteenth century, that provides a system for acquiring knowledge of the seven liberal arts and other forms of learning through a programme of prayer, fasting, and contemplation of the notae — elaborate geometric and symbolic figures accompanied by sequences of divine names, Greek voces magicae, and Hebrew words, arranged into extended series of prayers (orationes). The practitioner is promised that diligent use of the system will result in divine infusion of the knowledge of grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy, without the ordinary labour of study.

Structure and Use

The text exists in two main recensions: a shorter version and a longer version incorporating additional notae and prayers. The cycle of use for the complete system takes several months; intermediate cycles of shorter duration are also prescribed. The practitioner must observe strict conditions of ritual purity, undertake fasting and prayer at specified times, and contemplate the notae while reciting the associated prayers. The result is claimed to be not only the acquisition of encyclopedic knowledge but also prophetic dreams, visions of angels, and ultimately the direct perception of God.

Julien Véronèse's critical edition (L'Ars notoria au Moyen Âge: Introduction et édition critique, Sismel, 2007) is the scholarly standard. John of Morigny's Liber visionum (early fourteenth century), edited by Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson (Penn State, 2015), is the most important medieval response to the Ars Notoria — a visionary revision of the system undertaken after Marian apparitions. Frank Klaassen's work situates the text within the broader manuscript tradition of English learned magic.

Theological Status

The Ars Notoria occupied an unusual theological position: it claimed to work through divine grace rather than demonic pact, making it arguably licit. Thomas Aquinas condemned it in the Summa theologiae (II-II, q. 96, a. 1) as vain (the system cannot achieve what it claims) and as implicitly involving demonic assistance (the voces magicae and geometric figures have no natural relationship to the knowledge they are supposed to infuse). Nevertheless, the text circulated widely in monastic and university contexts, and its practitioners evidently found the theological condemnation less than conclusive.

texts.title: Sworn Book of Honorius
texts.description: The Sworn Book of Honorius is a major medieval ritual magic text concerned with divine vision, angelic hierarchy, and ritual discipline.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Sworn Book of Honorius (Liber juratus Honorii) is a Latin magical text, probably composed in the thirteenth century, that presents itself as the surviving essence of a great magical library compiled by Honorius of Thebes and preserved only because ninety masters of magic swore to keep it secret and to pass it on to no more than three persons each. The framing narrative — the masters of magic assembling against papal persecution to preserve their knowledge — is itself significant as an early articulation of the magician's self-understanding as a persecuted keeper of ancient wisdom.

Contents

The Sworn Book is organized around a programme for achieving the beatific vision — the direct sight of God — through a course of prayer, fasting, and ritual practice extending over several months. The operative core is a set of prayers and conjurations for summoning the angel Hochmel (associated with divine wisdom), other celestial spirits, and eventually God himself. The text also includes procedures for more conventional magical ends: spirit conjuration for practical purposes, the construction of the Seal of God (a complex diagram combining divine names, astrological symbols, and angelic seals), and instructions for achieving invisibility.

Gösta Hedegård's critical edition (Liber iuratus Honorii: A Critical Edition of the Latin Version of the Sworn Book of Honorius, Almqvist and Wiksell, 2002) provides the scholarly text. Joseph Peterson's edition (Ibis Press, 2016) makes it available with English translation. The text occupies an interesting position between the Ars Notoria tradition (angelic infusion of knowledge through prayer and contemplation) and the demonic conjuration tradition (explicit spirit-binding for practical ends), and has been analysed by Kieckhefer, Klaassen, and Sophie Page in terms of this generic ambiguity.

texts.title: Forbidden Rites
texts.description: Richard Kieckhefer's Forbidden Rites edits and studies a fifteenth-century necromantic manual.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Richard Kieckhefer's Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century (Penn State University Press, 1997) is both a critical edition and translation of the Munich Manual of demonic magic (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 849) and a sustained scholarly analysis of what the text reveals about medieval learned magic and the social world in which it circulated. The Munich Manual is a Latin miscellany copied around the 1440s containing illusionist tricks, love magic using spirits, and full demonic conjuration rituals — the most complete surviving medieval Latin handbook of its kind.

The Text and Its Contents

Clm 849 contains three distinct types of material. The first section comprises "illusionist" experiments — procedures for creating apparent wonders (making a horse seem to have no head, making a banquet appear where none exists) that exploit psychological suggestion and natural properties rather than demonic power. The second section covers experiments involving spirit assistance for practical ends: finding hidden treasure, compelling love, causing discord, revealing thieves. The third section contains formal demonic conjuration: complete ritual procedures for summoning, binding, interrogating, and dismissing named demons.

Kieckhefer's edition provides the Latin text with facing English translation and extensive annotation identifying the demons named, the ritual sources, and the parallels in other magical manuscripts. His introductory chapters situate the text within the broader tradition of medieval Latin magic, discuss the question of how such a text was used (by whom, in what circumstances, with what expectations), and address the relationship between demonic conjuration and the theological concept of demonic pact.

Significance

The Munich Manual is significant as a primary document for the "clerical underworld" that Kieckhefer theorized in Magic in the Middle Ages: a text clearly designed for a literate, Latinately educated practitioner who expected to perform its rituals, not merely read about them. Its survival is partly accidental (it was bound with more respectable medical and astrological texts), and its content is more explicitly demonic than most surviving magical manuscripts — raising the question of what was destroyed that no longer survives. Forbidden Rites remains the model for how to approach a practical magic manuscript with scholarly rigour.

texts.title: The Transformations of Magic
texts.description: Frank Klaassen's study examines illicit learned magic in the later Middle Ages and Renaissance.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic: Illicit Learned Magic in the Later Middle Ages (Penn State University Press, 2013) is the most rigorous analysis of what Klaassen calls the "experiment literature" — the practical ritual magic books (nigromantic handbooks, ars notoria texts, Solomonic conjuration manuals) that circulated in manuscript among clerically trained readers in medieval England and Continental Europe from approximately 1300 to 1500. The book argues against two misleading models: the model that treats medieval magic as a unified, coherent tradition with stable content, and the model that treats the learned magical tradition as a pale copy of, or preparation for, Renaissance Hermeticism. Instead, Klaassen documents what actually survived in English manuscripts and shows how the content, purposes, and social contexts of learned magic shifted substantially over two centuries.

Argument and Evidence

Klaassen's central methodological contribution is the systematic survey of a defined corpus: he identifies and analyses approximately 270 surviving manuscripts containing ritual magic material in the medieval English tradition, rather than relying on a handful of well-known texts. This allows him to distinguish majority practice (ars notoria texts, image magic, simple conjurations) from exceptional cases (full demonic pact rituals), to trace the social circulation of texts across different manuscript contexts, and to identify two distinct types of transformation across the later medieval period.

The first transformation Klaassen identifies is a shift from "Solomonic" ritual magic — which emphasised the magician's moral purity, his Solomonic authority, and the coercive binding of spirits within a broadly Christian ritual framework — toward a more openly demonic conjuration literature in which the pact and explicit appeal to demonic power become more visible. The second transformation, running in the opposite direction, is the gradual absorption of Solomonic and image magic into the emerging idiom of "natural philosophy": Klaassen documents how later medieval readers and scribes increasingly framed magical operations in naturalistic terms, aligning them with Albertan and Arabist accounts of occult properties and celestial influence, effectively naturalising what earlier manuscripts had treated as operations of religious power.

Significance for Grimoire Studies

The book makes three major contributions to the study of the grimoire tradition. First, by documenting the manuscript evidence rather than relying on printed editions, Klaassen corrects the distortions introduced by the selective survival and editorial intervention of printed magical texts. Second, by demonstrating that "the learned magical tradition" is not a single thing but a set of practices and texts that changed substantially across two centuries, the book warns against the anachronistic projection of later Renaissance or early modern magical theory back onto medieval texts. Third, by focusing on what scribes and readers actually did with manuscripts — how they copied, excerpted, combined, and reorganised texts — Klaassen provides a model of manuscript-culture analysis that influenced subsequent work on the Ars Notoria, the Munich Manual, and Solomonic texts.

Context and Reception

Klaassen's work was preceded by and engages throughout with Richard Kieckhefer's Forbidden Rites (1997), which edited and analysed the Munich Manual of demonic magic, and with Claire Fanger's edited volumes on medieval ritual magic. It has been widely cited in subsequent scholarship on the grimoire tradition, including Dan Harms and Joseph Peterson's work on specific texts and Sophie Page's studies of magical manuscripts in institutional collections.

texts.title: Magic in the Cloister
texts.description: Sophie Page's monograph examines monastic and clerical engagements with occult approaches to the medieval universe.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Sophie Page's Magic in the Cloister: Pious Motives, Illicit Interests, and Occult Approaches to the Medieval Universe (Penn State University Press, 2013) examines magical manuscripts in English monastic and collegiate library collections, demonstrating that monks, canons, and other religious not only possessed magical texts but engaged with them in ways that made sense within their intellectual and devotional frameworks. The book challenges the assumption that magic was simply suppressed by institutional Christianity and argues instead for a more complex picture of accommodation, curiosity, and practical use.

Evidence and Argument

Page's primary evidence consists of the magical manuscripts preserved in collections associated with specific English monastic and collegiate institutions — principally St Augustine's Canterbury, the Augustinian canons at Oxford, and related houses. By examining these manuscripts in their codicological context (what texts surround them, how the manuscripts are constructed, what marks of ownership and use they bear), Page reconstructs something of the reading practices of the religious who possessed them.

The picture that emerges is of a learned culture that maintained theoretical condemnations of magic while in practice preserving, copying, and apparently using magical texts for a variety of purposes: curiosity about the natural world and its hidden workings; practical medical applications (the boundary between healing and magic was genuinely ambiguous); interest in the cosmological frameworks that magical texts assumed; and possibly direct practical use of the simpler magical procedures. Page's argument that "pious motives" could coexist with "illicit interests" in the same practitioner is an important corrective to the tendency to treat magic and orthodoxy as simply opposed.

texts.title: Invoking Angels
texts.description: Claire Fanger's edited collection studies theurgic ideas and practices from the thirteenth to sixteenth centuries.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Claire Fanger (ed.), Invoking Angels: Theurgic Ideas and Practices, Thirteenth to Sixteenth Centuries (Penn State University Press, 2012) is the follow-up volume to Fanger's earlier Conjuring Spirits (1998) and represents the state of the field in the study of medieval and early Renaissance angel magic. The volume collects essays by leading scholars on the Ars Notoria tradition, the Liber visionum of John of Morigny, the Sworn Book of Honorius, and related texts, with particular attention to the relationship between angel magic, mysticism, and devotional practice.

Contents and Significance

The essays in Invoking Angels demonstrate how the category of "angel magic" — operations aimed at communication with angelic beings for the acquisition of knowledge or other benefits — overlaps with and cannot be cleanly separated from approved forms of medieval Christian contemplation and prayer. The practitioners of the Ars Notoria understood themselves as engaging in a form of pious enquiry for divine gifts of knowledge; John of Morigny's Marian angel magic was explicitly framed as a devotional practice. The volume's central argument is that the boundary between magic and mysticism in the medieval period was contested, permeable, and historically produced rather than given by the nature of the practices themselves.

Contributors include Julien Véronèse (on the Ars Notoria), Nicholas Watson (on John of Morigny), Sophie Page, and other leading historians of medieval magic. The volume is essential reading for the history of angelic magic and for understanding how the learned magical tradition intersected with the broader landscape of medieval Christian spiritual practice. Together with Fanger's Conjuring Spirits (1998), it constitutes the foundational edited collection for the study of medieval ritual magic.

texts.title: Unlocked Books
texts.description: Benedek Lang's study of manuscripts of learned magic in Central European libraries foregrounds codicology, ownership, and library context as evidence for learned magical transmission.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Benedek Láng's Unlocked Books: Manuscripts of Learned Magic in the Medieval Libraries of Central Europe (Pennsylvania State University Press, 2008) extends the systematic study of magical manuscripts in institutional library collections — pioneered for England by Kieckhefer, Klaassen, and Page — to the libraries of Hungary, Austria, Poland, and Bohemia. The result substantially expands the geographic scope of medieval magic scholarship and demonstrates that the learned magical tradition was a genuinely pan-European phenomenon with significant regional variation.

Findings and Significance

Láng's survey of Central European library collections reveals that magical manuscripts were present in significant quantities in the major institutional libraries of the region: the royal library at Buda, the chapter libraries of Esztergom and Krakow, the university libraries of Vienna and Prague. The types of magical material represented span the full range of the European learned tradition: astrological and geomantic texts, the Ars Notoria, Solomonic conjuration, natural magic, and miscellaneous practical magical material.

The book's title reflects its central argumentative point: the magical manuscripts were "unlocked" — that is, accessible in regular library collections, available to any reader with access to the institution, not hidden in restricted or clandestine locations. This accessibility suggests that the social reality of magical manuscript possession and circulation was more open than the theological rhetoric of condemnation implies. Readers who consulted a magical text in a chapter library were not necessarily engaging in transgressive behaviour; they were using the resources of a learned library in the same way as they would use other technical or philosophical texts. Láng's findings complement Klaassen's for England and Page's for monastic contexts, establishing the "open library" character of medieval magical manuscript culture as a European-wide phenomenon.

texts.title: Magic in Medieval Manuscripts
texts.description: Sophie Page's study examines medieval manuscript evidence for magical texts and the codicological contexts in which occult, devotional, and scientific materials circulated.
texts.analysis_html:
Magic in Medieval Manuscripts (2010): A Visual and Textual Survey

Sophie Page's Magic in Medieval Manuscripts (2010), published by the British Library, provides an accessible yet scholarly introduction to magical texts and their manuscript contexts through the British Library's extensive collections. The volume combines analysis of magical content with attention to the material and visual dimensions of magical manuscripts—their scripts, illustrations, diagrams, and physical form—demonstrating how the study of manuscripts as objects, rather than merely as vehicles for textual content, can illuminate the practices and communities that produced and used them. Page's expertise in medieval magic and manuscript culture makes the volume both an authoritative scholarly resource and an effective guide for general readers encountering this material for the first time.

The book's coverage ranges from the Anglo-Saxon period through the late Middle Ages, examining texts in Latin, Middle English, and other vernaculars. It addresses the full spectrum of magical literature from theoretical demonology and natural magic to practical grimoires and popular charms, situating each within its historical and cultural context. Particular attention is paid to the visual elements of magical manuscripts: the elaborate diagrams of the Ars Notoria, the spirit seals of Solomonic texts, the astronomical tables of astrological magic, and the illustrated charms of vernacular tradition. These visual components are integral to the magical function of the texts themselves, not merely decorative additions.

Page's approach illustrates a broader methodological turn in the study of medieval magic toward attention to the material dimensions of textual transmission. Rather than treating manuscripts as neutral containers for textual content, scholars in this tradition examine the physical properties of manuscripts—parchment type, binding, marginal annotations, signs of use—as evidence for how texts were read, stored, and transmitted. This material philology has revealed important information about the social contexts of magical text production and use, suggesting audiences and practices that analysis of content alone would miss. The British Library's collections, rich in magical manuscripts of all periods and traditions, make them an ideal platform for this kind of investigation.

texts.title: Hazards of the Dark Arts
texts.description: Richard Kieckhefer's translation and study of Johannes Hartlieb's advice for princes places witchcraft, magic, and prohibited arts within fifteenth-century political and moral counsel.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Richard Kieckhefer's Hazards of the Dark Arts: Advice for Medieval Princes on Witchcraft and Magic (Penn State University Press, 2017) compiles and translates a series of late medieval advisory texts — addressed to princes, rulers, and nobles — that address the dangers of magic and witchcraft from a practical political perspective. The volume demonstrates that the discourse about magic was not confined to theological treatises and inquisitorial manuals but extended into the genre of political advice literature, where magic was addressed as a practical concern for rulers who might be targeted by maleficium or who needed to adjudicate accusations of magical harm.

Contents and Significance

The texts compiled by Kieckhefer represent a rarely examined genre: advice for princes on how to recognize, respond to, and protect against magical attack, written by court-connected scholars and clerics who combined theological learning with political practicality. The texts address topics including how to evaluate accusations of witchcraft, how to distinguish natural from demonic causation in apparent marvels, and how a prince should comport himself in relation to practitioners of magic — whether to prosecute them, tolerate them, or employ them.

The volume contributes to the broader social-historical understanding of how magical discourse operated in political contexts, complementing the institutional history of the Inquisition and the theological history of demonological writing. Kieckhefer's introduction situates these texts within the broader landscape of medieval political thought and the history of magic, and the translations make them accessible to English-language readers for the first time.

texts.title: Liber Theysolius
texts.description: The Liber Theysolius is a medieval text associated in recent scholarship with wisdom, familiar spirits, and the pursuit of knowledge through ritualized contact.
texts.analysis_html:
Liber Theysolius: An Attributed Magical Compilation

The Liber Theysolius is a Latin magical text attributed to the otherwise obscure figure of Theysolius, belonging to the tradition of medieval learned magic compilations that claimed ancient authority through pseudepigraphical attribution. Like many texts in this genre, the Liber Theysolius draws on diverse sources—spirit lists, ritual procedures, divine name sequences, and operational instructions—assembled under a single attributed authority to constitute a usable magical reference. The text's content situates it within the broader experimental magic tradition of the thirteenth through fifteenth centuries.

The compilation's significance lies partly in what it reveals about the practices of magical text production and transmission in medieval Europe. Compilations like the Liber Theysolius were assembled by practitioners who drew on available sources—other magical texts, oral traditions, astrological lore, angelological speculation—and organized them under convenient attributed authorities. The resulting texts were neither simple copies of sources nor entirely original compositions, but products of a creative compilation process that was itself a recognized form of learned activity. The attribution to Theysolius, like attributions to Solomon, Hermes, or Apollonius elsewhere, served to anchor this compiled material in claimed ancient wisdom.

Scholarly recovery of texts like the Liber Theysolius has been part of the broader project, undertaken by researchers including Frank Klaassen and Richard Kieckhefer, to document the full range of medieval magical literature beyond the canonical texts most frequently discussed. Manuscript catalogues, critical editions, and comparative studies have gradually mapped the scope of this literature, revealing a much larger and more diverse corpus than earlier scholarship recognized. Minor texts like the Liber Theysolius contribute to this picture by providing evidence for the variety of practices, traditions, and attributed authorities that populated the medieval magical imagination beyond its most famous exemplars.

texts.title: Liber Juratus Honorii
texts.description: The Liber Juratus Honorii, or Sworn Book of Honorius, is a major Latin ritual text concerning divine vision, angelic hierarchy, and sworn secrecy.
texts.analysis_html:
Liber Juratus Honorii: The Sworn Book of Honorius

The Liber Juratus Honorii (Sworn Book of Honorius), also known as the Liber Sacer, is one of the most ambitious and complex magical texts of the medieval period, claiming to represent the distilled essence of the entire magical tradition assembled by a council of master magicians at the instigation of the angel Hocroel. The text's elaborate frame narrative presents it as the product of a congress of ninety magic masters who, threatened by papal and episcopal persecution, decided to preserve their knowledge in a single book to be sworn to secrecy and transmitted only to worthy initiates. This origin legend—itself a sophisticated piece of legitimating fiction—gives the text a self-conscious sense of representing a persecuted tradition of authentic wisdom.

The text's content reflects its synthetic ambitions: it includes a comprehensive theory of the created order, detailed instructions for achieving a vision of God (the beatific vision) through sustained magical practice, a lengthy ritual for summoning angels and spirits of the four directions, extensive lists of divine names, and practical operations for a wide range of goals. The beatific vision section is particularly distinctive, presenting the acquisition of divine knowledge as the highest goal of magical practice—a goal that claims to transcend mere practical magic and participate in the tradition of Christian mysticism. This theological ambition distinguishes the Sworn Book from purely operational texts and connects it to the learned magic tradition's persistent aspiration to reconcile magical practice with Christian spiritual aspiration.

Gösta Hedegård's critical edition (2002) established a reliable Latin text based on manuscript comparison and provided the scholarly foundation for subsequent analysis. Researchers including Julien Véronèse and Sophie Page have situated the Sworn Book within the broader context of clerical learned magic and the contested transmission of magical knowledge in medieval Europe. The text's claim to represent an endangered tradition preserved against persecution resonates with actual historical circumstances—the repeated condemnation of magical texts by councils, bishops, and papal authority—suggesting that its frame narrative, however fictive in its specifics, reflects genuine anxiety about the survival of this kind of knowledge.

texts.title: Liber Razielis
texts.description: The Liber Razielis is a Latin textual complex associated with angelic revelation, astral knowledge, and the figure of Raziel.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Liber Razielis (Book of Raziel) is a Latin magical compendium, probably compiled in the thirteenth century, that draws heavily on Jewish sources — particularly the Hebrew Sepher Raziel ha-Malakh (Book of Raziel the Angel) — and on Arabic astrological magic. The Latin text presents itself as a revelation from the angel Raziel to Adam, transmitted through Enoch, Noah, Solomon, and ultimately to the practitioner. Its content includes angel magic, conjuration, astrological talismans, and a cosmological account of the seven heavens and their angelic inhabitants.

Sources and Transmission

The Liber Razielis is one of the most important texts for tracing the transmission of Jewish magical traditions into Latin learned magic. Its Hebrew source, the Sepher Raziel, is a complex compilation that was probably assembled in the thirteenth century but incorporates much older material, including traditions related to the Sepher ha-Razim and Geonic angel magic. The Latin translation transformed a Hebrew text structured around Jewish liturgical and cosmological categories into a form legible and usable within the framework of Latin clerical magic.

The text circulated in association with other Solomonic and angel magic texts — it appears in several manuscripts alongside the Clavicula Salomonis and the Ars Notoria — and was known to be one of the principal sources of Solomon's magical knowledge. David Pingree's work on the text and Gideon Bohak's analysis of the relationship between the Hebrew and Latin traditions provide the best scholarly guides to its transmission history.

texts.title: De radiis
texts.description: De radiis, associated with al-Kindi in Latin tradition, theorizes rays, celestial causality, and the efficacy of words and images in medieval natural philosophy.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Al-Kindi's De radiis stellarum (On Stellar Rays) — surviving only in a medieval Latin translation, its Arabic original apparently lost — is the most theoretically systematic account of magical causation in the Arabic-Latin intellectual tradition and the primary source for the naturalistic theory that underlies astrological and talismanic magic. Probably written around 850 CE and translated into Latin in the twelfth century, the text argues from first principles that all causation in the cosmos operates through the radiation of qualities from every existing thing, and that this universal radiation system provides the mechanism by which magic works.

The Theory of Rays

Al-Kindi argues that every entity in the world — celestial and terrestrial, material and immaterial — continuously emits rays in all directions, analogous to the emission of light from a luminous body. These rays carry the specific qualities of their source and affect the things they strike, changing their qualities, movements, or states. Celestial bodies emit the most powerful and pervasive rays, because their nature is superior and their position gives them access to the entire sublunary world. But terrestrial things also emit rays; the human will and imagination, when intensely concentrated, can emit rays that affect other things at a distance — this is the theoretical basis for the magician's power.

The magician who understands the ray-system can work within it: by concentrating his will on a specific intention, using materials and words that resonate with specific celestial sources, timing his operations to celestial configurations that strengthen the relevant rays, he produces effects at a distance through purely natural (if hidden) causes. Al-Kindi is thus the philosopher of natural magic in its most rigorous form: magic is applied natural philosophy, and the boundaries between the two are established by knowledge rather than by essential difference.

Influence

The influence of De radiis on Latin natural philosophy was extensive. Thabit ibn Qurra's De imaginibus applies the ray theory to astrological image magic. Robert Grosseteste's metaphysics of light and Roger Bacon's multiplication of species draw on related principles. The Speculum astronomiae cites al-Kindi's works on images; Nicolas Weill-Parot's analysis of addressative magic situates De radiis as the theoretical foundation that subsequent scholastic discussion of image magic either accepted, qualified, or rejected. David Pingree's catalogue of al-Kindi's works provides the bibliographic context.

texts.title: De imaginibus
texts.description: De imaginibus is a Latin astral-image text attributed to Thabit ibn Qurra and important for theories of talismanic images and celestial timing.
texts.analysis_html:
De Imaginibus: Thabit ibn Qurra and Talismanic Magic

The text known in Latin as De imaginibus (On Images) and attributed to the ninth-century Sabian mathematician and astronomer Thabit ibn Qurra represents one of the most influential transmissions of Arabic talismanic magic into the medieval Latin West. The text provides instructions for creating astrological talismans—images, figures, or inscribed objects—at specific celestial conjunctions to capture and channel planetary or stellar influences for a variety of practical goals including healing, protection, and the influencing of persons and events. Its detailed operational instructions, combined with astrological rationale, made it a key source for Latin authors seeking to engage with image magic within a natural philosophical framework.

The text's attribution to Thabit ibn Qurra, while questioned by modern scholars, reflects the medieval strategy of anchoring magical texts in authoritative ancient or prestigious near-contemporary names. Thabit's genuine reputation as a mathematician and astronomer of the first rank—he translated Greek mathematical texts into Arabic and made original contributions to astronomy and number theory—lent credibility to a text making bold claims about celestial influence. Whether or not Thabit wrote anything like the text attributed to him, the attribution circulated widely and influenced the text's reception as legitimate natural philosophy rather than condemned superstition.

The De imaginibus occupies a central place in Nicole Weill-Parot's important study of "addressative" magic—that is, magic based on the idea that images or objects can be addressed to specific spiritual or celestial entities capable of conferring power. Her analysis situates the text within the debate about whether image magic relies on natural celestial causation (and is thus philosophically defensible) or on the implicit invocation of spiritual beings (and is thus condemned as demonic). This debate, which runs through the entire medieval treatment of talismanic and astrological magic, gave the De imaginibus its controversial significance: it was both a resource for those who sought to develop a natural philosophical account of magic and a target for those who insisted that any such account merely obscured underlying demonic dependency.

texts.title: Speculum astronomiae
texts.description: The Speculum astronomiae classifies astrological and image-making texts and became a crucial witness for scholastic attempts to distinguish licit astronomy from illicit image magic.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Speculum astronomiae (Mirror of Astronomy), attributed to Albertus Magnus though the attribution has been contested (Nicolas Weill-Parot argues against it; most scholars accept it), is the most systematic scholastic treatment of the boundary between legitimate and illegitimate astrological magic composed in the thirteenth century. Probably written in the 1260s, the text was addressed to the growing number of natural philosophers who were encountering Arabic astrological image magic and needed guidance on which procedures were compatible with Christian orthodoxy and which were not.

The Tripartite Classification

The Speculum's central contribution is a tripartite classification of astrological image-making. The first category — fully licit — comprises images that work through purely natural celestial causes: talismans whose figures, materials, and timing are keyed to the natural influences of specific planets, operating as material focal points for stellar power in the way that a burning glass concentrates light. The second category — potentially licit, depending on content — comprises images that may or may not involve demonic invocation: the key question is whether the text that accompanies the image explicitly addresses spiritual agents by name (thereby becoming "addressative" in Weill-Parot's terminology) or merely exploits natural stellar influence. The third category — clearly illicit — comprises images that explicitly invoke demonic names or require demonic cooperation: these are condemned without qualification.

This classification had significant consequences for subsequent natural philosophy and magic. It legitimated a domain of astrological talisman-making as natural philosophy, provided a framework for evaluating specific texts and procedures, and influenced later Renaissance defenders of natural magic (Ficino, Agrippa, della Porta) who sought to work within the licit category. It also identified the key diagnostic question — whether a magical procedure explicitly addresses spiritual agents — that Nicolas Weill-Parot's concept of addressative magic systematizes and applies to the broader history of medieval astrological image magic.

texts.title: A History of Magic and Experimental Science
texts.description: Lynn Thorndike's multi-volume history framed magic and experimental science as intertwined parts of medieval intellectual history, even where later scholarship has revised its assumptions.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Lynn Thorndike's A History of Magic and Experimental Science (Columbia University Press, 1923–1958), in eight volumes, is the most extensive survey of the relationship between magic and science in European intellectual history and remains, despite its limitations, an indispensable research tool for anyone working on the subject. The project covered the Roman Empire through the seventeenth century and drew on primary sources — often in manuscript — that Thorndike was the first modern scholar to examine systematically.

Argument and Organization

Thorndike's thesis — implicit in the title — is that magic and experimental science were parallel developments sharing an empirical orientation toward the investigation of nature's hidden properties. Medieval magic, he argued, was not mere superstition: it represented a serious attempt to understand and exploit natural forces, and the gradual differentiation of legitimate experimental science from magical practice is a key theme in the history of European thought from the Roman period through the Scientific Revolution. The work proceeds chronologically and person-by-person: each chapter treats a specific author, manuscript, or text, summarizing its contents and situating it in the broader intellectual history.

The work's strengths are its scope (no subsequent project has approached its coverage) and its primary-source depth (Thorndike read widely in manuscript collections and provides the first systematic accounts of dozens of texts). Its weaknesses include a tendency toward uncritical summary, an outdated historiographical framework (the "magic to science" teleology has been substantially revised), and factual errors in the earlier volumes that have been corrected by subsequent specialized scholarship. Despite these limitations, Thorndike's chapter-length surveys often remain the only readily available accounts of specific texts and authors, and the eight-volume index is an invaluable finding tool.

texts.title: Clavicula Salomonis
texts.description: The Key of Solomon is a major Solomonic grimoire tradition transmitted in late medieval and early modern manuscripts, important for ritual purity, seals, conjurations, and textual instability.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Clavicula Salomonis (Key of Solomon) is the most widely circulated and extensively copied of the medieval and early modern Solomonic grimoires, surviving in over one hundred manuscripts in Latin, Italian, Hebrew, French, and English, ranging from the fourteenth century to the nineteenth. It is attributed to Solomon himself or to the transmission from Solomon to his son Roboam, and presents itself as a comprehensive practical manual for the conjuration of spirits, the construction of magical implements, and the performance of a wide range of ritual operations.

Structure and Contents

The text is typically organized in two books. Book I covers the practical ritual operations: how to conjure spirits to achieve specific ends (finding hidden treasures, obtaining love, causing invisibility, healing disease, inflicting harm). Book II covers the preparation of the magician and his instruments: the days and hours of the planets under which various operations should be conducted, the making and consecration of the magic circle, the pentacles attributed to the seven planets (each accompanied by a figure and a conjuration), the preparation of magical tools (knife, wand, lamen, robe, etc.), and the ritual of suffumigation and prayer.

The manuscript tradition is enormously complex. Joseph Peterson's online edition (Esoteric Archives) documents over fifty Latin and vernacular manuscripts; his printed edition (Weiser, 2004) provides the most thorough textual analysis available. S.L. Mathers's 1889 edition, based on British Museum manuscripts, was the first modern printed edition and shaped the occult revival's understanding of the text, though it combined several divergent manuscript families without adequate documentation.

Historical Development

The earliest datable manuscripts of the Clavicula Salomonis are from the fourteenth century; the text clearly assembled over a long period from multiple source traditions, incorporating elements of older Solomonic demonology, astrological image magic, and ritual prayer. The Hebrew Mafteah Shelomoh (Key of Solomon) tradition is related but may represent an independent development rather than a simple translation from Latin. The Arabic tradition of Solomonic conjuration (Solomon as Sulayman, master of jinn) provides a parallel context rather than a direct source. Frank Klaassen's work on the medieval English manuscript tradition and Pablo Torijano's on the ancient background remain the principal scholarly frameworks.

texts.title: Hygromanteia
texts.description: The Hygromanteia is a Byzantine Greek Solomonic ritual tradition that stands behind later Key of Solomon materials and complicates Latin-centered grimoire histories.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Hygromanteia (Greek: divination from water) is a Byzantine Greek astrological magic text, attributed to Solomon and surviving in several Greek manuscripts from the thirteenth century onward, though its compilation likely predates the surviving witnesses. The text is one of the principal Greek Solomonic texts and was a source for, or parallel development to, the Latin Clavicula Salomonis tradition. It combines astrological procedures, planetary images and talismans, and conjuration formulae within a Solomonic attribution framework.

Contents and Structure

The Hygromanteia addresses a wide range of practical magical procedures organized around the planets and their governing periods. Its contents include: procedures for using water, fire, and other substances for divination; instructions for making and using planetary images and talismans; formulas for conjuring planetary spirits; and procedures for a range of practical operations (finding hidden things, causing love, defeating enemies, obtaining favour from authorities). The attribution to Solomon and the invocation of divine and angelic names as authorizing forces situate it firmly within the Solomonic tradition.

Scholarship

Ioannis Marathakis's critical edition and English translation (The Magical Treatise of Solomon or Hygromanteia, Golden Hoard Press, 2011) made the text accessible to scholars working in the Latin and vernacular magical tradition. The edition establishes the manuscript tradition, provides the Greek text with English translation, and discusses the relationship of the Hygromanteia to the Latin Clavicula Salomonis — a relationship of partial correspondence and partial independence that suggests a shared tradition of Solomonic magic rather than simple textual derivation.

texts.title: Testament of Solomon
texts.description: The Testament of Solomon is a late antique demonological text that made Solomon a paradigmatic commander of spirits in later magical and literary traditions.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Testament of Solomon is a Greek pseudepigraphic text, probably composed between the first and fifth centuries CE, that narrates how King Solomon, aided by a magic ring given by the archangel Michael, summoned and interrogated demons, learning their names, their functions, the afflictions they cause, and the angels capable of thwarting them. The demons are then set to work constructing the Temple in Jerusalem. The text is the earliest systematic demonology in Greek and the foundational text of the Solomonic grimoire tradition: its framework of named demons bound to named angels, organized by Solomonic authority, provides the template replicated across two millennia of magical literature.

Structure and Contents

The narrative frame has Solomon receive a ring from Michael, inscribed with a pentagram, that gives him power over demons. He then successively summons thirty-six demons (later expanded in some manuscript traditions), each of whom reveals his name and the specific affliction he causes. Typical entries follow a pattern: the demon appears, reveals his name (often etymologized or pun-connected to his function), describes the diseases or misfortunes he inflicts, and reveals the angel whose name, written or spoken, can neutralize him. Some entries include planetary associations, gemstone affinities, and brief ritual instructions.

The text exists in several manuscript recensions of varying length and arrangement: McCown identified five principal recensions in his 1922 critical edition. The most important manuscripts are in the Bibliothèque nationale de France and the Vienna National Library. Dennis Duling's translation in Charlesworth's Old Testament Pseudepigrapha (Doubleday, 1983) is the standard English version.

Historical Significance

The Testament of Solomon is significant for several reasons. First, as a demonological text, it represents the earliest comprehensive name-catalogue of demons with individual attributes — a structure replicated in the Ars Goetia (part of the Lemegeton), the Book of Abramelin, and dozens of medieval and early modern grimoires. Second, as a pseudepigraphic text, it establishes the attribution strategy that would legitimise the entire subsequent Solomonic corpus: magical knowledge is Solomonic in origin, transmitted by divine gift (Michael's ring), and serves ultimately to build the Temple — that is, to serve God's purposes. Third, its composite nature — drawing on Jewish, Christian, pagan Greek, and possibly Egyptian elements — makes it evidence for the multicultural magical milieu of the late antique Mediterranean.

texts.title: Liber de angelis
texts.description: The Liber de angelis names a family of Latin ritual texts concerned with angelic knowledge, invocation, and the textual authority of revealed ritual.
texts.analysis_html:
Liber de Angelis: Medieval Angel Magic and Practical Conjuration

The Liber de Angelis (Book of Angels) is a medieval Latin magical compilation preserved in several manuscript versions from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, providing practical instructions for invoking and working with angels for a variety of purposes including healing, protection, acquiring knowledge, and influencing persons and events. The text occupies the contested territory between legitimate Christian veneration of angels and condemned magical conjuration, claiming divine and angelic sanction for its procedures while providing operational instructions whose practical orientation connects it to the broader learned magic tradition.

The text draws on the rich medieval tradition of angelology that assigned specific names, powers, and spheres of responsibility to vast hierarchies of angels derived from Jewish, Christian, and ultimately Babylonian and Persian cosmological speculation. The association of specific angels with days, hours, planets, and zodiacal signs—elaborated in texts like the Sepher ha-Razim, the Heptameron, and countless liturgical and paraliturgical sources—provided practitioners with a systematic framework for identifying which angel to address for which purpose and when. The Liber de Angelis applied this angelological knowledge in explicitly operational directions, providing the names, seals, and ritual procedures for actual invocation.

Scholarly work on texts like the Liber de Angelis has been part of a broader effort to map the full range of medieval learned magical literature beyond its canonical exemplars. Researchers including Julien Véronèse, Claire Fanger, and Frank Klaassen have demonstrated that the medieval magical corpus encompasses a far greater variety of texts—in terms of content, purpose, and intended audience—than earlier scholarship recognized. The Liber de Angelis contributes to this picture by providing evidence for the persistence and practical application of angel magic traditions in contexts where practitioners sought benevolent spiritual assistance rather than the compulsion of demons.

texts.title: Liber visionum
texts.description: The Liber visionum is associated with John of Morigny's visionary and ritual reworking of Ars Notoria materials.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Liber visionum (Book of Visions), composed by the Benedictine monk John of Morigny between approximately 1301 and 1315, is the most remarkable response to the Ars Notoria tradition in the medieval period: an extended autobiographical visionary text in which John narrates his use of the Ars Notoria, his gradual disillusionment with it following Marian visions, and his composition of a new, purified form of angel magic under direct divine and angelic guidance. The Liber visionum survives in several manuscript versions representing different stages of John's ongoing revision of the text.

Narrative and Significance

John began using the Ars Notoria to acquire knowledge of the arts and sciences and experienced visions of the Virgin Mary and Christ in which the Notory Art was condemned as contaminated by demonic elements — the voces magicae and geometric notae of the Ars Notoria, John's visionary informants told him, worked through demonic rather than angelic mediation. Under continued visionary guidance, John composed a new system of Marian contemplation and prayer — the Liber florum celestis doctrine or Flowers of Heavenly Teaching — that he believed replaced the Ars Notoria with a purified form of angelic illumination.

The text is unique in the medieval magical tradition for its sustained autobiographical narrative of a practitioner's engagement with, critique of, and revision of a magical tradition in response to visionary experience. It demonstrates from within the tradition how practitioners understood and evaluated what they were doing, rather than from the external perspective of theological condemnation. Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson's critical edition and translation (Liber florum celestis doctrine / The Flowers of Heavenly Teaching, Penn State University Press, 2015) is the definitive scholarly treatment.

texts.title: Flowers of Heavenly Teaching
texts.description: The Flowers of Heavenly Teaching names John of Morigny's revised ritual and visionary project for divinely assisted knowledge.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Liber florum celestis doctrine (Book of the Flowers of Heavenly Teaching), the revised core of John of Morigny's angel magic system, is the operative text that John presented as the purified replacement for the Ars Notoria. Where the Ars Notoria used geometric notae accompanied by voces magicae and extended prayers to secure divine infusion of the liberal arts, John's system uses a series of elaborate figure-based prayers (flores, flowers) designed under visionary guidance by the Virgin Mary and Christ, addressed to the Marian figure and the Trinity rather than to ambiguous angelic intermediaries.

Structure and Content

The flores are prayers of extraordinary length and density, each associated with a visual figure (related to but distinct from the Ars Notoria's notae). The first flos — the "flower of the beginning" — establishes the practitioner's relationship with the Virgin and requests her intercession. Subsequent flowers address specific kinds of knowledge (theology, philosophy, the arts), virtues, and states of contemplative consciousness. The system is designed to take weeks or months of sustained practice, with each flower to be used at appropriate times in the liturgical day.

The Liber florum demonstrates how a medieval practitioner transformed the inherited categories of learned magic — figures, prayers, systematic cycles of practice — within a specifically devotional and visionary framework. John's insistence that his system worked through genuine divine grace rather than demonic mediation places it in the contested territory between approved contemplative practice and condemned magic, a territory that his visionary informants navigated for him but that the Inquisition would likely have assessed differently. Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson's Penn State edition (2015) is the essential scholarly resource.

texts.title: Munich Manual
texts.description: The Munich Manual is the fifteenth-century necromantic manuscript edited and analyzed by Richard Kieckhefer in Forbidden Rites.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Munich Manual of demonic magic (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 849) is a Latin miscellany copied in southern Germany around the 1440s and containing the most complete medieval Latin handbook of practical demonic magic to survive. The manuscript is significant precisely because it is unexceptional as an object: it is not a handsome presentation copy but a practical working document, bound with other material (medical and astrological texts), showing signs of use, and representing the kind of compiled magical resource that a learned practitioner — probably a clerk with university training — would assemble and use.

Contents

Clm 849 contains three main categories of material. The first is "illusionist" experiments: procedures for creating apparent wonders through sleight of hand, optical tricks, and psychological suggestion rather than demonic power. The second is practical experiments using spirit assistance: finding hidden treasure, compelling love or hate, discovering thieves, causing discord — operations that require the cooperation of named spirits but fall short of the full demonic conjuration of the third category. The third category is formal necromantic conjuration: complete rituals for summoning, binding, interrogating, and dismissing named demons, with all the ritual apparatus (magic circle, fumigations, prayers, conjuration formulas) specified in detail.

Richard Kieckhefer's Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century (Penn State University Press, 1997) provides the critical edition (Latin text with facing English translation) and the most thorough analysis. Kieckhefer's examination of the manuscript's social context — who would have possessed and used it, what the ritual apparatus implies about the practitioner's social position and resources — has been foundational for the concept of the "clerical underworld" in medieval magic scholarship.

texts.title: Book of Oberon
texts.description: The Book of Oberon is an early modern English ritual magic compilation that preserves and transforms medieval Solomonic and spirit-conjuring materials.
texts.analysis_html:
Book of Oberon: English Fairy Magic and Spirit Conjuration

The Book of Oberon is a substantial late sixteenth-century English magical compilation named for Oberon, the king of the fairies, whose invocation appears among its many spirit conjurations. The manuscript, held at the Folger Shakespeare Library, represents one of the most comprehensive surviving examples of Elizabethan practical magic, combining material from multiple traditions: Solomonic conjuration in the continental learned magic tradition, fairy lore drawn from English popular culture, astrological medicine, and experimental procedures drawn from various natural magical sources. Its juxtaposition of learned and popular elements makes it an invaluable witness to the actual practice environment of Elizabethan magical culture.

The inclusion of fairy conjuration alongside demonic conjuration and angelic invocation reflects the particular character of English magical culture, in which the category of fairy overlapped with but was distinct from the continental categories of demon and spirit. English fairies occupied an ambiguous ontological position: neither straightforwardly demonic nor clearly angelic, they were nonetheless powerful beings accessible to practitioners with appropriate knowledge and ritual technique. The appearance of Oberon—better known from literary contexts including Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream and the medieval romance Huon of Bordeaux—in a practical magical text illustrates the porous boundary between literary and operational magical traditions in the Elizabethan period.

The scholarly edition of the Book of Oberon by Daniel Harms, James Clark, and Joseph Peterson (2015) made this important manuscript accessible to researchers and practitioners alike. Their work situates the compilation within the broader context of Elizabethan magical culture as illuminated by studies like Frank Klaassen's examination of manuscript magic and the broader scholarship on occultism in Renaissance England. The Book of Oberon provides crucial evidence for the social and cultural context of magical practice—who compiled magical texts, what they hoped to achieve, and how they navigated the relationship between learned magic, popular belief, and official condemnation.

texts.title: Book of Soyga
texts.description: The Book of Soyga is an early modern angelological and cryptographic ritual text associated with John Dee and earlier learned magical traditions.
texts.analysis_html:
Book of Soyga: Alphabetic Tables and Angelic Secrets

The Book of Soyga (also known as Aldaraia sive Soyga vocor) is a sixteenth-century Latin magical manuscript whose contents center on a set of complex alphabetic tables—36 matrices each containing 36 rows of 36 letters—believed to encode divine and angelic secrets. The text was famously owned by John Dee, who in 1583 asked the angel Uriel through his scryer Edward Kelley to explain the tables' significance; Uriel reportedly said that only the angel Michael could explain them and that the original was given to Adam in Paradise. This anecdote, recorded in Dee's diaries, has made the Soyga particularly resonant in the history of early modern esotericism.

The manuscript's scholarly fortunes changed dramatically when Jim Reeds, a mathematician at Bell Labs, cracked the algorithm generating the Soyga's tables in 1994—demonstrating that they were produced by a systematic procedure involving a keyword, a specific alphabet, and a recursive generation rule. Reeds' analysis, published in a paper circulated within Dee scholarship, showed that the tables were not random or arbitrary but encoded according to a consistent method, though the specific magical significance of the content remains unclear. This computational analysis illustrated how modern mathematical tools can illuminate aspects of historical magical texts that traditional philological methods cannot address.

Deborah Harkness's research on John Dee brought renewed scholarly attention to the Soyga as part of her investigation of Dee's magical projects and his relationship to Elizabethan learned culture. The text exemplifies the category of magical manuscript that circulated among educated practitioners in the sixteenth century—learned enough to require Latin literacy and mathematical sophistication, yet concerned with operations (angelic communication, access to divine secrets) that placed it firmly outside the bounds of orthodox religious practice. Its association with Dee connects it to the broader project of Enochian magic and the Elizabethan search for pristine angelic knowledge.

texts.title: Heptameron
texts.description: The Heptameron is a ritual magic text attributed to Pietro d'Abano in print tradition and central to early modern angelic and planetary conjuration.
texts.analysis_html:
Heptameron seu Elementa Magica: Planetary Angels and Ritual Hours

The Heptameron seu Elementa Magica (Heptameron, or Elements of Magic), attributed to Peter of Abano (c. 1250–1316) though likely composed by a later author, is one of the most widely circulated practical magical texts of the Renaissance period. Organized around the seven days of the week and the angels governing each day's hours, the text provides detailed instructions for summoning angels through properly constructed circles, appropriate fumigations, and specific divine and angelic names. Its combination of celestial organization, ritual precision, and Solomonic authority made it a foundational reference for practical ceremonial magic in the fifteenth through seventeenth centuries.

The attribution to Peter of Abano—the prominent Italian physician and philosopher whose Conciliator and other works made him a leading figure in the Latin reception of Arabic natural philosophy—is almost certainly pseudepigraphical, exploiting his established reputation as a learned investigator of hidden natural powers. Peter's genuine work engaged seriously with astrological medicine and occult qualities, making him a plausible attributed author for a text claiming that planetary angels could be summoned through celestially synchronized ritual. Whether or not he wrote anything resembling the Heptameron, the attribution placed the text's practical magic within a framework of natural philosophical investigation rather than mere superstition.

The text's practical instructions are detailed and systematic: for each day and hour, it specifies the governing angel, the appropriate circle construction, the names to be used in invocation, and the fumigations suitable for the planetary hour. This systematic completeness—covering all days, all hours, all planets—gave the text a comprehensive character that made it useful as a practical reference. Its wide circulation in manuscript and early printed editions (often appended to editions of Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia or published with the spurious Fourth Book) made it one of the most accessible and influential practical magic texts of the Renaissance period, exercising formative influence on the later Solomonic tradition.

texts.title: Ars Almadel
texts.description: The Ars Almadel is a Solomonic angelic ritual text transmitted in early modern grimoire compilations and linked to older angelic invocation traditions.
texts.analysis_html:
Ars Almadel: Angelic Conjuration through the Wax Tablet

The Ars Almadel constitutes one of the five books typically assembled in the seventeenth-century compilation known as the Lemegeton or Lesser Key of Solomon, though it circulated independently in earlier manuscript traditions. Its distinguishing feature is its method of angelic invocation: the practitioner constructs a wax tablet (almadel) engraved with divine names and symbols, lights candles upon it, and invokes angels associated with specific chora or quarters of the heavens. Unlike the demonic conjuration of the Goetia, the Almadel presents itself as a form of angelic magic seeking benevolent assistance with healing, knowledge, and protection from a class of angelic beings divided into four celestial regions.

The text's origins are obscure, with manuscript versions appearing in the later medieval period. Its title derives from Arabic al-mandal, a term associated with a class of divinatory and magical mirror or surface practices, suggesting a transmission history involving Arabic magical literature. The specific angelic names and the fourfold division of celestial regions connect it to broader traditions of Jewish and Christian angel lore elaborated in texts like the Sepher ha-Razim and the Liber Razielis, which similarly assigned angels to cosmic zones and described procedures for invoking their assistance.

The Almadel's compilation into the Lemegeton placed it within a systematized presentation of Solomonic magic that became influential in seventeenth-century England and subsequently in the modern occult revival. The Lemegeton assembly—combining the demonic Goetia with the Theurgia Goetia, Pauline Art, Almadel, and Notory Art—created a comprehensive manual of spirit magic that purported to cover the full range of spiritual beings from demons to angels, all framed within Solomonic authority. This compilation strategy reflects the early modern consolidation of previously dispersed magical texts into integrated systems, a process paralleled in contemporary publications like the Heptameron and the various editions of the Key of Solomon.

texts.title: Ars Paulina
texts.description: The Ars Paulina is a Solomonic text of planetary and zodiacal angelic invocation preserved in early modern Lemegeton traditions.
texts.analysis_html:
Ars Paulina: Angelic Governors of Hours and Degrees

The Ars Paulina forms the third book of the Lemegeton compilation and represents a sophisticated integration of astrological and angelic lore. The text describes two classes of angels: those governing the twenty-four hours of the day (Book One), and those governing the 360 degrees of the zodiac (Book Two). Unlike the demonic conjuration of the Goetia, the Pauline Art claims to operate through angels who are benevolent ministers of the celestial order, accessible to practitioners who know their proper names and the astrological conditions under which they exert influence. The text attributes its transmission to the apostle Paul, citing Paul's account in 2 Corinthians of being "caught up to the third heaven"—an attribution that claimed apostolic authority for practices that the institutional Church would otherwise condemn.

The text's astrological framework connects it to the broader tradition of astrological magic elaborated in texts like the Picatrix and the writings of Thabit ibn Qurra. The assignment of angels to specific hours and zodiacal degrees reflects the medieval understanding of celestial influence as operating through hierarchically ordered spiritual beings who transmitted planetary or stellar virtue to the sublunary world. This conceptual framework allowed magical practitioners to present their operations as working in harmony with—rather than against—the divinely ordained cosmic order, since invoking the angel of a particular celestial configuration was ostensibly different from commanding demons.

The Pauline Art's place within the Lemegeton compilation illustrates the synthetic character of seventeenth-century learned magic: the assembler drew together texts of diverse origin—demonic conjuration, angelic invocation, talismanic magic, the Notory Art—and presented them as components of a unified Solomonic system. This synthetic presentation was itself a form of intellectual legitimation, suggesting that the various operations constituted parts of a coherent magical philosophy rather than a miscellaneous collection of techniques. The attribution to Paul, like the attribution to Solomon elsewhere in the compilation, served to anchor the entire system in ancient sacred authority.

texts.title: Ars Goetia
texts.description: The Ars Goetia is an early modern Solomonic demon catalogue and conjuring text whose roots and reception belong to the wider grimoire tradition.
texts.analysis_html:
Ars Goetia: The Seventy-Two Demons of Solomon

The Ars Goetia (or simply the Goetia) is the first and most famous book of the seventeenth-century compilation known as the Lemegeton or Lesser Key of Solomon. It presents a systematic catalogue of seventy-two demons whom Solomon allegedly bound under his seal and confined in a brass vessel, together with detailed descriptions of each spirit's appearance, rank, powers, and the method of compelling it to appear and perform service. The spirits are organized hierarchically into kings, dukes, princes, marquises, presidents, earls, and knights, with each rank commanding specified numbers of lesser spirits and possessing particular areas of competence ranging from knowledge of hidden things to the teaching of arts and sciences to the creation of illusions.

The catalogue's origins lie in earlier medieval demonological literature. Several of the spirit names and their attributed powers show connections to the Jewish Testament of Solomon, to Arabic magical compilations, and to the expanding demonological encyclopaedias assembled by late medieval learned magic practitioners. The specific list of seventy-two, however, appears to crystallize in the sixteenth century, with manuscript versions circulating before the compilation of the Lemegeton. Johann Weyer's Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1577), appended to his De praestigiis daemonum, provided an early printed list of these spirits that served as a source for subsequent compilations including the Goetia itself.

The Goetia became enormously influential in the modern Western magical tradition following Aleister Crowley and Samuel Liddell Mathers' edition of 1904, which combined the manuscript text with Crowley's extended commentary and additional material. This edition transformed a seventeenth-century manuscript compilation into a foundational text of twentieth-century ceremonial magic. Historical scholarship, including the work of Joseph Peterson and Daniel Harms, has subsequently worked to reconstruct the earlier manuscript traditions and disentangle the authentic seventeenth-century text from later accretions, establishing the Goetia's place within the broader history of Solomonic magic rather than treating it primarily through the lens of modern occultism.

texts.title: Lemegeton
texts.description: The Lemegeton or Lesser Key of Solomon is an early modern Solomonic compilation whose parts preserve angelic, demonic, and planetary ritual traditions.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Lemegeton (also called the Lesser Key of Solomon) is a compilation of five distinct magical texts, probably assembled in its current form in England in the seventeenth century, though each component text has earlier sources. The five parts are: the Ars Goetia (a catalogue of seventy-two demons with their seals and powers); the Ars Theurgia-Goetia (spirits of the cardinal and intermediate directions); the Ars Paulina (planetary angels of the hours); the Ars Almadel (angels of the four altitudes); and the Ars Notoria (a memory and wisdom system using prayer and divine names). The compilation circulated extensively in seventeenth-century English manuscript culture — surviving in dozens of copies — before its first modern printed edition by Mathers and Crowley in 1904.

The Ars Goetia

The most influential component is the Ars Goetia, which catalogues seventy-two demons in the tradition of the Testament of Solomon: each demon is given a name, rank (king, duke, marquis, count, etc.), seal, number of legions commanded, and special powers (knowledge of arts and sciences, revealing hidden things, building structures, inciting love or discord, etc.). The catalogue derives from earlier sources — particularly the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum appended to Johann Weyer's De praestigiis daemonum (1563) — and represents a systematic elaboration of the Solomonic spirit catalogue tradition. Joseph Peterson's 2001 edition of the complete Lemegeton is the standard scholarly resource, documenting the manuscript sources and their relationships.

The Ars Notoria

The Ars Notoria (Notory Art) is the oldest component and the most distinct in character: rather than conjuring demons, it seeks knowledge and wisdom through a system of prayer, meditation, and contemplation of divine words and figures (notae). The text claims that by meditating on the notae and reciting the associated prayers over a period of weeks, the practitioner will acquire the seven liberal arts and other forms of knowledge infused by divine grace. This tradition, which emphasizes the practitioner's religious purity and the angelic mediation of knowledge, is analyzed in detail by Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson in their editions of John of Morigny's Liber visionum (a related text) and by Julien Véronèse in his critical edition of the Notory Art.

texts.title: Grimorium Verum
texts.description: Grimorium Verum is an early modern printed grimoire important for the post-medieval reception and reorganization of spirit conjuration traditions.
texts.analysis_html:
Grimorium Verum: The True Grimoire and Its Hierarchy of Spirits

The Grimorium Verum (True Grimoire) is an eighteenth-century magical text, first published purportedly in Memphis in 1817 (though earlier manuscript versions likely exist) and attributed to "Alibek the Egyptian." Despite its relatively late appearance in print, the text draws on earlier magical traditions—particularly the Solomonic and demonic conjuration literature of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—and has attracted significant scholarly and practitioner interest because of its frank presentation of demonic magic without the apologetic framing found in texts like the Arbatel. The Grimorium Verum presents itself as providing access to real demonic powers for practical ends, without much attempt to disguise this character under philosophical or theological legitimation.

The text's spirit hierarchy is distinctive: rather than the seventy-two demons of the Goetia or the planetary angels of more celestially-oriented texts, the Grimorium Verum organizes its spirits under three principal demons (Lucifer, Beelzebuth, and Astaroth) with subordinate spirits possessing specific practical competences. This organizational scheme reflects the demonological systematizing characteristic of grimoire literature while presenting it in a more baldly operational register than texts claiming philosophical foundations. The practical focus—obtaining specific results through specific demons—aligns the text with the tradition of "experimental" or "practical" magic that bypassed theoretical justification in favor of tested procedures.

Jake Stratton-Kent's modern scholarly edition and study of the Grimorium Verum (2009) has brought this text to new scholarly attention, situating it within the broader tradition of grimoire literature and arguing for its connections to earlier, possibly ancient, magical traditions. While Stratton-Kent's arguments have been received with varying degrees of scholarly acceptance, his work exemplifies the contemporary intersection of academic historical research and living magical practice that characterizes much current scholarship on grimoire texts, where critical engagement with historical evidence coexists with interest in the texts as functional magical resources.

texts.title: Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses
texts.description: The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses are early modern/modern grimoire traditions relevant to the long reception of biblical magical authority.
texts.analysis_html:
Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses: Kabbalistic Magic and Popular Tradition

The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses is an eighteenth-century German magical compilation that presents itself as the continuation of the Pentateuch—the five books attributed to Moses—providing the secret magical knowledge that Moses supposedly possessed but withheld from public scripture. First printed in German in the 1780s and repeatedly reprinted thereafter, the text synthesizes learned Kabbalistic material, divine names, seals, and practical magic instructions within a frame that claims Mosaic authority for its contents. This attribution strategy represents a late example of the pseudepigraphical tradition that had long legitimated magical texts by attaching them to biblical figures.

The text achieved remarkable cultural reach, spreading far beyond its German origins through immigration and diaspora networks. German immigrants to Pennsylvania brought it to North America in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, where it became foundational for the Pennsylvania German Pow-Wow tradition of folk magic. More dramatically, it was carried to West Africa and the Caribbean through the slave trade and colonial networks, where it was integrated into syncretic religious and magical traditions including Hoodoo, Obeah, and various Afro-Caribbean spiritual practices. This global trajectory—from German printing house to African American conjure tradition—illustrates the extraordinary mobility of printed magical texts and the creative adaptations they underwent as they crossed cultural boundaries.

Scholarly study of the Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses has been enriched by ethnographic and folklore research on its reception communities alongside historical research on its textual origins. Sabina Magliocco and other folklorists have documented its persistence in living traditions, while historians of print culture have traced its publication history and textual evolution.
