Davies's central argument is that the grimoire is not a timeless repository of esoteric knowledge but a historically conditioned object that changes with its means of production, its social context, and its intended audience. The ancient and medieval manuscript grimoire (expensive, restricted, circulating among literate elites) differs fundamentally from the eighteenth-century French chapbook grimoire (Grand Albert, Petit Albert, Dragon Rouge), which was designed for a literate popular market. The nineteenth-century occult revival editions of Mathers and Waite imposed scholarly apparatus and ritual significance on texts that had long circulated as practical handbooks. The twentieth-century paperback grimoire (Llewellyn, Weiser) addresses a self-identified magical community with different needs and assumptions.

The book's chapters proceed chronologically and by geography: ancient Mesopotamian and Egyptian magical books; Jewish and Christian late antique texts; medieval European manuscripts; the Arabic and Mediterranean traditions; the early modern print era; the French chapbook tradition; American popular magic (hoodoo, Pennsylvania Dutch hex); the Victorian occult revival; and twentieth-century print and digital magic. Each chapter combines primary-source analysis with attention to the social history of production, circulation, and use.

Significance

Davies's book is particularly important for two contributions. First, it documents the role of popular print culture — the chapbook, the pamphlet, the cheap pamphlet grimoire — in transmitting magical tradition to social strata far below the learned clerical elite that had been the focus of most previous grimoire scholarship. Second, it demonstrates the global reach of the grimoire tradition, including its transmission to colonial and post-colonial contexts in Africa, the Caribbean, and North America, where texts like the Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses entered African-American hoodoo practice.

texts.title: The Book of Oberon
texts.description: Critical transcription and annotated translation of Folger Shakespeare Library MS Vb.26, a late sixteenth-century English manuscript of approximately 450 pages. Edited by Daniel Harms, James R. Clark, and Joseph H. Peterson, published by Llewellyn in 2015. The manuscript combines Solomonic spirit lists drawn from Agrippa and related sources with vernacular fairy magic, conjuring for treasure and love, and practical operations in both Latin and English. The edition exemplifies how the Elizabethan period combined learned Continental magic traditions with native English vernacular practices. Klaassen's Making Magic in Elizabethan England examined related manuscripts from the same period.
texts.analysis_html:
The Book of Oberon: A Sourcebook of Elizabethan Magic (2015 Edition)

The modern scholarly edition of the Book of Oberon, published by Llewellyn in 2015 and edited by Daniel Harms, James R. Clark, and Joseph H. Peterson, represents a major contribution to the history of Elizabethan magical culture. The editors transcribed and annotated the previously unstudied Folger Shakespeare Library manuscript (MS V.b.26), a late sixteenth-century English magical compilation of roughly 300 pages covering spirit conjuration, astrological medicine, fairy lore, and experimental magic. Their editorial work made accessible a primary source that substantially enriches understanding of how learned magic actually operated in the hands of practitioners rather than in the abstract discussions of theologians and demonologists.

The edition's scholarly apparatus—introductions, footnotes, glossaries, and comparative references to parallel texts—situates the manuscript within the context of late sixteenth-century English magical culture. The editors trace the manuscript's sources, identifying material derived from continental learned magic traditions (Solomonic conjuration, astrological medicine) alongside characteristically English elements (fairy conjuration, charms in the vernacular tradition). This comparative work illuminates the processes of textual transmission and cultural adaptation through which a broadly European learned magical tradition was transformed into something distinctively Elizabethan.

The publication history of the edition itself reflects the contemporary landscape of magical text scholarship, where academic presses and popular occult publishers both compete for and sometimes collaborate on the audience for historical magical texts. The Llewellyn edition, while produced to high scholarly standards, was published by a firm primarily serving practitioners of contemporary paganism and magic rather than academic historians. This positioning illustrates the complex relationship between historical scholarship on magic and contemporary magical practice—a relationship in which historical research serves simultaneously as academic contribution and as resource for living traditions that claim historical roots.

texts.title: Making Magic in Elizabethan England
texts.title_original: Making Magic in Elizabethan England: Two Early Modern Vernacular Books of Magic
texts.description: Edited volume published by Frank Klaassen at Penn State University Press (2019), providing critical editions and analysis of two Elizabethan vernacular magic manuscripts. The volume demonstrates how early modern English practitioners engaged with Continental learned magic traditions including Agrippa, Dee, and earlier Solomonic texts while producing vernacular adaptations that combined learned and popular elements. Klaassen situates these manuscripts within his broader argument about the continuity of medieval ritual magic into the early modern period, showing that sixteenth-century English practitioners drew on the same core of medieval spirit-conjuring texts as their fifteenth-century predecessors, supplemented by printed Renaissance sources.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Frank Klaassen and Sharon Hubbs Wright's The Magic of Roger Bacon: Practical Magic in Medieval and Early Modern England (Penn State University Press, forthcoming) and, more broadly, the body of scholarship focused on practical magic in the Elizabethan and early Stuart periods, examines the continuity between medieval learned magic and its early modern English manifestations. The primary source record for Elizabethan practical magic includes the Folger Book of Oberon (edited by Harms, Clark, and Peterson, 2015), the British Library's Sloane manuscripts, and the Ashmole collection at the Bodleian.

The Elizabethan Magical Milieu

Elizabethan England provides unusually rich documentation of practical magic at multiple social levels. At the learned end: John Dee's angel conversations (1582–1589), documented in meticulous diaries. At the middling level: the Sloane and Ashmole magical manuscripts, collections of astrological, Solomonic, and natural magical material assembled by practitioners like Simon Forman and Richard Napier. At the popular level: the cunning folk documented in quarter sessions records and pamphlet literature, offering services that included healing, divination, and counter-magic. Keith Thomas's Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) provided the foundational social-historical account of Elizabethan magical practice; Frank Klaassen's subsequent manuscript-based scholarship has refined and corrected Thomas's picture by showing the continuity between medieval and Elizabethan learned magic that Thomas's "decline of magic" framework obscured.

texts.title: The Magic of Rogues
texts.description: Published by Frank Klaassen and Sharon Hubbs Wright at Penn State University Press (2021) in the Magic in History Sourcebooks series. Examines legal documents and magic texts from two early Tudor cases where English authorities confronted practicing magicians, exploring how practitioners thought about the world, where they obtained their ideas, and how their magic was supposed to work. The volume provides critical editions of the relevant manuscripts and legal records alongside analysis of the practices involved. Demonstrates the vitality of the medieval necromantic tradition in early sixteenth-century England and the social networks through which magical manuscripts circulated among clerics, practitioners, and curious laypeople.
texts.analysis_html:
Magic of Rogues: The Underworld of Late Medieval Magic

The study of what might be called "rogue magic"—magical practices operating outside the learned clerical tradition, in the spaces of urban popular culture, traveling entertainers, confidence men, and social margins—reveals dimensions of medieval and early modern magical culture that the learned tradition's self-representation often conceals. Richard Kieckhefer's analysis in Magic in the Middle Ages and related work, along with studies by Michael Bailey and others, has attended to the intersection of learned and popular magic in social contexts where the boundaries between legitimate and condemned practice were negotiated in everyday life rather than in academic treatises.

The figure of the professional magician—the itinerant practitioner who offered magical services for payment, sometimes drawing on genuine learned texts and sometimes fabricating claims to knowledge—occupies an important but elusive place in the history of magic. Such figures appear in court records, in satirical literature, and in moralizing condemnations, but rarely left self-descriptions that would allow reconstruction of their actual practices. The overlap between their operations and those of more respectable practitioners (court astrologers, university-trained physicians, learned clerics who wrote magical texts) was considerable, suggesting that the social boundary between legitimate and illegitimate magic was less about the content of practices than about the social position and institutional affiliation of practitioners.

The study of rogue magic intersects with broader social histories of poverty, migration, gender, and religious marginality in medieval and early modern Europe. Women healers, cunning folk, itinerant charm-sellers, and others who operated outside institutional structures of learning and ecclesiastical authority practiced forms of magic that drew on the same cosmological assumptions as learned magic while operating through different social channels. Understanding this dimension of magical culture requires sources—court records, ecclesiastical visitiation documents, folk narrative collections—that complement the learned texts typically studied by historians of magic, producing a more complete picture of magic as a social and cultural phenomenon.

texts.title: The Magus
texts.description: Compiled by Francis Barrett and published in London in 1801. A substantial compilation drawing heavily on Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia, Robert Turner's seventeenth-century English translations of magical texts, and related Renaissance and medieval sources. The Magus marks the transition from manuscript and early print circulation of learned magic to Romantic-era popular occultism. Barrett organized his compilation in three parts: natural magic, magnetism and alchemy, and ritual and talismanic magic. The Magus served as a conduit bringing Agrippa's framework and associated Renaissance material to nineteenth-century English-language audiences and influenced later figures including Edward Bulwer-Lytton and Eliphas Lévi.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Francis Barrett's The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer; Being a Complete System of Occult Philosophy (London: Lackington Allen and Co., 1801) is the most ambitious English-language compendium of occult philosophy produced in the early nineteenth century and a crucial text in the transmission of Renaissance learned magic from its early modern manuscript and print forms into the Victorian occult revival. Barrett compiled and republished large portions of the 1651 English translation of Agrippa's De occulta philosophia, alongside material from Peter d'Abano's Heptameron, mediaeval lapidary traditions, and other sources, presenting them as a comprehensive and still-applicable system of magical knowledge.

Contents and Sources

The three-book structure follows Agrippa's: Book I covers natural magic (occult properties of things, the four elements, alchemical principles); Book II covers magnetism, the Kabbalah, and the construction of talismans and magical seals; Book III covers celestial intelligences and demonology, with a catalogue of demons and their seals derived from the Goetic tradition. The striking copperplate engravings — particularly the demon portraits, each shown in a distinctive form — were influential on subsequent visual representations of demonic beings in the occult tradition.

Barrett also advertised himself as a teacher of the occult sciences and sought to attract private students, suggesting that the book was meant to serve both as an encyclopedic reference and as a prospectus for his teaching. His audience was the educated but non-specialist English reader interested in occult subjects — a market that expanded substantially through the nineteenth century. Owen Davies's Grimoires (2009) situates The Magus in the longer history of magical publication; the book's place as a bridge between early modern learned magic and the Victorian occult revival (the Golden Dawn, Aleister Crowley) makes it an important transitional text.

texts.title: Sepher ha-Razim
texts.description: The Book of Mysteries (Sepher ha-Razim) is a Hebrew magical handbook whose compilation is usually dated to the 7th–10th century CE, though it draws on much older traditions of angel magic. Attributed to Noah and transmitted through Shem, the text organizes the seven heavens and their angelic inhabitants, providing adjurations, incantations, and ritual procedures keyed to each heavenly realm. Its framework of named angels ordered by celestial sphere connects to both the Solomonic grimoire tradition and broader Jewish mystical cosmology. The standard critical edition is Mordecai Margalioth's 1966 Hebrew text; Morgan's English translation appeared in 1983.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Sepher ha-Razim (Book of Mysteries) is a Hebrew magical handbook whose compilation is usually dated to the Geonic period (sixth to tenth centuries CE), though it draws on material that is almost certainly earlier — some scholars detect traditions going back to the Second Temple period. It is attributed to Noah, who received it from the angel Raziel, transmitted it through Shem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and ultimately Solomon, who used it in the construction of the Temple. This chain of transmission connects the text to the Solomonic authority framework while locating its ultimate origin in antediluvian divine revelation.

Structure and Contents

The text is organized around the seven heavens, each presided over by a named angelic prince and populated by named angelic servants whose functions and the periods of their activity are specified. For each heavenly realm, the text provides: the names of the ruling angel and his subordinates, the days and hours of their activity, adjurations invoking them, and specific practical procedures (prescriptions for achieving various ends through the proper invocation of the appropriate heaven's angels). Operations range from healing and protection through love magic, invisibility, and the harming of enemies.

The standard critical edition is Mordecai Margalioth's 1966 Hebrew text. Michael Morgan's English translation (Scholars Press, 1983) made the text accessible to non-Hebrew readers and remains the standard English version. The text is a key document for the history of Jewish magical practice and provides essential context for understanding the relationship between Jewish angel magic and the Latin and Greek Solomonic tradition.

Significance

The Sepher ha-Razim is significant for several reasons. Its hierarchical organization of named angels by heavenly sphere anticipates the spirit catalogues of the medieval Solomonic grimoires. Its adjuration formulas — commands addressed to named spirits invoking God's authority — provide the direct precedent for the Latin conjuration literature. Its attribution to Noah and Raziel rather than Solomon marks a distinct tradition of antediluvian revealed magic that parallels the Solomonic tradition without being identical to it. Gideon Bohak's Ancient Jewish Magic (2008) situates it within the wider context of Jewish magical practice.

texts.title: Solomon the Esoteric King
texts.description: Pablo Torijano's Solomon the Esoteric King: From King to Magus, Development of a Tradition (Brill, 2002) traces the transformation of the biblical Solomon into a master of demons, occult knowledge, and magical authority across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic sources from the Second Temple period through the medieval era. Torijano analyzes the Testament of Solomon, Solomonic adjurations, and the pseudepigraphic authority of the Solomonic corpus as a cross-cultural phenomenon. Reviewed by Frank Klaassen and others as foundational for understanding Solomonic attribution as a legitimating strategy.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Pablo Torijano's Solomon the Esoteric King: From King to Magus, Development of a Tradition (Brill, 2002) is the foundational scholarly study of how the biblical King Solomon was transformed across late antique and medieval sources into the supreme master of demons, angelic revelation, and occult knowledge, and of how this transformation operated across three religious traditions — Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — simultaneously. The book is the essential starting point for any serious engagement with the Solomonic magical tradition.

Argument and Evidence

Torijano's argument is that Solomonic esoteric authority was not a fixed body of tradition but a dynamic attribution strategy: the name "Solomon" carried an authority — royal, prophetic, divinely-gifted — that different communities in different periods attached to different textual traditions for legitimating purposes. The strategy was available across religious boundaries because all three traditions shared the biblical narrative of Solomon's divinely-granted wisdom, while differing in how they elaborated and applied it.

The book proceeds through four main areas of evidence. First, the Second Temple Jewish pseudepigraphic literature (Wisdom of Solomon, Psalms of Solomon, and related texts) that first established Solomon as a figure of cosmic wisdom and spiritual authority. Second, the Testament of Solomon and related texts (the Solomonic adjurations, the Hygromanteia) that developed the demonological dimension: Solomon as master of individual named demons. Third, the Islamic tradition of Sulayman as a prophet-king given power over jinn by divine command, and the Islamic magical texts that drew on Qurʾanic Solomonic traditions. Fourth, the Latin and Hebrew grimoire tradition (the Clavicula Salomonis, the Mafteah Shelomoh, the Lemegeton) as the medieval crystallization of Solomonic magical authority.

texts.title: Ancient Jewish Magic: A History
texts.description: Gideon Bohak's Ancient Jewish Magic: A History (Cambridge University Press, 2008) surveys Jewish magical practice from the biblical period through the end of antiquity, drawing on amulets, magical papyri, incantation bowls, genizah fragments, and rabbinic literature. The book argues that Jewish magic was a coherent and distinctive tradition with identifiable practices, texts, and practitioners, and that it contributed substantially to the broader Mediterranean magical culture from which Christian and Islamic magical traditions emerged. Essential for the pre-history of the Solomonic grimoire corpus.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

Gideon Bohak's Ancient Jewish Magic: A History (Cambridge University Press, 2008) is the most comprehensive and analytically rigorous account of Jewish magical practice from the biblical period through the end of late antiquity, and the essential foundation for understanding the Jewish roots of the Solomonic grimoire tradition. Bohak draws on an extraordinary range of material and textual evidence: biblical and deuterocanonical literature, Dead Sea Scrolls, Greek magical papyri, Aramaic incantation bowls, lead curse tablets, Genizah fragments, and rabbinic literature.

Argument and Evidence

Against the tendency to treat "ancient Jewish magic" as simply one local variant of a homogeneous Mediterranean magical culture, Bohak argues that Jewish magical practice was a distinctive tradition with identifiable features, practices, and practitioners — even as it both borrowed from and contributed to the broader magical cultures of Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Hellenistic world. The distinctively Jewish features include: the use of specific divine names (YHWH rendered in Greek as IAO, SABAOTH, ADONAI) as compelling forces in adjuration; the invocation of biblical patriarchs and figures (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Solomon) as authorizing precedents; the use of Hebrew and Aramaic in formulas where other languages would serve equally well magically; and the integration of magical practice with a specifically Jewish cosmology of angels, demons, and divine names.

The book proceeds chronologically: biblical period attestations (the urim and thummim, the bronze serpent, prophylactic and curative procedures); Second Temple literary sources (Dead Sea Scrolls, Enochic literature, early Solomonic traditions); the Greek magical papyri and their Jewish elements; Aramaic incantation bowls from Babylonian Jewish communities; and Genizah magical texts. The final chapters discuss the relationship between Jewish magic and rabbinic authority, arguing that the rabbis both condemned and participated in magical practice.

Significance

For the history of the Solomonic tradition specifically, Bohak provides the indispensable pre-history: the early Jewish foundations of Solomonic magical authority, the angelic adjuration traditions that the Sepher ha-Razim and Testament of Solomon develop, and the role of Hebrew divine names in creating the distinctive character of Solomonic conjuration. Together with Pablo Torijano's Solomon the Esoteric King (2002), Bohak's work establishes the Jewish scholarly foundation for the entire Solomonic corpus.

texts.title: Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 1
texts.description: James H. Charlesworth's Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 1 (Doubleday, 1983) contains Dennis Duling's annotated English translation of the Testament of Solomon, with introduction covering date, provenance, original language (Greek), manuscript tradition, and theological significance. The volume remains the standard reference collection for pseudepigraphic literature adjacent to the Hebrew Bible and New Testament, placing Solomonic demonology within the context of Jewish apocalyptic and early Christian writing.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

James H. Charlesworth's The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, Volume 1: Apocalyptic Literature and Testaments (Doubleday, 1983) is the standard English reference collection for Jewish and Jewish-Christian pseudepigraphic literature adjacent to the Hebrew Bible and New Testament. Volume 1 contains Dennis Duling's annotated translation of the Testament of Solomon (pp. 935–987) — the standard English text of this foundational Solomonic document — alongside other apocalyptic and testamentary literature including 1 Enoch (translated by E. Isaac), 2 Enoch, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, and the Apocalypse of Abraham.

Significance for Solomonic Studies

The inclusion of the Testament of Solomon in a scholarly reference collection designed for mainstream biblical scholarship was significant for the history of magic: it placed Solomonic demonology within the context of Jewish apocalyptic and early Christian writing rather than treating it as an isolated curiosity of the magical tradition. Duling's introduction addresses the text's date, provenance, original language (Greek), and manuscript tradition with full scholarly apparatus, situating it within New Testament scholarship's engagement with the pseudepigraphic literature that surrounded the canonical texts.

The volume's theological context — the OTP was explicitly designed to serve biblical scholarship and seminary education — meant that Duling's translation reached audiences that would not typically have encountered the Testament of Solomon in the history-of-magic literature. This cross-disciplinary availability helped establish the text as a recognized reference point in New Testament studies as well as in the history of magic, and facilitated the subsequent scholarly conversation between Solomonic magic specialists (Torijano, Bohak) and biblical scholars working on pseudepigraphy and late antique Jewish-Christian relations.

texts.title: Mafteah Shelomoh
texts.description: The Mafteah Shelomoh (Key of Solomon in Hebrew) survives in several medieval and early modern manuscripts, of which the most significant for scholarship is British Museum MS Oriental 14759, edited by Herman Gollancz in 1914. The Hebrew recension of the Clavicula Salomonis tradition shows independence from the Latin manuscript families while sharing ritual categories including conjurations, pentacles, and spirit hierarchies attributed to Solomon. Its relationship to the Latin Clavicula Salomonis remains debated: whether the Hebrew text preceded or derived from Latin versions is a key question in Solomonic textual scholarship.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Mafteah Shelomoh (Hebrew: Key of Solomon) is a Hebrew recension of the Solomonic grimoire tradition, of which the most important surviving manuscript is British Museum MS Oriental 14759 (now British Library MS Or. 14759), edited by Herman Gollancz in 1914. Additional Hebrew manuscripts of the Key of Solomon tradition exist in the British Library, the Jewish Theological Seminary, and other collections. The Hebrew text provides independent evidence for the Solomonic spirit-binding and pentacle tradition, demonstrating that Hebrew-language versions of the Key of Solomon circulated alongside the Latin Clavicula Salomonis tradition and maintained distinctive features not found in the Latin manuscripts.

Relationship to the Latin Clavicula

The precise relationship between the Hebrew Mafteah Shelomoh and the Latin Clavicula Salomonis tradition is one of the unresolved questions of Solomonic textual scholarship. Several possibilities have been proposed: the Hebrew text preceded the Latin and the Latin tradition represents a Christian adaptation; the Hebrew text derived from Latin or Greek sources; or both derive independently from a common earlier (possibly Greek or Aramaic) tradition. The manuscripts share ritual categories — conjurations, pentacles, spirit hierarchies, ritual preparation requirements — but differ in specific content, formulary, and organizational structure in ways that suggest neither is simply a translation of the other.

Gollancz's 1914 edition, based on the Or. 14759 manuscript, was the first critical edition of any Hebrew recension and established the scholarly framework for discussing the Hebrew tradition. Joseph Peterson's online edition and commentary have extended this work using additional manuscripts. Gideon Bohak's analysis of the relationship between the Hebrew Solomonic tradition and the broader Jewish magical corpus provides essential context. Pablo Torijano's comparative approach in Solomon the Esoteric King (2002) situates the Hebrew Key of Solomon within the long development of Solomonic magical authority across religious traditions.

texts.title: Summa theologiae
texts.description: Thomas Aquinas's Summa theologiae (c. 1265–1274), composed at Paris, Naples, and Rome, contains the most systematic scholastic treatment of divination, astrology, demonic magic, and the limits of natural philosophy in medieval Latin thought. Questions in the Secunda secundae (ST II-II, qq. 92–96) address superstition, divination, and the pact with demons; earlier sections treat angels and demons as rational creatures with limited but real causal powers. Aquinas's framework dominated university theology through the fifteenth century and informed every major scholastic classification of magic.
texts.analysis_html:
Overview

The Summa theologiae of Thomas Aquinas, composed between approximately 1265 and 1274 at Paris, Naples, and Rome (left incomplete at his death in 1274), is the most systematic and authoritative synthesis of medieval scholastic theology and the work that dominated Catholic theological education from the fourteenth century through the Second Vatican Council. For the history of magic, two sections are of primary importance: the treatment of angels and demons in the Prima Pars (qq. 50–64, 106–114) and the discussion of superstition, divination, and forbidden arts in the Secunda secundae (qq. 92–96).

Angels, Demons, and Causal Powers

In the Prima Pars, Aquinas treats angels as pure intellectual substances, created good by God, some of whom fell through pride — the demons. As intellectual substances, both angels and demons have real causal powers: they can move bodies, affect the imagination and senses, influence the passions, and produce what appear to be marvellous effects through their superior knowledge of natural causes and their capacity to move matter more rapidly than human agents. However, they cannot override free will (because the will is moved only by the intellect and by God), and they cannot perform genuine miracles (which are reserved to God alone). The demonic wonders described in scripture are either real natural effects produced through superior knowledge, or illusions (praestigia) affecting only the senses or imagination.

This framework — demons as real agents with limited natural powers — was not merely theological but had direct practical implications for how inquisitors, theologians, and natural philosophers assessed magical claims. A phenomenon could be miraculous (divine), natural (explicable through natural causes), or diabolical (a real effect produced through demonic cooperation or a demonic illusion). Aquinas's framework licensed the investigation of natural causes without immediately condemning them as demonic, while insisting that any operation requiring demonic cooperation was illicit.

Superstition and the Forbidden Arts

The Secunda secundae, qq. 92–96 define superstition (Latin superstitio) as a species of irreligion: the attribution to creatures of what belongs to God alone, or the worship of God in an improper manner. Divination (divinatio) is the attempt to know hidden or future things by means of creatures — stars, spirits, lots, dreams — rather than through divine revelation or legitimate causal reasoning. Aquinas condemns all forms of divination as implicitly or explicitly involving demonic pact, even when the practitioner does not consciously intend this: the desire to obtain occult knowledge from spiritual agents that are not God constitutes a tacit invitation to demonic assistance.

Observations (observationes) — magical rituals using material objects, words, or procedures — are similarly condemned when they operate through demonic agency rather than natural causes. However, Aquinas acknowledges that some material things have natural occult powers (occult qualities) that can produce unusual effects without supernatural intervention; his De occultis operibus naturae (a brief treatise addressed to a soldier) develops this naturalistic alternative more fully.

persons.name: Richard Kieckhefer
persons.description: Learned magic, necromancy, and the social history of medieval ritual texts.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Richard Kieckhefer is a historian of medieval religion and magic at Northwestern University, where he taught for over three decades before retirement. His scholarship has been central to establishing the history of medieval magic as a legitimate and rigorous subdiscipline of medieval studies, combining careful archival work with broad synthetic analysis. He received his doctoral training at the University of Texas at Austin and has published across the history of medieval religion, spirituality, and the relationship between official theology and popular practice.

Major Works

Magic in the Middle Ages (Cambridge University Press, 1989; revised edition 2000) is Kieckhefer's most widely read work and the standard introduction to the field. The book surveys the full range of medieval magical practice — from village charms and protective amulets through learned necromancy — and introduces the crucial analytical distinction between "common tradition" (widely shared magical practices embedded in everyday life) and "specific tradition" (the specialized learned magic of the educated clergy and university-trained). Kieckhefer's concept of the "clerical underworld" — the social milieu of clergy and university students who circulated practical magic manuscripts alongside more respectable texts — has been widely adopted and debated.

Forbidden Rites: A Necromancer's Manual of the Fifteenth Century (Penn State University Press, 1997) offers an edition, translation, and analysis of the Munich Manual (Clm 849), a Latin necromantic handbook from the 1440s. The edition is a model of how to approach a practical magic manuscript: Kieckhefer situates the text in its manuscript context, analyses its ritual structure and theoretical assumptions, and uses it to illuminate the social world of learned clerical magic. The book is essential reading for anyone working on the Latin grimoire tradition.

His edited volume Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic (Penn State, 1994), co-edited with Claire Fanger, assembled key essays on medieval ritual magic and helped define the field's scope and methods. Theology in Stone: Church Architecture from Byzantium to Berkeley (2004) represents his parallel work on medieval religious culture. His work on medieval devotion and mysticism (Unquiet Souls: Fourteenth-Century Saints and their Religious Milieu, 1984; Mystics and Miracles, 2015) provides the broader religious-historical context within which the history of magic is properly situated.

persons.name: Claire Fanger
persons.description: Medieval ritual magic, angelic theurgy, and visionary autobiographical writing.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Claire Fanger is a scholar of medieval religion and ritual magic at Rice University whose editorial and interpretive work has been central to establishing the study of medieval ritual magic as a rigorous historical subdiscipline. Her work focuses on the intersection of magic, mysticism, and religious experience in the later Middle Ages, with particular attention to texts that blur the boundaries between legitimate contemplative practice and condemned magical operation.

Editorial Work

Fanger edited the landmark volume Conjuring Spirits: Texts and Traditions of Medieval Ritual Magic (Penn State University Press, 1998), which brought together essays on the Ars Notoria, the Munich Manual, the Liber visionum of John of Morigny, and other key texts, establishing the field's scope and methods. A follow-up volume, Invoking Angels: Theurgic Ideas and Practices, Thirteenth to Sixteenth Centuries (Penn State, 2012), extended the analysis to the relationship between angel magic and mysticism across three centuries.

Her edition (with Nicholas Watson) of John of Morigny's Liber florum celestis doctrine (The Flowers of Heavenly Teaching, Penn State, 2015) is the critical scholarly edition of this extraordinary visionary text, providing Latin text, English translation, and extensive introduction. The edition demonstrates the kind of careful textual and contextual analysis that distinguishes modern grimoire scholarship from earlier occultist editions.

Interpretive Contributions

Fanger's interpretive work addresses the relationship between magical and mystical traditions in medieval Christianity, arguing against sharp categorical distinctions between "magic" (condemned) and "mysticism" (approved). Her analysis of John of Morigny shows how a practitioner could engage with the Ars Notoria tradition, receive visionary critique of it, and produce a revised system that was itself neither purely magical nor purely contemplative. This blurring of categories is characteristic of the learned magical milieu and important for understanding how magical practice was experienced by its practitioners.

persons.name: Frank Klaassen
persons.description: Manuscript culture and transformations of learned magic in late medieval and early modern England.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Frank Klaassen is a historian of medieval magic and learned culture at the University of Saskatchewan. His research focuses on the practical ritual magic texts of medieval England — the manuscripts that circulated among literate clergy and university-trained practitioners — and on what their content and manuscript contexts reveal about the culture of learned magic in the later Middle Ages. He studied at the University of Toronto and completed his doctorate there.

The Transformations of Magic

The Transformations of Magic: Illicit Learned Magic in the Later Middle Ages (Penn State University Press, 2013) is Klaassen's major monograph and the most rigorous systematic study of the English learned magic manuscript tradition. The book surveys approximately 270 manuscripts containing ritual magic material, providing a quantitative foundation for generalizations about what types of magic circulated, in what social contexts, and how the tradition changed between c.1300 and c.1500. Klaassen identifies two transformations: a shift in some parts of the tradition toward more explicit demonic conjuration, and a counter-trend of naturalization in which ritual operations were increasingly framed within the idiom of scholastic natural philosophy and celestial influence theory.

The book's methodological contribution — the systematic manuscript survey rather than focus on a few canonical texts — was influential in subsequent grimoire scholarship, demonstrating that the selection bias of printed editions had significantly distorted earlier accounts of what medieval learned magic actually looked like.

Other Work

Klaassen has edited and introduced key primary texts in the medieval magic corpus. His edition (with Christopher Phillips) of the Ars Notoria tradition and his contributions to Claire Fanger's Invoking Angels (Penn State, 2012) expand the manuscript base for understanding angelic magic in the medieval period. He has also published on the relationship between learned magic and early modern print culture, on the transition from manuscript to print in the magical tradition, and on the Solomonic attribution as a legitimating strategy.

persons.name: Sophie Page
persons.description: Monastic, clerical, and manuscript contexts for medieval occult learning.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Sophie Page is a historian of medieval intellectual and religious culture at University College London, specializing in magical manuscripts, their institutional contexts, and their relationship to natural philosophy and theology in medieval England. Her work addresses questions about how magical texts were collected, stored, used, and theorized within institutional (especially monastic) settings, challenging the assumption that magical manuscripts were only or primarily the product of disreputable clerical subculture.

Magic in the Cloister

Magic in the Cloister: Pious Motives, Illicit Interests, and Occult Approaches to the Medieval Universe (Penn State University Press, 2013) is Page's major work. The book examines the manuscript evidence for magical texts in English monastic and collegiate libraries — principally the collections associated with St Augustine's Canterbury, the Augustinian canons at Oxford, and related institutions — and argues that monks and other religious who possessed and used magical texts did so for reasons that made sense within their own religious framework: curiosity about the natural world, the pursuit of practical knowledge (medical, astronomical, calendrical), and a genuine interest in the relationship between the observable world and its hidden causes.

Page's approach, combining codicological analysis (examining how magical texts are bound, where they appear in manuscript collections, what they are associated with) with intellectual history (what theoretical frameworks the possessors brought to the texts), has been influential in demonstrating that magical manuscripts cannot be understood in isolation from their manuscript contexts. A text appearing in a miscellany alongside medical recipes, astronomical tables, and grammatical exercises tells a different story than the same text appearing alone or in a collection of overtly transgressive material.

persons.name: Michael D. Bailey
persons.description: Medieval religion, superstition, witchcraft, and magic as contested categories.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Michael D. Bailey is Professor of History at Iowa State University and one of the leading historians of medieval and early modern magic and witchcraft. His scholarship focuses on the intersection of magic, heresy, and religious reform in the late medieval period, with particular attention to the construction of the diabolical witch concept and the social history of magical practice in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

Major Works

Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages (Penn State University Press, 2003) is Bailey's most important work and the most thorough analysis of the emergence of the diabolical witch concept in the early fifteenth century. Bailey argues that the witch-sabbath construct was not a simple outgrowth of popular belief but was created by a specific group of reform-minded clerics — primarily in the Alpine regions of the Diocese of Lausanne and the western Alps — who combined the inquisitorial concern with heretical conspiracy with the pastoral concern over maleficium and with learned demonological theory. The book identifies Johannes Nider's Formicarius (c.1437) as the key text in which these elements first coalesce into the full diabolical witch concept.

Magic and Superstition in Europe: A Concise History from Antiquity to the Present (Rowman and Littlefield, 2006) provides a broader synthetic overview of European magical practice and its regulation from ancient Rome through the twentieth century. The book is notable for its clarity and its attention to the problems of definition that have bedevilled the historiography of magic.

Fearful Spirits, Reasoned Follies: The Boundaries of Superstition in Late Medieval Europe (Cornell University Press, 2013) examines how late medieval thinkers — theologians, inquisitors, pastoral writers — drew and defended the boundaries between licit religious practice and condemned superstition, and how these boundary-drawing efforts both reflected and shaped the prosecution of magic and witchcraft.

persons.name: Catherine Rider
persons.description: Medieval magic, medicine, fertility, charms, and pastoral contexts.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Catherine Rider is an Associate Professor in the Department of History at the University of Exeter and one of the leading historians of medieval magic with a focus on the relationship between magic, medicine, and gender in medieval England and Europe. Her research examines how magic was discussed and regulated in pastoral and scholastic contexts and how magical texts and practices intersected with medical knowledge and practice.

Magic and Impotence

Rider's major monograph, Magic and Impotence in the Middle Ages (Oxford University Press, 2006), examines a specific body of medieval magical literature — texts dealing with magically caused impotence and the remedies for it — as a window into how medieval people thought about the relationship between magic, medicine, sexuality, and religious authority. The study demonstrates how texts that combined medical and magical approaches to a practical problem circulated in manuscript collections across the medieval period, and how the institutional Church — in canon law, in pastoral literature, and in theological discussion — responded to the claim that magic could render men unable to perform sexually.

Beyond its specific subject, the book is important as a methodological model: by focusing on a specific, well-documented type of magical practice and tracing it across multiple textual and institutional contexts, Rider shows how the history of magic can be practised with the same archival rigour as other branches of medieval social history. Her subsequent work, including her contributions to Sophie Page and Catherine Rider (eds.), The Routledge History of Medieval Magic (2019), has extended this approach across a wider range of topics in medieval magic history.

persons.name: Dan Attrell
persons.description: Translator and scholar of the Latin Picatrix and astral magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Dan Attrell is a scholar of Renaissance magic and esotericism whose primary contribution to the field is his co-translation (with David Porreca) of the Picatrix — the most comprehensive medieval Latin text of astrological magic — into English, published by Penn State University Press in 2019. The translation, the first complete scholarly English rendering of the Latin text, makes David Pingree's 1986 critical edition accessible to readers without Latin and provides an extensively annotated version that identifies sources, parallels, and scholarly context throughout.

Picatrix Translation

The Attrell-Porreca translation draws on Pingree's two-volume critical edition and the earlier Spanish translation (by Maslama al-Majriti, 1256) to produce an English text that is both readable and scholarly. The introduction and notes situate the text within its Arabic and Latin transmission history, identifying the philosophical sources (Neoplatonic, Hermetic, Aristotelian) that underpin the Picatrix's theory of astral magic and providing the contextual information that readers need to use the text as a historical source. The translation has been widely adopted in university courses on Renaissance magic and the history of science.

Attrell's broader scholarly interests include Renaissance Neoplatonism, the history of Western esotericism, and the theory of magic in early modern Europe. His work contributes to the continuing project of making primary sources in the medieval and Renaissance magical tradition available in rigorous scholarly editions — essential infrastructure for a field that has long suffered from a gap between specialist manuscript scholarship and popular occultist editions.

persons.name: David Porreca
persons.description: Medieval Latin Hermetica, Picatrix studies, and transmission of Arabic astral magic.
persons.bio_html:
David Porreca: Scholar of Hermes Trismegistus and Medieval Magic

David Porreca is a contemporary scholar whose research has contributed significantly to understanding the reception of Hermetic texts in medieval Europe, particularly the figure of Hermes Trismegistus as an attributed authority in philosophical, astrological, and magical literature. His work situates the medieval Hermes within the broad tradition of pseudepigraphical attribution through which ancient wisdom figures were invoked to legitimize learned texts of uncertain or composite origin, examining how particular texts came to be associated with Hermes and what this association meant to their medieval readers and users.

Porreca's scholarship addresses the complex question of Hermes' identity and function in medieval intellectual culture. Unlike the Renaissance recovery of Greek Hermetic texts that Frances Yates analyzed in her foundational work, the medieval Hermes was primarily known through Latin translations of Arabic astrological and talismanic texts—particularly the Picatrix and Liber Hermetis—rather than through the philosophical Corpus Hermeticum that became central to Renaissance Neoplatonism. This medieval Hermes was above all an astrologer and sage of natural powers, not the mystic theologian of Ficino's synthesis. Understanding this distinction is essential for accurate histories of Hermetic tradition that avoid anachronistically projecting Renaissance categories onto medieval materials.

His contributions to the study of medieval magic place him within a generation of scholars who have significantly expanded and revised the historical understanding of learned magic's textual foundations. By attending carefully to the specific textual traditions—manuscripts, translations, attributions, and readership—through which magical knowledge circulated, researchers like Porreca have replaced earlier, more impressionistic accounts of a unified "Hermetic tradition" with a more nuanced picture of multiple, partially overlapping textual lineages with distinct histories and audiences.

persons.name: Apollonius of Tyana
persons.description: Ancient sage whose name became attached to medieval ritual and talismanic traditions.
persons.bio_html:
The Figure

Apollonius of Tyana (c.15–100 CE) was a first-century CE Neopythagorean philosopher from Cappadocia who, in the hagiographic biography written by Philostratus (c.220–230 CE), was presented as a wandering sage and wonder-worker whose miracles — healing the sick, raising the dead, appearing simultaneously in different places — rivalled those of Jesus Christ. The Life of Apollonius made him an important figure in late antique pagan responses to Christianity and established him as a type of the philosopher-magus whose wisdom gave him power over nature.

Magical Attribution

In the medieval and Renaissance magical tradition, Apollonius of Tyana was one of the figures to whom magical texts and procedures were attributed as a legitimating pseudepigraphic strategy. The Kitab al-istimaas (Book of the Consultation of the Spirits), known in Latin as the Liber Lunae or related texts, and various other Arabic magical compilations circulated under his authority. The Arabic tradition knew Apollonius as Balinus and attributed to him the discovery of the Emerald Tablet of Hermes — perhaps the most important single document of alchemical tradition — in a vault beneath a statue. This attribution of the Emerald Tablet to Apollonius-Balinus, transmitted through Arabic into Latin, connected him to the Hermetic-alchemical tradition alongside his association with the broader magical tradition.

For historians of magic, Apollonius is significant primarily as a vector of pseudepigraphic attribution: texts circulated under his name exploit the authority of a figure known for wonder-working and ancient wisdom. The historical Apollonius himself remains poorly documented; Philostratus's biography is hagiography rather than history, and modern scholarship (G.R.S. Mead, Maria Dzielska) has found it impossible to determine what is historical in the Philostratan portrait.

persons.name: Thabit ibn Qurra
persons.description: Ninth-century Sabian scholar associated in Latin reception with astral image theory.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Thabit ibn Qurra al-Harrani (c.836–901 CE) was a Sabian mathematician, astronomer, and philosopher from Harran (in modern southern Turkey), working in Baghdad under the patronage of the Banu Musa brothers and later of the ʿAbbasid court. The Sabians of Harran were a pagan community who preserved Neoplatonic and Hermetic traditions alongside astronomical and mathematical learning; their religious practice involved planetary worship and ritual addressed to the celestial bodies, which gave Thabit both theoretical and practical interest in the relationship between celestial bodies and terrestrial things. He is one of the most productive and original scientists of the ninth century, contributing to mathematics, astronomy, mechanics, and medicine.

De imaginibus and Astral Magic

De imaginibus (On Images) is Thabit's treatise on astral image magic, surviving in Latin translation (the Arabic original does not appear to be extant, though similar texts exist in Arabic). The work provides practical instructions for making talismans keyed to the planets and fixed stars: for each operation, it specifies the appropriate planetary hour and configuration, the materials to be used (each planet corresponds to specific metals, plants, and stones), the image to be engraved or cast, the fumigations and prayers to accompany the operation, and the practical ends that can be achieved. The theoretical basis is al-Kindi's ray theory combined with Neoplatonic doctrine of the world-soul and planetary intelligences.

David Pingree edited and analysed De imaginibus in the context of the broader tradition of Arabic astrological magic. The text was known to and used by Latin natural philosophers from the twelfth century: the Speculum astronomiae cites Thabit's works on images as examples of potentially licit astrological magic (those operating through natural celestial causes rather than demonic names). Nicolas Weill-Parot's work on addressative magic situates De imaginibus within the scholastic controversy over image magic.

persons.name: Benedek Lang
persons.description: Central European manuscript libraries, learned magic, and the codicological history of ritual texts.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Benedek Láng is a Hungarian historian of medieval science and magic at the Budapest University of Technology and Economics whose systematic research on Central European manuscript collections — libraries in Hungary, Austria, Poland, and Bohemia — has substantially extended the geographic scope of medieval magic scholarship beyond its traditional focus on English and French manuscripts. His work demonstrates that the learned magical tradition was pan-European in distribution and shows regional variations that earlier scholarship had not documented.

Unlocked Books

Unlocked Books: Manuscripts of Learned Magic in the Medieval Libraries of Central Europe (Pennsylvania State University Press, 2008) is Láng's major contribution. The book surveys magical manuscripts in the major medieval library collections of Central Europe, providing a systematic catalogue and analysis of the distribution, types, and manuscript contexts of learned magic texts in a region largely ignored by earlier grimoire scholarship. The survey reveals that Central European libraries contained substantial quantities of magical material — from astrological and geomantic texts through Solomonic conjuration and the Ars Notoria — circulating in manuscript contexts very similar to those identified by Klaassen for England and by Page for monastic contexts.

The book's title reflects its central argumentative point: the magical manuscripts were accessible in regular library collections rather than hidden or restricted locations. Many readers who consulted a magical text in a chapter or university library were using the resources of a learned institution in the same way as they used other technical or philosophical texts. This "open library" character of medieval magical manuscript culture appears to be a European-wide phenomenon, as Klaassen found for England and Page for monastic contexts. Láng's comparative framework, situating Central European collections alongside English and French evidence, helps establish the learned magical tradition as genuinely pan-European in its institutional presence.

persons.name: Lynn Thorndike
persons.description: Early twentieth-century historian whose multi-volume history made magic and experimental science a continuous object of medieval intellectual history.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Lynn Thorndike (1882–1965) was an American historian at Columbia University whose monumental A History of Magic and Experimental Science (8 volumes, Columbia University Press, 1923–1958) remains the most extensive survey of the relationship between magic and science in European intellectual history. The project covered the Roman Empire through the seventeenth century and drew on an extraordinary range of primary sources, many of which Thorndike was the first modern scholar to examine systematically.

A History of Magic and Experimental Science

The eight-volume work is organized chronologically, with each chapter or section treating a specific author, text, or topic. Thorndike's thesis — stated in the title — is that magic and experimental science developed in parallel, sharing an empirical orientation toward the investigation of nature's hidden properties; that medieval magic was not mere superstition but represented a serious attempt to understand and manipulate natural forces; and that the history of science cannot be properly understood without attention to the magical and astrological context within which early scientific observation and experiment took place.

The work's strengths are its scope and its primary-source depth: Thorndike read vast quantities of manuscript material and provides the first systematic accounts of dozens of texts previously unknown to scholarship. Its weaknesses, identified by subsequent scholars, include a tendency toward uncritical summary (Thorndike often paraphrases his sources at length without sustained analysis), an outdated historiographical framework that treats the relationship between magic and science as straightforwardly progressive, and significant factual errors in the earlier volumes that have been corrected by subsequent specialized work.

Legacy

Despite its limitations, A History of Magic and Experimental Science remains an indispensable research tool for anyone working on medieval and early modern natural philosophy and magic. The index volumes provide access to an enormous range of authors and texts; the primary-source descriptions, where later scholarship has not superseded them, remain valuable. Thorndike's work is the principal example of the encyclopedic historical approach to the subject that was standard before the development of more theoretically sophisticated methods in the 1980s and 1990s.

persons.name: Nicolas Weill-Parot
persons.description: Historian of astral image theory, scholastic natural philosophy, and the boundary between licit and illicit image practices.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Nicolas Weill-Parot is a French historian of science and philosophy at the École pratique des hautes études in Paris, specializing in medieval and Renaissance natural philosophy, astrology, and the history of learned magic. His work is distinguished by its combination of rigorous philological analysis of primary sources with sophisticated philosophical reconstruction of the theoretical frameworks within which medieval natural philosophers discussed magical phenomena.

Addressative Magic and the Speculum astronomiae

Weill-Parot's most important contribution is his development of the concept of "addressative magic" (magie addressative), elaborated in his monumental study Les "images astrologiques" au Moyen Âge et à la Renaissance: Spéculations intellectuelles et pratiques magiques (XIIe–XVe siècle) (Honoré Champion, 2002). Addressative magic designates magical operations that explicitly address spiritual agents — demons, angels, or planetary spirits — as personal, rational beings responsive to command or invocation, as opposed to operations that merely exploit impersonal natural forces. Weill-Parot argues that the scholastic condemnation of image magic targeted specifically the addressative dimension: images that worked through natural celestial causes (as Albertus Magnus attempted to defend) were potentially licit; images that required explicit invocation of spirits were condemned as demonic.

His analysis of the Speculum astronomiae and its attribution dispute — Weill-Parot argues against the attribution to Albertus Magnus on both historical and internal grounds — has been controversial but has significantly advanced the historiography. His broader work on the relationship between natural philosophy and magic in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, particularly his account of William of Auvergne as the key transition figure, provides the indispensable context for understanding scholastic engagement with the Arabic magical tradition.

persons.name: Jean-Patrice Boudet
persons.description: Historian of medieval astrology, divination, learned magic, and manuscript transmission in the Latin West.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Jean-Patrice Boudet is a French historian of medieval science and magic at the Université d'Orléans whose research focuses on astrology, divination, and learned magic at the French royal court and in the broader context of late medieval French intellectual culture. His work documents how astrological and divinatory practices were integrated into the culture of the Valois court and how the relationship between learned magic and royal patronage shaped the production and circulation of magical texts in fourteenth and fifteenth-century France.

Entre science et nigromance

Boudet's major work, Entre science et nigromance: Astrologie, divination et magie dans l'Occident médiéval (XIIe–XVe siècle) (Publications de la Sorbonne, 2006), provides the most comprehensive account of the relationship between astrological science and nigromanric practice in medieval Western Europe from the twelfth through the fifteenth centuries. The book traces the gradual development of a learned culture of astrological and divinatory practice — initially dependent on Arabic translation, then increasingly elaborated in Latin and vernacular contexts — and examines how this culture intersected with court patronage, university education, and ecclesiastical regulation.

Boudet's research on the court of Charles V of France — a monarch who patronized astrologers, owned magical texts, and commissioned translations of astrological works — demonstrates how royal courts provided spaces in which learned magic could be practised under aristocratic protection. His analysis of the relationship between Nicole Oresme's critique of astrology and the court culture that simultaneously employed and critiqued astrological practitioners illuminates the contradictory position of learned magic within late medieval intellectual life. His work on the Picatrix and other astrological magic texts at the French court complements the English-focused scholarship of Klaassen and Page.

persons.name: Julien Veronese
persons.description: Scholar of ritual magic, the Ars Notoria, and manuscript traditions of angelic and learned ritual practice.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Julien Véronèse is a French historian of medieval magic at the Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne whose critical edition of the Ars notoria tradition — L'Ars notoria au Moyen Âge: Introduction et édition critique (Sismel/Edizioni del Galluzzo, 2007) — is the definitive scholarly treatment of the most widely circulated system of medieval angel magic. Véronèse's work combines rigorous manuscript philology with attention to the liturgical and theological contexts within which the Ars Notoria operated.

Ars Notoria Edition

The critical edition documents the manuscript tradition of the Ars Notoria in its two principal recensions (the shorter Ars notoria brevis and the longer version including the Flores aurei), identifies the relationship between the different manuscript families, and provides a text with full critical apparatus and extensive annotation. The introduction situates the Ars Notoria within the broader context of medieval ritual magic (especially its relationship to the Sworn Book of Honorius and to the Ars Almadel), discusses the theological debate over its licitness (from Aquinas's condemnation onward), and analyses the visual dimension of the tradition — the distinctive geometric notae that give the system its name and that survive in sometimes spectacular form in the illustrated manuscripts.

Véronèse's edition replaced earlier incomplete studies and for the first time provided historians with a reliable text of what was, in terms of manuscript circulation, one of the most popular learned magic texts of the medieval period. His collaboration with Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson on the related Liber visionum of John of Morigny (Penn State, 2015) has extended the analysis to the Ars Notoria's most creative medieval response.

persons.name: Johannes Hartlieb
persons.description: Fifteenth-century Bavarian physician and author of advice literature on forbidden arts, witchcraft, and princely governance.
persons.bio_html:
Johannes Hartlieb (c. 1400–1468): Court Physician and Expositor of Forbidden Arts

Johannes Hartlieb was a Bavarian court physician and author who served the Wittelsbach dynasty and produced one of the most significant vernacular treatments of magic in fifteenth-century Germany. His Buch aller verbotenen Kunst, Unglaubens und der Zauberei (Book of All Forbidden Arts, Superstition, and Sorcery, c. 1456) provided a systematic vernacular taxonomy of magical practices organized around the traditional schema of the seven forbidden arts—nigromancy, geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, pyromancy, chiromancy, and spatulamancy—supplemented by discussions of other condemned practices including witchcraft and demonic compacts.

Hartlieb's text is particularly valuable for historians because it was written for a courtly lay audience rather than for academic theologians, reflecting the dissemination of anti-magical discourse beyond the Latin-literate clerical and university world. His patron, the Margrave Johann von Brandenburg, received a text that combined moralizing condemnation with practical description, giving readers enough information about magical practices to recognize and avoid them while making the material accessible through vernacular German prose rather than scholastic Latin. This pedagogical strategy—explaining in order to condemn—characterized much early vernacular demonological literature and inadvertently preserved detailed descriptions of magical practices.

As a physician, Hartlieb occupied a professional position at the intersection of natural philosophy, medicine, and magic. Medical practitioners of the fifteenth century regularly encountered questions about the boundary between natural cures, learned magic, and popular healing practices, and Hartlieb's exposition of forbidden arts likely drew on his professional experience with cases where patients had sought magical remedies. His work thus illuminates both the learned discourse about magic and the social reality of magical practice in late medieval German urban and courtly culture, providing a perspective that complements the more abstract theoretical treatments produced by theologians and inquisitors.

persons.name: Ulrich Molitor
persons.description: Late medieval jurist and author associated with learned discussion of witchcraft and demonic magic.
persons.bio_html:
Ulrich Molitor (c. 1442–1507): Legal Humanist and Skeptic of Witchcraft

Ulrich Molitor was a German jurist and legal humanist whose 1489 treatise De lamiis et phitonicis mulieribus (On Witches and Female Soothsayers) represents a significant early contribution to debates about witchcraft that would intensify dramatically over the following decades. Written in the form of a dialogue and illustrated with woodcuts depicting witches engaged in various supposed activities, Molitor's text engaged directly with the questions raised by the Malleus Maleficarum (1487) while adopting a notably skeptical position on the reality of witches' powers. His legal training and humanist sensibilities led him to question whether the feats attributed to witches—flight, metamorphosis, weather-working—could be literally real or were rather diabolical illusions and melancholic delusions.

Molitor's argument drew on the canon Episcopi, the influential ninth-century ecclesiastical text which had long asserted that beliefs about nocturnal flight and transformation were illusory—the product of demonic deception rather than actual supernatural events. Against demonologists who were increasingly arguing that the Episcopi's skepticism had been superseded by accumulated evidence of witch activity, Molitor maintained that God would not permit demons to possess such comprehensive power over creation. This position aligned with a tradition of qualified skepticism about witch powers that persisted alongside the more credulous demonological consensus emerging in the late fifteenth century.

The visual apparatus of Molitor's text—its woodcut illustrations depicting stereotypical witch activities—is as significant as its arguments. These images circulated widely and contributed to the visual iconography of the witch, even as the text they illustrated maintained skeptical positions about witch powers. This paradox illustrates the complexity of the early modern witch debate, where visual, literary, legal, and theological discourses operated on partially independent tracks, sometimes reinforcing and sometimes contradicting each other. Molitor's work thus occupies an important position in the historiography of witchcraft as evidence of the diversity of learned opinion before the hardening of consensus in the sixteenth century.

persons.name: John of Morigny
persons.description: Fourteenth-century Benedictine monk whose visionary autobiography and ritual book reworked the Ars Notoria in Marian and monastic terms.
persons.bio_html:
Life

John of Morigny (active c.1301–1315) was a Benedictine monk, probably from the monastery of Morigny near Étampes in the Île-de-France, who composed the Liber visionum (Book of Visions) — a visionary mystical work that began as an adaptation of the Ars Notoria tradition and was progressively transformed into an original form of contemplative angel magic through direct visionary experience. His career is unusually well documented for a medieval magical author because the Liber visionum is itself autobiographical: it narrates John's encounter with the Ars Notoria, his initial use of it, his visions of the Virgin Mary and angels, and the progressive revision of his practice under visionary guidance.

The Liber visionum

John began using the Ars Notoria — a widely circulated prayer-based system for acquiring knowledge of the arts and sciences through divine infusion — and experienced visions in which the Virgin Mary and Christ appeared to him, apparently validating but also transforming the practice. Over a period of years, he composed a new version of the Notory Art that replaced the original Latin prayers and notae (geometric figures) with new formulas revealed in his visions, insisting that his version was purified of the diabolical contamination he had come to detect in the original Ars Notoria.

Claire Fanger and Nicholas Watson's edition and translation (Liber florum celestis doctrine / The Flowers of Heavenly Teaching, Penn State University Press, 2015) is the critical edition of this remarkable text. John of Morigny is significant as an example of a medieval practitioner who engaged critically with the learned magical tradition from within, revising its texts in response to visionary experience rather than simply transmitting or condemning them.

persons.name: Honorius of Thebes
persons.description: Attributed authorial figure attached to the Sworn Book of Honorius and traditions of angelic ritual magic.
persons.bio_html:
The Legendary Figure

Honorius of Thebes is a legendary magical authority rather than a historical person: a figure to whom the Sworn Book of Honorius (Liber juratus Honorii) and related magical texts are attributed, presented as a master magician who compiled the surviving essence of a vast magical library and established the fraternal oath of secrecy that preserved it against papal persecution. The text's framing narrative — ninety masters of magic assembling to protect their tradition against ecclesiastical attack — has no historical basis but provides the legal and social self-understanding of the tradition it represents.

The Sworn Book of Honorius

The Sworn Book of Honorius is a Latin magical text probably compiled in the thirteenth century, combining the programme of the Ars Notoria (seeking divine knowledge through prayer and contemplation) with explicit spirit conjuration and a series of operations for achieving the beatific vision. Its central feature — the Seal of God (Sigillum Dei), a complex geometric figure combining divine names, angelic seals, and astrological symbols — was understood as the supreme magical talisman, conferring authority over all spirits. John Dee's obsession with the Sigillum Dei (he commissioned a large wax seal based on a version of the figure in 1582) demonstrates the continuing influence of the Honorian tradition in the Elizabethan period.

The text attributes its origin to Honorius, son of Euclid, Master of the Theban School — a fantastical genealogy designed to give it intellectual authority (Euclid as mathematical wisdom) and exotic provenance (Thebes as ancient Egyptian learning). The fraternal oath that opens the text — each member of the original ninety swears to transmit the book to no more than three persons, and those three must be men of good character — frames the text as a consciously counter-cultural preservation of forbidden knowledge. Gösta Hedegård's critical edition (2002) and Joseph Peterson's English translation (2016) are the scholarly standards.

persons.name: Raziel
persons.description: Angelic authority associated with the Liber Razielis and related Jewish and Latin traditions of revealed esoteric knowledge.
persons.bio_html:
The Angelic Figure

Raziel (Hebrew: רזיאל, "Secret/Mysteries of God") is an angel in Jewish mystical and magical tradition, known primarily as the celestial scribe who compiled and transmitted the Sepher Raziel ha-Malakh (Book of Raziel the Angel) — a compendium of magical and cosmological knowledge — to Adam after the Fall, and who served as the intermediary between divine wisdom and human magical knowledge. Raziel appears in post-biblical Jewish literature; his name does not occur in the Hebrew Bible.

Textual Traditions

In the Midrashic tradition, Raziel stands at the veil separating the heavenly court from the divine presence and overhears all divine decrees, making him a natural intermediary of celestial secrets. The Sepher Raziel ha-Malakh — a Hebrew magical compendium probably assembled in the Geonic period (sixth to tenth centuries) but presented as Raziel's transmission to Adam — draws on this identification to claim the oldest possible authority for its contents: knowledge revealed before the Fall, preserved through the patriarchs, and eventually reaching Solomon. The text incorporates material related to the Sepher ha-Razim alongside kabbalistic material, amulet formulas, and angel names.

In Latin European magic, Raziel appears primarily through the Liber Razielis — a thirteenth-century Latin compilation drawing on Hebrew sources — which attributes its contents to Raziel's original revelation to Adam. The figure of Raziel thus serves the same pseudepigraphic function in the angelic knowledge tradition as Solomon serves in the demonic conjuration tradition: an ancient, divinely-authorized source whose name legitimates later compiled content. David Pingree's work on the Liber Razielis and Gideon Bohak's on the Hebrew Sepher Raziel tradition provide the scholarly foundations.

persons.name: Solomon
persons.description: Biblical king whose attributed authority structures major medieval and early modern traditions of spirit command, talismanic lore, and ritual experiment.
persons.bio_html:
The Biblical and Legendary Solomon

Solomon, son of David and King of Israel (traditionally c.970–931 BCE), is one of the most important figures in the history of religion and magic: a historical ruler about whom almost nothing can be independently verified, but whose legendary attributes — surpassing wisdom, fabulous wealth, architectural achievement (the Temple), and mastery of demons and spirits — made his name the primary authorizing signature of the learned magical tradition across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic cultures for two millennia.

Biblical Solomon

The biblical accounts of Solomon in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles establish the basic attributes: the gift of divinely-granted wisdom (surpassing all other men), wealth beyond ordinary description, the construction of the Temple in Jerusalem, and ultimately the apostasy into which his foreign wives led him. The Wisdom literature of the Hebrew Bible was attributed to Solomon (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, and in the Septuagint, the Wisdom of Solomon and Psalms of Solomon), establishing him as the paradigmatic wise man and author of authoritative texts.

The Magical Solomon

The magical attributes not found in the main biblical narrative developed in Second Temple Jewish literature and in the Hellenistic and late antique period. Josephus (first century CE) describes Solomon as an expert in exorcism using a ring and the plant baaras, and notes that his craft was still practised in Josephus's own time. The Testament of Solomon (probably second to fifth centuries CE) provided the fullest narrative account of Solomon's magical career: the ring given by Michael, the summoning and interrogation of thirty-six demons, their compelled labour in building the Temple. This text established the structural template — named demons, Solomonic authority, divine names as binding force — that the entire subsequent grimoire tradition replicates.

In Islam, Sulayman is a prophet-king granted power over jinn, wind, and animals by divine command (Qurʾan 27, 34). Islamic commentators elaborated his magical power extensively. In late medieval and early modern European magic, "Solomon" functions primarily as an authorizing label: the texts' claim to Solomonic origin is a pseudepigraphic strategy, not a historical claim. Pablo Torijano's Solomon the Esoteric King (2002) provides the most thorough cross-cultural analysis.

persons.name: Theysolius
persons.description: Attributed or textual authority associated with the Liber Theysolius and traditions concerning familiar spirits and wisdom.
persons.bio_html:
Theysolius: Legendary Magician and Attributed Author

Theysolius represents one of the more obscure attributed authorities in the medieval magical corpus, a figure whose historical reality is uncertain and whose significance lies primarily in his role as a legitimating name attached to particular texts. The Liber Theysolius, a Latin magical compilation associated with this name, belongs to the tradition of texts claiming transmission from ancient wisdom figures—a strategy common to the grimoire genre as well as to alchemical and astrological literature. By invoking an exotic, semi-legendary sage as original author, compilers signaled the text's claim to ancient authority while insulating it from immediate contemporary accountability.

The practice of pseudepigraphical attribution in medieval magic drew on multiple models: biblical figures like Solomon and Raziel, ancient philosophers like Aristotle and Apollonius of Tyana, and semi-legendary sages like Hermes Trismegistus and, in this case, Theysolius. Such attributions were not necessarily understood as deliberate fabrications; medieval textual culture often accepted the transmission of ancient wisdom through chains of unnamed intermediaries, and the claim that a text ultimately derived from an ancient wise man carried cultural weight regardless of the chain's verifiability.
