The specific content attributed to Theysolius—ritual procedures, spirit names, and operational instructions characteristic of the learned magic tradition—places this compilation within the broader experimental magic literature of the twelfth through fourteenth centuries.

Scholarly recovery of texts attributed to marginal figures like Theysolius has been part of a broader project to map the full range of the medieval Latin magical corpus beyond its canonical exemplars. Manuscript catalogues and critical editions of minor texts have gradually revealed the scope and variety of this literature, demonstrating that named authorities like Theysolius functioned within a recognizable economy of legitimation in which ancient, exotic, or divine origin served to authorize otherwise suspect practices. The study of such figures illuminates the sociology of magical textual production as much as the content of any particular text.

persons.name: David Pingree
persons.description: Historian of exact sciences, astrology, and astral magic whose work is essential for Arabic, Greek, Sanskrit, and Latin transmission histories.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

David Pingree (1933–2005) was Professor of History of Mathematics and History of Science at Brown University and the most productive editor and translator of mathematical, astronomical, and magical texts in the Western historical tradition. His output — spanning Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Greek, and Latin — was extraordinary in its scope and precision. He is described by colleagues as having produced more critical editions of primary sources in the history of science and astrology than any other scholar of his generation.

Work on the Magical Tradition

For the history of magic, Pingree's most important contributions are his critical editions of the Picatrix (2 vols., Warburg Institute Studies 39, 1986) — the standard scholarly edition of both the Latin text and the related Arabic tradition — and of Thabit ibn Qurra's De imaginibus, al-Kindi's astrological works, and numerous other texts in the astrological-magical tradition. His edition of the Picatrix established the manuscript tradition, identified the Arabic sources, and provided the essential tools for all subsequent scholarship on the most comprehensive medieval text of astrological magic. Without Pingree's editions, systematic scholarly work on the Arabic-Latin transmission of astral magic theory would be impossible.

Pingree also produced critical editions of several Sanskrit astrological texts, Persian astronomical tables, and Greek astrological compilations, demonstrating through these comparative editions the transmission routes through which ancient Babylonian and Hellenistic astronomy and astrology reached Arabic, Persian, and eventually Latin learning. His contributions to understanding the exact bibliographic and textual transmission paths of magical and astrological knowledge set the standard for subsequent work in the field.

Legacy

Pingree's students and successors — including Charles Burnett, Julio Samsó, and others working on the Arabic-Latin transmission — continue the philological tradition he established. His Picatrix edition, in particular, remains the indispensable scholarly resource for anyone working on astrological magic theory in the medieval Latin tradition.

persons.name: Valerie Flint
persons.description: Historian of early medieval religion and magic whose work shaped debates about Christianization, pastoral care, and magical survivals.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Valerie I.J. Flint (1936–2009) was a historian of medieval religion and culture at the University of Hull and later the University of Auckland, whose work challenged the dominant historiographical model of the early medieval Church as simply suppressive of pagan and magical practices. Her scholarship argued for a more complex and ambivalent relationship between institutional Christianity and the popular magical practices it officially condemned.

The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe

The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe (Princeton University Press, 1991) is Flint's major work and one of the most provocative interventions in the historiography of medieval magic. Flint argues that the early medieval Church did not simply condemn and suppress popular magic: it deliberately accommodated, Christianized, and in some respects promoted forms of magical practice that it reframed as compatible with orthodox Christianity. Healing rituals, protective charms, divination, and even some forms of spirit-consultation were tolerated or transformed rather than eliminated, because the Church needed to win converts from precisely the social world where such practices were embedded.

The argument rests on close reading of pastoral texts, penitentials, canon law collections, and hagiography from the sixth through eleventh centuries. Flint shows how the same practices (using written texts for healing, consulting the calendar for lucky and unlucky days, employing protective objects) appear in both condemned and approved contexts, and argues that the difference is often one of authorization and framing rather than content. A charm using the Lord's Prayer rather than a pagan deity's name is structurally identical to its pagan predecessor but theologically transformed.

Reception and Significance

Flint's thesis was controversial: critics argued that she overstated the degree of ecclesiastical endorsement and understated genuine suppression. Richard Kieckhefer, Karen Louise Jolly, and others have engaged with and refined her argument. Her work is significant for insisting that the relationship between institutional Christianity and popular magic was not simply one of condemnation and resistance, and for drawing attention to the pastoral and missionary contexts within which early medieval attitudes toward magic were formed.

persons.name: Robert Mathiesen
persons.description: Scholar of ritual magic manuscripts and Solomonic textual traditions, especially relevant to Ars Notoria and grimoire transmission.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Robert Mathiesen is a scholar of Slavic languages and literatures and the history of magic, best known for his collaboration with Theitic (Mark Stavish) and his work on the Solomonic magic tradition in Eastern European contexts, particularly his research into the manuscript tradition of Solomonic and related magical texts in Slavic and Cyrillic manuscripts. His academic career was at Brown University, where he worked in the Slavic Studies department.

Contributions to Magic History

Mathiesen's contributions to grimoire scholarship include his documentation of Solomonic magical texts in Eastern European manuscript collections — a tradition less well studied than the Western Latin manuscripts but connected to the same Solomonic framework through Byzantine Greek intermediaries. The Byzantine Greek Hygromanteia and related Solomonic texts were transmitted into Slavic manuscript culture, providing a southeastern European branch of the Solomonic tradition that complements the Latin Western tradition documented by Kieckhefer, Klaassen, and Page.

His work on the relationship between Greek, Slavic, and Latin Solomonic traditions contributes to the broader picture of Solomonic magic as a truly pan-European phenomenon with parallel transmission histories across multiple linguistic and cultural zones. His collaborative work with Dan Harms and Joseph Peterson on specific grimoire texts situates this Eastern European dimension within the wider comparative grimoire scholarship that has developed since the 1990s.

persons.name: Jan R. Veenstra
persons.description: Historian of magic, learned culture, and intellectual history whose work connects medieval classifications to Renaissance magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Jan R. Veenstra is a Dutch historian of medieval and Renaissance literature and magic at the University of Groningen whose work focuses on the intersection of political thought, court culture, and learned magic in late medieval Europe, with particular attention to France and the Low Countries. His research addresses how magical texts and magical practitioners operated within the specifically political contexts of the late medieval court and how the definition and condemnation of magic served political as well as theological purposes.

Magic and Divination at Court

Veenstra's most important work for magic history is his study of Jean de Bar and his magical activities at the French court, and more broadly his analysis of how divination and political prophecy intersected in late medieval French court culture. His book Magic and Divination at the Courts of Burgundy and France: Text and Context of Laurens Pignon's 'Contre les devineurs' (Brill, 1998) provides an edition of a fifteenth-century French treatise against divination alongside a rich contextual analysis of the political and social dimensions of divinatory practice in the Burgundian court milieu.

The analysis shows how the condemnation of divination and magic served specific political functions: attacks on court diviners could be instruments of factional politics as much as expressions of theological principle, and the definition of what counted as illicit divination was shaped by the specific political circumstances of specific moments. Veenstra's work thus connects the history of magic to the political history of late medieval France and Burgundy in ways that purely theological or natural philosophical analyses miss.

persons.name: Charles Burnett
persons.description: Historian of Arabic-Latin transmission, astrology, natural philosophy, and occult sciences in the medieval Latin West.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Charles Burnett is Professor of the History of Islamic Influences in Europe at the Warburg Institute, University of London, and the leading authority on the twelfth-century Arabic-Latin translation movement — the systematic transfer of Arabic scientific, philosophical, and magical learning into Latin that transformed European intellectual culture between approximately 1100 and 1200. His work spans Arabic astronomy, astrology, mathematics, philosophy, and magic, with particular attention to the scholars who performed the translations (Adelard of Bath, Hermann of Carinthia, Robert of Ketton, Gerard of Cremona, and others) and to the texts they chose to translate.

Work on Magic

For the history of magic, Burnett's most important contributions are his studies of specific translated magical texts and of the translators who brought them into Latin. His work on Adelard of Bath (including editions of several of Adelard's translations) documents the early phase of Arabic-Latin transmission. His studies of the Picatrix tradition, of al-Kindi's works on astrology and magic, and of the astrological-magic texts translated in the twelfth century provide the documentary basis for understanding how Arabic natural magic theory entered Latin learned culture.

Burnett has also worked on Arabic-Hebrew and Arabic-Latin transmission routes for magical texts, contributing to the understanding of how Solomonic and angel magic traditions moved between Jewish, Islamic, and Christian learned cultures. His editions and studies of specific texts — including works attributed to Michael Scot and to the Toledo translation circle — provide essential primary-source documentation. His broad command of the primary languages (Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Greek) and his commitment to rigorous philological method make him indispensable to anyone working on the transmission of magical knowledge in the medieval period.

persons.name: Paola Zambelli
persons.description: Historian of astrology, magic, scholastic debates, and the Speculum astronomiae tradition.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Paola Zambelli (1929–2020) was an Italian historian of science and philosophy at the University of Florence whose work on Renaissance magic, natural philosophy, and the history of astrology and divination shaped the field across half a century. Her approach combined rigorous archival research with philosophical analysis, situating figures like Agrippa, Pomponazzi, and Cecco d'Ascoli within the social and institutional history of the Renaissance university and court.

Major Contributions

Zambelli's study of Cornelius Agrippa — developed across several articles and culminating in her analysis of the relationship between De occulta philosophia and De incertitudine — provided one of the most sophisticated accounts of Agrippa's intellectual development, arguing that his scepticism in De incertitudine was not simply a repudiation of the magical programme but a complex rhetorical and theological response to the dangers of public exposure. Her reading of Agrippa as a fideist sceptic — using Pyrrhonist arguments to defend religious faith against both scholastic rationalism and magical speculation — influenced Charles Nauert's biography and subsequent Agrippa scholarship.

Her work on Pietro Pomponazzi's De naturalium effectuum causis sive de incantationibus (On the Causes of Natural Effects, or On Incantations) — an Aristotelian argument that all apparently magical effects, including those attributed to demons and angels, can be explained through natural causes — placed this controversial text in its Paduan university context and illuminated the connection between Pomponazzi's radical Aristotelian naturalism and the broader Renaissance debate about magical causation. Her essays on astrological determinism and its condemnation, collected in White Magic, Black Magic in the European Renaissance (Brill, 2007), provide the best overview of her contributions to the history of magic.

persons.name: Agostino Paravicini Bagliani
persons.description: Historian of medieval learned culture, astrology, medicine, and courtly/scientific contexts relevant to occult knowledge.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Agostino Paravicini Bagliani is a Swiss-Italian medievalist and emeritus professor at the University of Lausanne whose work on the medieval papacy, papal court culture, and the relationship between medicine, natural philosophy, and ecclesiastical authority has contributed important context for understanding how learned magic operated at the highest levels of medieval institutional life. His research on the papal court's engagement with natural philosophy, alchemy, and the prolongation of life is particularly relevant to the history of magic at the intersection of medicine, natural philosophy, and theology.

The Pope's Body

Paravicini Bagliani's most widely read work in English translation is The Pope's Body (Il corpo del Papa, 1994; English translation University of Chicago Press, 2000), which examines how the medieval papacy constructed the physical person of the pope as a sacred body — simultaneously ordinary (the pope could die, be ill, become old) and extraordinary (his office conferred unique spiritual authority). The book's treatment of the papal court's engagement with medical practitioners, alchemists, and natural philosophers seeking to prolong the pope's life provides context for understanding how the highest levels of medieval institutional Christianity were implicated in the same natural philosophical and proto-magical projects that the Church officially condemned in other contexts.

His broader work on Roger Bacon's relationship to the papal court, on the Speculum astronomiae and its attribution, and on the culture of thirteenth-century natural philosophy at the Roman curia contributes to the history of magic by documenting how natural philosophy — including astrological and alchemical projects with magical dimensions — was pursued at and for the papacy even as the same papacy condemned learned magic in its judicial capacity. This irony — the institutional Church both sponsoring and condemning the same kinds of natural philosophical enquiry — is central to the social history of medieval magic.

persons.name: Don C. Skemer
persons.description: Manuscript scholar whose work on textual amulets and written protection is central for charms and apotropaic writing.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Don C. Skemer is a curator and historian at Princeton University Library whose scholarly work on medieval textual amulets — objects on which written texts are inscribed or enclosed for protective or magical purposes — has been foundational for understanding the material culture of medieval magic. His book Binding Words: Textual Amulets in the Middle Ages (Pennsylvania State University Press, 2006) is the most comprehensive study of this topic in any language and the essential reference for the history of written magic as a material practice.

Binding Words

Binding Words examines the production and use of written protective objects across medieval Europe from approximately the sixth through the fifteenth centuries, with particular attention to England, France, and the Italian peninsula. Skemer's approach is broadly interdisciplinary: he combines codicological analysis (examining the physical properties of surviving objects — the materials on which texts are written, their size and form, their marks of wear and use), textual criticism (establishing what texts were inscribed and how they changed across the tradition), and social history (who commissioned, who produced, and who used these objects).

The book's central argument is that textual amulets were not simply residual paganism or popular superstition but a coherent and sophisticated material practice embedded in medieval literate culture at multiple social levels. The same person who read a scholastic theological text might commission or wear a written amulet bearing divine names or Gospel passages. The boundary between legitimate religious use of sacred texts (devotional books, relics) and illicit magical use of the same texts (written charms worn on the body) was a genuine object of theological debate rather than a simple institutional given. Skemer's documentation of the enormous variety of textual amulets in circulation — from simple Gospel inscriptions to complex Solomonic seal-sequences — demonstrates the richness of this material tradition.

persons.name: Lea T. Olsan
persons.description: Scholar of charms, healing prayers, and vernacular ritual language in medieval manuscript contexts.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Lea T. Olsan is a scholar of medieval literature and magic, best known for her foundational research on medical charms in Middle English manuscripts. Her work examines the verbal and material culture of healing magic in medieval England, focusing on the charm tradition as it appears in manuscript collections that combined medical, devotional, and magical material. She has taught at the University of Louisiana Monroe.

Charms and Medical Manuscripts

Olsan's research on Middle English medical charms — her articles in Magic, Ritual, and Witchcraft, Traditio, and related journals — has been foundational for establishing medical charms as a legitimate subject of scholarly analysis rather than dismissing them as mere superstition or residual paganism. Her work examines how charms functioned within the practical medical culture of medieval England: how they were copied, how they were organized in manuscript collections (typically alongside recipes, herbal lore, and surgical instructions), and how their users understood their efficacy.

A key contribution is her analysis of the relationship between the verbal form of charms and their claimed efficacy: Olsan shows that medieval charm-users had sophisticated understandings of how different types of verbal formula (prayer, adjuration, narrative charm, protective verse) worked through different mechanisms — prayer through divine petition, adjuration through divine authority, narrative charm through analogy and precedent — and that the choice of verbal form was not random but reflected practitioners' views about the nature of magical causation. Her work connects the popular charm tradition to the theoretical debates of scholastic natural philosophy and pastoral theology that addressed the same questions about the power of words and the mechanism of magical causation.

persons.name: Katelyn Mesler
persons.description: Scholar of Jewish, Christian, and ritual magic traditions, including Solomonic and angelological transmission.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Katelyn Mesler is a historian of medieval science and magic at Northwestern University whose work focuses on the transmission of knowledge — particularly magical and astrological knowledge — between Jewish, Christian, and Islamic cultures in the medieval Mediterranean world. Her research addresses how Hebrew magical texts entered Latin circulation, how Jewish scholars participated in or resisted the transmission of magical learning to Christian audiences, and how the boundaries between licit and illicit knowledge were negotiated across religious and cultural divides.

Research Contributions

Mesler's contributions to the history of medieval magic centre on the role of Jewish intermediaries and translators in the transmission of magical texts from Arabic and Hebrew into Latin, and on the specific textual traditions (amulet texts, Solomonic conjurations, astrological magic) that crossed religious boundaries. Her work on the Latin reception of Hebrew magical material illuminates a dimension of the Arabic-Latin translation movement that has been understudied: the translation of specifically Jewish magical texts (the Liber Razielis, Hebrew angel magic) into Latin, and the transformation of their meaning and authority in the process.

Her research engages with the broader question of how Jewish scholars in medieval Christian Europe navigated the demand for their expertise in magical and astrological matters while managing the religious and social risks that such engagement entailed. The essays collected in Sophie Page and Catherine Rider (eds.), The Routledge History of Medieval Magic (2019), to which Mesler contributed, provide the broader scholarly context for this research. Her work connects the Jewish magical tradition analysed by Bohak and Torijano to the Latin learned magic tradition analysed by Kieckhefer and Klaassen.

persons.name: Florence Chave-Mahir
persons.description: Scholar of exorcism, liturgy, ritual authority, and the borderlands of religious and magical practice.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Florence Chave-Mahir is a French medievalist whose research focuses on exorcism, demonic possession, and the relationship between pastoral practice and the demonic in the medieval Church. Her work provides essential context for understanding how the Church's institutional responses to demonic activity — through exorcism and related ritual practices — intersected with the learned magical tradition that also claimed to control demons.

L'exorcisme des possédés

Chave-Mahir's major work, L'exorcisme des possédés dans l'Église d'Occident (Xe–XIVe siècle) (Brepols, 2011), provides the most comprehensive account of medieval exorcism practice from the tenth through the fourteenth centuries, examining both the liturgical and canonical framework of exorcism as an official Church rite and the actual practice of exorcism as documented in hagiographical and pastoral sources. The work illuminates the relationship between official exorcism and the unofficial, learned magical procedures for commanding demons that the same Church condemned: both claim authority over demonic beings through divine power, and the boundary between a legitimate exorcism and an illicit conjuration was contested and context-dependent.

For the history of magic, Chave-Mahir's work is significant for demonstrating that the Church's relationship to demonic power was not simply one of condemnation and suppression. The institutional practice of exorcism constituted an acknowledged, officially sanctioned form of commanding demons — not through magical art but through divine authority delegated through the Church's priesthood. Understanding this institutional framework helps explain why practitioners of learned demonic magic could frame their operations within a broadly Christian devotional structure and claim to work within divine authority rather than against it.

persons.name: Béatrice Delaurenti
persons.description: Historian of medieval knowledge, marvels, nature, and the conceptual edges of natural and occult causality.
persons.bio_html:
Life and Scholarship

Béatrice Delaurenti is a French historian of medieval philosophy and medicine at the École des hautes études en sciences sociales (EHESS) in Paris whose research focuses on the relationship between fascination, enchantment, and natural philosophy in medieval scholastic thought. Her work examines how medieval philosophers and physicians theorized the power of the gaze, voice, and imagination to produce real physical effects on other persons — the natural philosophical account of what popular tradition called "the evil eye" or fascination.

La puissance des mots

Delaurenti's major work, La puissance des mots: «Virtus verborum»: débats doctrinaux sur le pouvoir des incantations au Moyen Âge (Éditions du Cerf, 2007), examines the medieval scholastic debate about the power of incantations — whether words could produce physical effects and, if so, by what mechanism. The book traces the debate from the twelfth century through the late medieval period, analysing how philosophers and theologians argued about whether the efficacy of spoken words in healing or harming required natural, angelic, or demonic causation.

This debate was directly relevant to the status of charms, adjurations, and conjuration formulas in the magical tradition: if words had no natural causal power (a position held by some scholastics), then their use in magical operations necessarily presupposed supernatural — and therefore demonic — assistance. If words had genuine natural power through their association with the speaker's intention and the qualities of sound, then at least some verbal magic could be defended as natural philosophy. Delaurenti's careful reconstruction of this debate provides essential philosophical context for understanding why the condemnation of verbal magic was not as straightforward as it might appear.

persons.name: Roger Bacon
persons.description: Thirteenth-century Franciscan philosopher whose discussions of experiment, language, optics, astrology, and natural powers are central to medieval debates over knowledge and magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Roger Bacon (c.1214/20–1292) studied at Oxford and Paris, entered the Franciscan Order probably in the 1250s, and spent periods under house restriction at Paris, apparently because of his controversial promotion of an experimental, mathematically-based natural philosophy and his attacks on the established university curriculum. His three major works — the Opus maius, Opus minus, and Opus tertium — were written at the request of Pope Clement IV (1265–1268) and represent a systematic programme for the reform of Christian education through the integration of mathematics, languages, optics, and experimental science.

Magic and Experimental Science

Bacon occupies a complex position in the history of learned magic. His works contain some of the most sophisticated engagement with the theory of magical causation in the thirteenth century — his account of the power of celestial influence, the action of the imagination, and the mechanism of "opus manus" (art or skill) that produces marvellous effects — alongside some of the most aggressive naturalization of magical phenomena. Bacon consistently argued that apparently magical effects could be explained through natural philosophy properly understood: through knowledge of celestial influences, optical phenomena, and the hidden properties of things.

His concept of scientia experimentalis (experimental science) as the crown of the philosophical sciences was explicitly connected to the production of marvellous effects: knowledge of the secret causes of things gave the philosopher the ability to produce effects that would strike the ignorant as magical. At the same time, Bacon drew a sharp distinction between legitimate philosophical investigation and demonic magic: the latter, he argued, was inferior to the former because it depended on cooperation with deceptive spiritual agents rather than true knowledge of natural causes. Lynn Thorndike's assessment of Bacon in his History of Magic and Experimental Science (vol. 2, 1923) remains the most extensive treatment, though subsequent scholarship (especially by David Lindberg) has refined the picture considerably.

persons.name: Albertus Magnus
persons.description: Thirteenth-century Dominican philosopher whose authority shaped scholastic natural philosophy, astrology, minerals, animals, and debates over occult properties.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Albertus Magnus (c.1200–1280) — Albert of Cologne, Albert the Great — was the most encyclopedic natural philosopher of the thirteenth century and the teacher of Thomas Aquinas at Cologne and Paris. Born in Lauingen on the Danube into a noble family, he entered the Dominican Order around 1223, studied and taught theology at Paris from around 1240, and then moved to the Cologne studium generale (1248), where he established the Dominican school for advanced studies and remained the dominant intellectual figure for three decades. He served briefly as Bishop of Regensburg (1260–1262) before returning to Cologne. He was beatified in 1622 and declared a Doctor of the Church and patron saint of natural scientists by Pius XII in 1941.

Natural Philosophy and the Occult

Albert's massive natural philosophical project — an attempt to paraphrase and comment on the entire Aristotelian corpus, supplemented with Arabic sources — was the primary conduit through which Arabist natural philosophy, including the doctrines of occult qualities, astral influence, and image magic, entered systematic Latin scholastic discussion. His De mineralibus (c.1262) treats the occult properties of stones and metals with a naturalistic framework: stones have powers exceeding their elemental composition, derived from stellar influence during their formation, and these powers can be used medicinally and magically without appeal to demonic causes. His commentaries on the pseudo-Aristotelian De plantis and Pseudo-Dionysius also bear on questions of magical causation.

The Speculum astronomiae, whose attribution to Albert has been debated (Nicolas Weill-Parot argued against it; most scholars maintain it), is the most systematic scholastic treatment of the boundary between legitimate and illegitimate magic in the thirteenth century. It distinguishes three categories of astrological image magic: fully licit images (talismans operating through natural celestial causes, analogous to medicinal plants), potentially licit images (whose licitness depends on whether demonic invocation is involved), and clearly illicit images (requiring demonic names and pact). This classification remained influential through the fourteenth century and was cited repeatedly in subsequent natural magical literature.

Pseudo-Albertine Literature

Albert's enormous authority generated a substantial pseudo-Albertine literature: practical magic texts circulated under his name as a legitimating attribution. The Liber aggregationis (Secrets of Albertus Magnus), De virtutibus herbarum, and Experimenta Alberti are the most widely circulated of these pseudo-attributions, and all went through numerous printed editions after 1500. Their circulation under Albert's name represents the same pseudepigraphic strategy visible in the Solomonic tradition: attributing practical magic to an authoritative figure domesticates its transgressive potential by connecting it to a recognized and respected intellectual tradition.

persons.name: Thomas Aquinas
persons.description: Thirteenth-century Dominican theologian whose discussions of demons, superstition, divination, and illicit pact shaped later scholastic classifications of magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), born into a noble family at Roccasecca near Aquino in southern Italy, entered the Dominican Order in 1244, studied under Albertus Magnus at Cologne (1248–1252), and spent his career teaching at Paris and in Italy. He died at the monastery of Fossanova while travelling to the Council of Lyon. He was canonized in 1323 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1567; his Summa theologiae was placed alongside the Bible on the altar at the Council of Trent. His theology and philosophy dominated the Catholic university curriculum from the thirteenth century to the twentieth.

Scholastic Demonology and Magic

Aquinas's treatment of magic appears principally in three locations: the Prima Pars of the Summa theologiae (on angels and demons as intellectual substances with limited causal powers), the Secunda secundae (qq. 92–96, on superstition, divination, and the pact with demons), and his shorter treatise De occultis operibus naturae (On the Occult Works of Nature), which addresses the natural philosophical limits of non-supernatural causation.

The Summa theologiae II-II, qq. 92–96 provide the most systematic scholastic condemnation of divination and magic as illicit forms of inquiry. Aquinas distinguishes superstition (which attributes to creatures — stars, images, demons — what belongs to God alone) from legitimate religious practice. Divination is always illicit when it involves implicit or explicit demonic pact; the desire to know the future by consulting anything other than legitimate causes or divine revelation is in itself a turning toward demonic power, even if the practitioner does not explicitly intend it. This framework made even passive or "natural" divination theologically suspect, and shaped the Inquisition's approach to magical practice for centuries.

On the natural philosophical side, De occultis operibus naturae argues that natural things can have properties exceeding ordinary causation (occult qualities) that produce apparently marvellous effects without supernatural intervention. This argument, against those who too quickly attributed unusual natural phenomena to demonic agency, licensed a domain of natural magical phenomena that could be studied and used without moral hazard. Combined with the condemnation of demonic magic, this position creates the characteristic Thomistic double gesture: nature can produce marvels; but any operation that requires demonic cooperation is illicit regardless of the intended end.

persons.name: William of Auvergne
persons.description: Thirteenth-century bishop and theologian whose treatment of demons, image magic, and illicit ritual is central to medieval demonological classification.
persons.bio_html:
Life

William of Auvergne (c.1180–1249) was born in Aurillac, studied and taught theology at Paris, and was appointed Bishop of Paris in 1228 — an office he held until his death. His episcopate coincided with the consolidation of the University of Paris as an institution and with the introduction of Arabic and Aristotelian philosophy into the curriculum, developments he monitored with a combination of intellectual engagement and occasional alarm.

Natural Philosophy and Magic

William's major philosophical works — the encyclopedic Magisterium divinale et sapientiale, comprising De trinitate, De universo, De anima, De virtutibus et moribus, De fide et legibus, De legibus, and De causis cur Deus homo — constitute the most ambitious attempt before Aquinas to systematically address the new Aristotelian and Arabic philosophy from within a Christian framework. For the history of magic, the most important are De universo and De legibus, composed in the 1230s.

William distinguished sharply between natural powers (admissible) and demonic cooperation (always forbidden). He engaged seriously with Arabic astrological image magic — the theory that planetary images, properly made and timed, could attract and concentrate celestial influences through purely natural causation — and subjected it to sustained philosophical criticism. His conclusion was that image magic as described in Arabic sources like the Picatrix and Thabit ibn Qurra's De imaginibus was impossible through natural causes alone and therefore necessarily involved demonic cooperation, whether the practitioners knew it or not. This argument anticipates the structure of Aquinas's later condemnation.

Nicolas Weill-Parot identifies William as the key transition figure between twelfth-century natural philosophy (which had been relatively permissive about natural magic) and the thirteenth-century scholastic framework that became more restrictive. William's engagement with Arabic sources represents the first serious scholastic confrontation with the sophisticated astrological magic theory of al-Kindi, Thabit ibn Qurra, and the Picatrix tradition.

persons.name: Pietro d'Abano
persons.description: Italian physician and philosopher associated with astrology, astral causality, and later magical attributions.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Pietro d'Abano (c.1257–c.1316) — known in Latin sources as Petrus de Abano — was an Italian physician and natural philosopher from Abano Terme near Padua who became one of the most influential medical and astrological authorities of the early fourteenth century. He studied medicine at Paris and was associated with the University of Padua, where he may have taught. He was twice accused of heresy before the Inquisition — once acquitted during his lifetime, once condemned posthumously — for astrological claims touching on determinism and for allegedly possessing a philosopher's stone.

Works and Significance for Magic

Pietro's Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum (Conciliator, printed 1472) was his most influential work: a vast reconciliation of the disagreements between Arabic and Galenic medicine and between Arabic astrology and Aristotelian natural philosophy, organized in 210 "differences" (disputationes). Several differences address the relationship between celestial influence and terrestrial events, including the production of marvellous effects through astrological knowledge.

The pseudo-Abanian Heptameron, seu elementa magica was attributed to Pietro d'Abano and circulated extensively in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, often appended to Agrippa's De occulta philosophia. The Heptameron provides a system of spirit conjuration organized by the days of the week and the angels and spirits associated with each day, with conjuration formulas, magic circles, and fumigations. Whether Pietro had any connection to this text is unclear; the attribution exploited his authority as a naturalistic philosopher to legitimate a practical conjuration system. Nicolas Weill-Parot's work on Pietro's engagement with image magic theory in the Conciliator clarifies his genuine contribution to the scholastic debate about astrological causation.

persons.name: Arnald of Villanova
persons.description: Physician and religious writer whose attributed corpus became entangled with medical, alchemical, and astrological materials.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Arnald of Villanova (c.1240–1311) was a Catalan physician, theologian, and spiritual writer who served as physician to three popes (Nicholas IV, Boniface VIII, and Clement V) and to the Aragonese royal family, while simultaneously producing an extraordinary range of works on medicine, alchemy, astrology, and Joachite prophecy that brought him into conflict with Parisian theologians and eventually with the Inquisition. Born probably in Valencia, he studied medicine at Montpellier and Naples, where he learned Arabic and had access to the latest Arabic medical literature. He translated several Arabic medical texts, including works of Avicenna's school, into Latin.

Medicine, Astrology, and Magic

Arnald's medical works — including his Regimen sanitatis ad regem Aragonum, his commentaries on Avicenna, and his treatise on poisons — engaged seriously with astrological medicine: the timing of medical interventions by planetary configurations, the use of lapidary and herbal remedies keyed to celestial influence, and the production of medical images and talismans. His engagement with astrological image magic brought him into the same contested territory as Albertus Magnus and Pietro d'Abano: the question of whether specific medical procedures worked through natural celestial causes or required demonic assistance.

Nicolas Weill-Parot's work on addressative image magic treats Arnald's engagement with the Picatrix tradition and with astrological talisman-making as an important case study in the negotiation of the licit/illicit boundary at the interface of medicine and magic. Arnald accepted the naturalistic theory of celestial influence in medicine while resisting the explicitly addressative elements of astrological magic that would have put him clearly outside orthodox bounds.

Prophecy and Condemnation

Arnald's most controversial works were his Joachite prophetic writings, in which he predicted the imminent coming of Antichrist and the end of the present ecclesiastical order. These writings were condemned at Paris in 1300 and brought him into ongoing conflict with the Dominicans and the Parisian theological faculty. His connections to the Franciscan Spirituals and to the Valencian Beguins complicated his relationship with the papacy even as he served as personal physician to three popes. He died at sea in 1311 before a planned second confrontation with the theological authorities.

persons.name: John of Salisbury
persons.description: Twelfth-century cleric whose critique of courtly divination and occult practices is important for earlier medieval moral classification.
persons.bio_html:
Life

John of Salisbury (c.1115/20–1180) was an English humanist scholar and ecclesiastical administrator who studied in Paris under Peter Abelard, Robert of Melun, William of Conches, and — most importantly for his intellectual formation — Thierry of Chartres, before serving as secretary to Archbishop Theobald and then Thomas Becket of Canterbury. He witnessed the murder of Becket in 1170 and ended his career as Bishop of Chartres (1176–1180). He was the most accomplished Latinist of his generation in northern Europe and the best witness to the intellectual culture of the Paris schools in the 1130s–40s.

The Policraticus and Magic

John's Policraticus sive de nugis curialium et vestigiis philosophorum (Statesman's Book, 1159), a wide-ranging treatise on political philosophy, contains important material on divination and magic in Books I–II. John distinguishes legitimate from illegitimate forms of divination with considerable sophistication, drawing on classical sources (Cicero's De divinatione) alongside patristic authorities. He is familiar with Arabic astrological categories and with the debate over whether celestial influence can legitimately serve as a basis for natural prognostication.

John's own experience of magic is personal and sceptical: he describes (I.11) how as a child he was used by a priest who attempted to see spirits in a polished nail or basin through a boy's eyes — an experience John found unproductive and disturbing. This autobiographical account makes him one of the few medieval writers to describe a magical operation from personal experience, however sceptical. For the history of magic, John is important as a twelfth-century voice engaging with astrological and divinatory theory before the main Arabic transmission had been fully absorbed, and as evidence for the persistence of practical magical experiment alongside learned theological discussion.

persons.name: Nicole Oresme
persons.description: Fourteenth-century philosopher and bishop whose criticism of astrology and divination belongs to late medieval debates over celestial influence.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Nicole Oresme (c.1320–1382) was a French philosopher, mathematician, and theologian who studied at the Collège de Navarre in Paris under Jean Buridan, became Master of the Collège de Navarre, was appointed canon of Rouen (1362), and eventually served as Bishop of Lisieux (1377). He was a close advisor to King Charles V of France and translated several Aristotelian works into French at royal request. He is recognized as one of the most original thinkers of the fourteenth century for his mathematical and physical innovations (the latitude of forms, the graphical representation of change, proto-impetus theory).

Magic and Wonders

Oresme wrote two works directly relevant to the history of magic. De causis mirabilium (On the Causes of Wonders, c.1360) argues systematically that all apparent marvels and wonders — including those typically attributed to demons or supernatural forces — can be explained through natural causes: optical illusions, the imagination's influence on the body, unusual properties of specific places or times, the suggestibility of the human mind. This systematic naturalization of the marvellous was not intended as a denial of the supernatural but as a methodological first step: natural explanation should be attempted before supernatural causes are invoked.

Tractatus contra astronomos (also called Livre de divinacions in its French version) attacked judicial astrology — the prediction of specific future events from horoscopes — as neither scientifically valid nor morally permissible. Oresme's arguments anticipate later sceptical challenges to astrology: celestial influence on terrestrial matter may be real, but the precision required for horoscopic prediction far exceeds what the theory can deliver, and the claim to determine the future of individuals undermines free will. His critique of astrology was influential on subsequent natural philosophical discussions of celestial influence and its limits.

persons.name: Augustine of Hippo
persons.description: Late antique Christian theologian whose account of demons, signs, superstition, and illicit curiosity shaped medieval classifications of magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE) was born in Thagaste in Roman North Africa (modern Algeria), educated in rhetoric at Carthage, and converted to Christianity in Milan in 386 under the influence of Ambrose of Milan and after years of engagement with Manichaeism and Neoplatonism. He returned to North Africa, was ordained priest, and became Bishop of Hippo Regius in 396, a position he held until his death during the Vandal siege of the city. He is the most influential theologian in the history of Western Christianity, and his writings established the conceptual foundations for medieval demonology, the theology of magic, and the critique of divination.

Demonology and Magic

Augustine's engagement with magic and demonology is dispersed across his enormous output but concentrated in several key texts. De civitate Dei (City of God, completed c.426) Books VIII–X — written in response to pagan accusations that Rome's sack in 410 was caused by the abandonment of the old gods — provides the most systematic Christian demonological framework. Augustine argues that the Neoplatonic daemons are real spiritual beings capable of apparent wonders, that all pagan religion constitutes effective (if unwitting) demon-worship, and that theurgic practices like those of Porphyry and Iamblichus are diabolical regardless of their philosophical pretensions. His distinction between divine miracles and demonic wonders (praestigia) — the latter real but limited in scope and always deceptive in intent — became the canonical framework for all subsequent medieval discussion.

De divinatione daemonum (On the Divination of Demons) argues that demons can appear to predict the future not because they have genuine foreknowledge (which belongs to God alone) but because they have sharper senses and faster movement than humans, enabling them to observe and report on distant events before human messengers could arrive. This naturalistic reduction of demonic prophecy — demons are cleverer and faster, not genuinely omniscient — became a standard resource for scholastic accounts of what demons could and could not do.

De doctrina christiana II.20–23 defines superstition and condemns all magical practices as implicit demonic pact: any appeal to non-divine agents for knowledge or power constitutes the worship of demons and is illicit regardless of outcome or intent.

Legacy

Augustine's framework dominated medieval thinking about magic for a millennium. Gratian's Decretum (c.1140) transmitted his anti-divination arguments into canon law; Thomas Aquinas's Summa theologiae repeatedly cites and develops his positions; the Malleus Maleficarum (1486) and subsequent witch-trial literature are unthinkable without the Augustinian framework of demonic pact and diabolical power.

persons.name: Isidore of Seville
persons.description: Early medieval encyclopedist whose etymological classifications of magic, divination, and pagan learning shaped later reference traditions.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Isidore of Seville (c.560–636 CE) was Archbishop of Seville from around 600 CE until his death, a central figure in the Visigothic Spanish church, a church council president, and the most important encyclopedist between late antiquity and the twelfth-century renaissance. Born into a noble Hispano-Roman family that included two other bishops, he was educated in the episcopal school at Seville, possibly under his brother Leander. He presided over the Third Council of Toledo (589) that oversaw the Visigothic conversion from Arianism to Catholicism, and continued to shape Spanish ecclesiastical and intellectual culture until his death.

The Etymologiae and Magic

Isidore's Etymologiae or Origines (completed c.623–636, in twenty books) was the most widely copied reference work in medieval Europe from the seventh through twelfth centuries — over one thousand manuscripts survive. It is organized as an encyclopedia of all knowledge, proceeding by etymology (tracing the origins of words) on the principle that a thing's name reveals its nature. Book VIII, chapter 9 (on the magicians) provides the taxonomy of forbidden arts that dominated medieval Christian classification of magic for six centuries: magi (magicians, from the Persian priestly caste), malefici (evildoers), mathematici (those who predict through stars), haruspices (from entrails), augures (from birds), pythones (those speaking through demons), arioli (who prophesy through demons), astrologi, and sortilegi (casters of lots). Each term is given an etymology and a brief characterization.

This taxonomy was transmitted into the medieval canon law tradition — Rabanus Maurus's De magicis artibus (c.842) follows it closely; Burchard of Worms's Decretum (c.1012) incorporates it; and ultimately Gratian's Decretum (c.1140) enshrined it in the canonical legal collection that governed the medieval Church's response to magic and divination. When Thomas Aquinas in the Summa theologiae asks whether divination is sinful, he is working within a framework whose categories ultimately derive from Isidore. Richard Kieckhefer and Michael Bailey both identify the Etymologiae as the starting point for any history of medieval magic classification.

persons.name: al-Kindi
persons.description: Arabic philosopher associated in Latin reception with De radiis and theories of rays, causality, words, and celestial influence.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Abu Yusuf Yaʿqub ibn Isḥaq al-Kindi (c.800/01–873 CE) was the first great Arab philosopher and a central figure in the translation movement that transmitted Greek philosophical and scientific learning into Arabic. Born in Basra to an aristocratic Yemeni family and educated in Baghdad, he served at the ʿAbbasid court as a physician and intellectual under al-Maʾmun and al-Muʿtasim, overseeing translations and contributing his own extensive philosophical and scientific writings. He was called "the Philosopher of the Arabs" by later writers. His works cover mathematics, astronomy, optics, medicine, philosophy, and music — as well as astrology and magic.

De radiis and the Theory of Rays

De radiis stellarum (On Stellar Rays) — the Latin title of a work whose Arabic original does not survive — is al-Kindi's most influential contribution to the history of magic. The work, probably written around 850 CE and surviving only in a medieval Latin translation (probably twelfth century), argues that all things in the world continuously emit rays in all directions, analogous to the way light radiates from a luminous body. These rays carry the qualities of their source and affect the things they strike. Celestial bodies emit the most powerful rays, but sublunary things also emit them; the human voice, when charged with intense mental concentration, can similarly emit effective rays. A person with the right knowledge can exploit this ray-system to produce effects at a distance — which is what magic is.

This theory had enormous influence on Latin natural philosophy and magic theory. Robert Grosseteste's metaphysics of light and optics drew on similar principles. Roger Bacon's theory of "multiplication of species" — the fundamental causal mechanism in his account of perception and celestial influence — is closely related. Thabit ibn Qurra's De imaginibus, which provides practical instructions for astrological image magic, presupposes al-Kindi's theoretical framework. David Pingree's analysis of al-Kindi's place in the tradition and Betsey Barker Price's work on the Latin reception of De radiis provide the scholarly context.

persons.name: Abu Ma'shar
persons.description: Ninth-century astrologer whose works shaped Latin astrology and the learned background for astral magic and image theory.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Abu Mashar al-Balkhi (787–886 CE) — known in Latin as Albumasar — was the most influential Islamic astrologer and astronomer of the ninth century, whose works became the primary channel through which Aristotelian cosmology and astrological theory were transmitted to the Latin West in the twelfth century. Born in Balkh (in modern Afghanistan), he moved to Baghdad, initially as a hadith scholar, and converted to astrology under the influence of al-Kindi. He spent most of his career in Baghdad, dying at the remarkable age of ninety-nine.

Works and Influence

Abu Mashar's Kitab al-madkhal al-kabir (Great Introduction to Astrology) — translated into Latin by Hermann of Carinthia in 1140 as Introductorium maius in astronomiam — provided the most systematic account available in the Latin West of the theoretical basis for astrology. The prologue, in which Abu Mashar argued that Aristotle himself had acknowledged celestial influence on terrestrial change, was enormously influential: it gave astrology a philosophical pedigree and made it appear as a straightforward application of Aristotelian natural philosophy. Roger Bacon cited Abu Mashar extensively in his arguments for the legitimacy of astrological enquiry.

Abu Mashar's De magnis coniunctionibus (On Great Conjunctions), translated by John of Seville, applied astrological theory to historical prophecy: the conjunctions of Jupiter and Saturn every twenty years, and of all planets at longer intervals, determined the rise and fall of religions, dynasties, and civilisations. This historico-astrological theory was taken up by medieval and Renaissance political astrologers and contributed to the tradition of prophetic astrology that intersected with learned magic. David Pingree's work on Abu Mashar's sources and influence provides the scholarly context.

persons.name: Adelard of Bath
persons.description: Twelfth-century translator and natural philosopher whose Arabic-Latin learning helped shape Latin debates about astrology, natural causality, and experiment.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Adelard of Bath (c.1080–c.1152) was an English natural philosopher and translator who made crucial early contributions to the transfer of Arabic natural philosophy and mathematics into Latin Europe. Born probably in Bath, he studied in Tours and Laon, then travelled extensively in southern Italy, Sicily, and probably the Arabic-speaking world (Antioch, possibly further east), learning Arabic and gaining access to the learned culture of the Islamic world before its full transmission to northern Europe. He returned to England and served at the court of the young King Henry II.

Translations and Natural Philosophy

Adelard's translations introduced foundational texts to the Latin West: Euclid's Elements (from Arabic, c.1120) in a translation that remained standard for centuries; al-Khwarizmi's astronomical tables (Zij); and Abu Mashar's Introductorium minus (the shorter introduction to astrology). His own Quaestiones naturales — a dialogue framed as a conversation with his nephew — introduced naturalistic explanations of a wide range of phenomena (why plants grow from seeds, why the sea is salty, how the senses work) that he attributed to "the Arabs," framing natural philosophy as the distinctive achievement of Arabic learning that Latin Europe lacked.

For the history of magic, Adelard is important as one of the earliest Latin conduits for Arabic astrological and natural magical theory, and for his methodological commitment to natural explanation: the Quaestiones naturales consistently seeks natural causes for apparently marvellous phenomena, prefiguring the naturalization strategies of Albertus Magnus and Roger Bacon. His translations of astronomical tables also enabled the precise timing of astrological and magical operations that the more sophisticated Latin magical tradition required.

persons.name: Hugh of Saint-Victor
persons.description: Twelfth-century theologian whose classifications of arts, knowledge, and illicit curiosity form part of the scholastic background for later treatments of magic.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Hugh of Saint-Victor (c.1096–1141) was the most important theologian and biblical exegete of the Parisian abbey of Saint-Victor, a house of Augustinian canons that was one of the principal intellectual centres of twelfth-century Europe. Born possibly in Saxony (his origins are uncertain), he spent his career at Saint-Victor, where he wrote an extraordinary range of works on theology, biblical exegesis, philosophy, and the classification of the arts and sciences.

The Didascalicon and the Classification of Magic

Hugh's Didascalicon de studio legendi (c.1120s) — a guide to reading and learning — contains the most systematic twelfth-century classification of the arts and sciences, including a treatment of the "mechanical arts" (practical skills) and, crucially, an account of the "adulterate arts" — divination and magic — that defined their status for subsequent generations. Hugh distinguished between legitimate inquiry into hidden natural causes (which he approved) and the arts that sought to penetrate the future or command spirits through illicit means (which he condemned). His taxonomy of divination — augury, auspicy, haruspicy, and various forms of sortilege — drew on Isidore but integrated it into a more philosophical framework.

For the history of magic, Hugh is important as an early twelfth-century voice insisting on the distinction between natural philosophy (which can study hidden causes) and magic (which transgresses into demonic territory). His classification influenced the subsequent scholastic discussion: the Victorine tradition's integration of natural inquiry with theological propriety provided one model for how learned magic could be discussed and evaluated within an orthodox framework. Richard Southern's Scholastic Humanism and the Unification of Europe and the relevant sections of Winthrop Wetherbee's work on twelfth-century Platonism provide the intellectual context.

persons.name: Bernard Silvester
persons.description: Twelfth-century intellectual associated with cosmological and astrological learning in the Latin schools, important for the learned background of celestial influence.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Bernardus Silvestris (Bernard Silvester, fl. c.1150) was a French scholar associated with the intellectual circle of Tours in the mid-twelfth century, most likely a master in the cathedral school there. He is best known for his Cosmographia (also called De mundi universitate, c.1147–1148), an elaborate allegorical cosmological work in mixed prose and verse (a prosimetrum) that narrates the creation and ordering of the universe through personified cosmic powers. His work is important for the history of magic because it transmits a specifically magical dimension of the twelfth-century Neoplatonic cosmology that influenced the subsequent learned magical tradition.

The Cosmographia and Natural Magic

The Cosmographia presents a Neoplatonic cosmology derived from Plato's Timaeus, Macrobius, Martianus Capella, and the Latin Asclepius, in which the universe is created and ordered by cosmic powers — Nous (Mind), Natura (Nature), and Physis (the lower world) — and in which the elemental world is permeated by a world-soul (Endelechia) that connects all things through sympathetic bonds. This framework — a living, intelligent cosmos pervaded by sympathetic connections — is precisely the theoretical basis for natural magic: if all things are connected through the world-soul's sympathies and antipathies, then operations that exploit these connections are natural philosophy rather than demonic practice.

The Cosmographia's presentation of astrology (the influence of the fixed stars and planets on terrestrial generation) and its treatment of the hidden properties of things as expressions of the world-soul's creative activity provided twelfth-century readers with a Neoplatonic framework for natural magic before the main wave of Arabic natural philosophical translation had reached northern France. Winthrop Wetherbee's work on the twelfth-century Platonists and the relevant sections of Brian Stock's Myth and Science in the Twelfth Century (1972) provide the intellectual context for Bernardus's place in the history of learned magic theory.

persons.name: Peter Abelard
persons.description: Twelfth-century theologian whose discussions of divination and astrology belong to earlier scholastic attempts to delimit illicit knowledge.
persons.bio_html:
Peter Abelard (1079–1142): Logic, Theology, and the Boundaries of Inquiry

Peter Abelard stands as one of the most intellectually combative and personally dramatic figures of the twelfth-century renaissance. Born near Nantes to a minor noble family that valued learning, Abelard abandoned his inheritance to pursue the new scholastic philosophy emerging in the cathedral schools of northern France. His mastery of logic—then the cutting edge of intellectual culture—brought him to Paris, where he challenged and defeated his teacher William of Champeaux in public disputation, establishing himself as the preeminent dialectician of his generation. His school at Mont Sainte-Geneviève drew students from across Europe, making him the most sought-after master of his era.

Abelard's contributions to the intellectual history relevant to magic and natural philosophy were primarily methodological. His Sic et Non (c. 1120) assembled contradictory authorities on 158 theological questions, demonstrating through sheer juxtaposition that received tradition required critical interpretation rather than passive reception—a method that empowered subsequent thinkers to subject natural phenomena, including magical claims, to rational scrutiny. His ethical philosophy, particularly his emphasis on intention as the determinant of moral character, had implications for assessments of magical practice: was an act sinful because of its external form or because of the practitioner's interior orientation toward demonic powers? This question would recur throughout later debates about the moral status of magical arts.

Abelard's turbulent life—his secret marriage to Heloise, his castration by her uncle's hired men, his subsequent monastic career, and his repeated condemnations at the Councils of Soissons (1121) and Sens (1140) at the instigation of Bernard of Clairvaux—made him a symbol of the tensions between intellectual innovation and ecclesiastical authority. Though not himself a practitioner or theorist of magic, his logical method and his willingness to subject theological tradition to critical analysis helped create the scholastic culture in which natural philosophy and demonological theory were elaborated with unprecedented rigor.

persons.name: Cecco d'Ascoli
persons.description: Fourteenth-century astrologer and poet whose condemnation and execution made him a key figure in debates over astrology, determinism, and forbidden knowledge.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Francesco Stabili, known as Cecco d'Ascoli (c.1257–1327), was an Italian astrologer, physician, and poet from Ascoli Piceno in the Marche, who became a professor of astrology at Bologna and physician to Charles of Calabria in Florence. He was burned at the stake in Florence on 16 September 1327 — the most dramatic example in the fourteenth century of a university-trained natural philosopher condemned for heretical astrological claims. His execution illustrates with unusual clarity the limits of what the medieval university could tolerate in the name of natural philosophy.

Works and Condemnation

Cecco's principal works are his commentary on John of Sacrobosco's De sphaera (a standard university astronomy text) and L'Acerba, a vernacular encyclopedic poem on cosmology, natural philosophy, and astrology that remained unfinished at his death. His commentary on the Sphaera was condemned at Bologna in 1324 for including discussions of astral determinism and related matters that the theological faculty found heretical: specifically, the claim that specific celestial configurations at the moment of Christ's conception and birth determined his nature and fate — a position that could be construed as denying the freedom of the Incarnation.

After his first condemnation (he was required to recant and fined), Cecco continued in his astrological work. His second condemnation, in Florence, was more severe: the inquisitor Accursio Bonfantini found him guilty of relapse into heresy and of affirming doctrines that effectively denied free will and reduced human affairs to celestial determination. Cecco was burned. His case is significant for the history of magic because it shows that astrological determinism — when applied to sacred history — could attract capital punishment even for a university-trained philosopher with noble patronage. Paola Zambelli's work on Cecco and the Florentine condemnation provides the most thorough scholarly analysis.

persons.name: Michael Scot
persons.description: Thirteenth-century translator, astrologer, and court intellectual associated with Arabic-Latin science and later magical reputation.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Michael Scot (c.1175–c.1232) was a Scottish scholar whose career exemplifies the role of the Arabic-Latin translator in transmitting Aristotelian and astrological learning to the Latin West. Educated probably in Oxford and Paris, he spent time in Toledo (where he learned Arabic) and eventually in Palermo at the court of Frederick II of Sicily — one of the most intellectually adventurous courts in medieval Europe. He served Frederick as court astrologer and intellectual advisor, and Dante placed him in the Inferno among the sorcerers (Inferno XX, 116), attributing to him magical knowledge that was almost certainly legendary.

Translations and Works

Michael's translations from Arabic into Latin were among the most important of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. He translated Averroes's (Ibn Rushd's) commentaries on Aristotle's natural philosophical works — the De caelo, De anima, De generatione et corruptione, and the zoological works — introducing the "Commentator" (Averroes's standard scholastic title) to Latin scholasticism. He also translated Aristotle's De animalibus directly from Arabic and Alpetragius's astronomical work De motibus celorum. These translations transformed Latin natural philosophy by making the Arabic Aristotelian commentaries available.

Michael's own works include an Introductorium (introduction to astrology and physiognomy), a Liber particularis (on physiognomy and astronomy), and a work on alchemy attributed to him. The reputation for magical knowledge that Dante attributes to him was built up in the Italian literary tradition and probably reflects the same tendency to ascribe occult knowledge to learned Arabic-Latin translators visible in the pseudo-Albertine literature: proximity to Arabic learning was construed as magical expertise. Charles Burnett's work on Michael Scot and the Toledo translation tradition provides the scholarly context.

persons.name: Marsilio Ficino
persons.description: Florentine philosopher, physician, and priest who directed Cosimo de' Medici's Platonic Academy and produced the first Latin translation of the Corpus Hermeticum (1463). Ficino's De Vita (1489), especially the third book De Vita Coelitus Comparanda, formulated an influential theory of stellar and spiritus magic drawing on Neoplatonism, astral medicine, and what he took to be ancient Hermetic wisdom. Frances Yates argued that Ficino inaugurated a distinctly Renaissance magical tradition; Frank Klaassen has argued the continuities with medieval learned magic are stronger than Yates recognized. D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic (1958) remains the standard treatment of Ficino's magical theory.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was born in Figline Valdarno, near Florence, the son of a physician who served the Medici. Cosimo de' Medici, recognizing the young scholar's promise, placed him under the tutelage of humanist teachers and eventually entrusted him with the translation of the newly acquired manuscripts of Plato and the Neoplatonists — a project that would occupy Ficino's entire career and reshape European intellectual life. Ficino spent most of his adult life at the Medici villa at Careggi, the nominal centre of what later scholars called the "Platonic Academy." He was ordained a priest in 1473, an event that introduced productive tensions between his philosophical commitments and his theological obligations that run through all his major works.

The Translation Project

Ficino's first major task, at Cosimo's urgent request, was to interrupt his Platonic translation project to render the newly arrived Corpus Hermeticum — fourteen Greek treatises attributed to Hermes Trismegistus — into Latin. This translation, completed in 1463 and circulated in manuscript before its 1471 printed edition, introduced the Hermetica to Latin Europe. Ficino accepted the traditional attribution: Hermes Trismegistus was, he believed, a real Egyptian sage of Mosaic antiquity, and the Hermetica preserved a primordial philosophical theology (prisca theologia) that anticipated Christian truth. This conviction structured his entire philosophical project: the recovery of ancient wisdom was also a preparation of pagan learning for Christian reception.

His translations of Plato's complete dialogues (1484), Plotinus's Enneads (1492), Iamblichus, Porphyry, Proclus, and Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite established Latin versions that remained standard for centuries. His commentaries — especially the Commentarium in Convivium Platonis de amore (1469, printed 1484) — transmitted Platonic philosophy in a form accessible to humanist readers across Europe.

Magia and De vita

The most controversial element of Ficino's intellectual production was the third book of his De vita trilogy, De vita coelitus comparanda (On Drawing Life from the Sky, 1489). Here Ficino outlined a system of therapeutic astral magic. The basis was Neoplatonic: the spiritus mundi, a subtle intermediary pervading the cosmos, linked the celestial bodies to all terrestrial things through bonds of sympathy and antipathy. A philosopher-physician — especially one of melancholic constitution (Saturn's children were the scholars and intellectuals) — could mitigate the excessive cold and dryness of Saturnine influence by attracting solar or Jovian spiritus through the use of appropriate materials: gold, amber, saffron, wine, images of the sun, solar music, exposure to sunlight and cheerful company.

D.P. Walker, in Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella (1958), was the first modern scholar to analyse this system in depth, arguing that it occupies an ambiguous position: Ficino consistently insisted that his magic operated through purely natural celestial causes, yet the Neoplatonic framework it drew on — especially from Iamblichus and Proclus — involved genuine spirit-working that could not easily be naturalised. Brian Copenhaver's subsequent work has been more sympathetic to Ficino's self-presentation as a natural philosopher, while acknowledging the philosophical instability of the position. The 1489 text caused Ficino genuine anxiety; he was investigated by the Florentine curia and appended a lengthy self-defence to subsequent editions.

Influence and Reception

Ficino's influence on the subsequent century of European thought was immense. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola absorbed and radicalised his synthesis, adding Christian Kabbalah. Lefèvre d'Étaples translated and promoted his work in France. Cornelius Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (1531) drew extensively on Ficino for its theory of the world-soul and elemental magic. John Colet in England and the German humanists engaged his Platonic commentaries. His influence on English Neoplatonism reached from the Cambridge Platonists of the seventeenth century to the Romantic poets.

For the history of magic specifically, the key secondary literature includes Brian Copenhaver's edition and translation of the Hermetica (1992) and his philosophical studies of Ficino's sources; D.P. Walker's foundational 1958 monograph; Michael Allen's work on Ficino's Platonic commentaries; and Stéphane Toussaint's studies of Ficino's natural magic and its reception.

persons.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
persons.description: Italian Renaissance philosopher who attempted to synthesize Christian theology, Neoplatonism, Hermeticism, and Jewish Kabbalah. His 900 Theses (1486) and Oration on the Dignity of Man presented magic as a natural science capable of uniting all human knowledge. Pope Innocent VIII condemned thirteen of his theses. Pico distinguished magia naturalis from goetia and was among the first Renaissance writers to incorporate Hebrew Kabbalah into a Christian magical synthesis. His early death in 1494 left his synthesis incomplete but enormously influential on Agrippa, Trithemius, Dee, and later Renaissance occultists.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was born into the ruling family of Mirandola in Emilia, studied canon law at Bologna, philosophy at Ferrara and Padua, and Arabic and Kabbalah in Florence and Perugia. He was a prodigy in multiple languages (Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, Aramaic) and in philosophy, and his short career — he died at thirty-one, possibly of poisoning, in the year the French invaded Italy — produced works of extraordinary ambition and originality. He was closely associated with Ficino's Florentine milieu but also a distinctly independent and more radical thinker.

The 900 Conclusiones and Christian Kabbalah

Pico's Conclusiones nongentae (900 Conclusions, 1486) — 900 theses drawn from ancient, medieval, and contemporary sources, including 72 Kabbalistic and 26 "magical" theses — were intended for a public debate in Rome that Pope Innocent VIII refused to permit. Thirteen of the theses were condemned as heretical; Pico fled to France, was arrested, and returned to Florence under Medici protection. The condemned theses included claims that Kabbalistic art confirmed the divinity of Christ and that no science demonstrates the resurrection more effectively than natural magic and Kabbalah.

Pico's contribution to the history of magic was twofold. First, he added Christian Kabbalah to the Renaissance occult synthesis as the highest form of magical technology: manipulating the Hebrew divine names and sefirot could accomplish what natural magic and astral magic could not, because it operated at the level of the divine intellectual world rather than the elemental or celestial. Second, his Oratio de dignitate hominis (Oration on the Dignity of Man, composed as a preface to the 1486 debate but not delivered) articulated the vision of the magus as the person who unites all the worlds within himself — elemental, celestial, intellectual — and thereby achieves a form of deification. This vision became the standard Renaissance image of the philosopher-magician.

Later Work

After his condemnation and pardon, Pico moved toward a more sceptical position on magic: his posthumously published Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem (Disputations against Divinatory Astrology, 1496) constitutes one of the most systematic Renaissance attacks on judicial astrology, anticipating many of the arguments that Kepler and later sceptics would make. His Heptaplus (1489) and De ente et uno (1492) represent a more orthodox Neoplatonist theology, less explicitly magical than the Conclusiones.

persons.name: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
persons.description: German polymath and lawyer who produced the most comprehensive Renaissance synthesis of occult philosophy. De Occulta Philosophia circulated in manuscript from c.1510 and was published in Cologne in expanded form (1531-1533). Agrippa drew on Ficino, Pico, Trithemius, and medieval magical sources to construct a three-tiered system of natural, celestial, and ceremonial magic. Klaassen has shown that Agrippa's third book draws directly on late medieval demonic and angelic magic manuscripts, undermining the clean break often claimed between medieval and Renaissance magic. He was at various times physician, courtier, legal scholar, and itinerant lecturer across Germany, France, and Italy.
persons.bio_html:
Life

Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535) was born in Cologne into a minor noble family. His education at the University of Cologne gave him the Latin learning and Scholastic philosophy that underpin his major works, while his subsequent wandering career — soldier, diplomat, court physician, lecturer, and perennial debtor — exposed him to the intellectual currents of humanist Italy, French and English royal courts, and the reform milieu of early German Lutheranism. He served in Maximilian I's campaigns in northern Italy around 1511, where contact with Italian Platonists (including possibly pupils of Ficino's circle) sharpened his interest in occult philosophy. He lectured on Reuchlin's Kabbalistic works at Dôle in 1509 and at a young age completed a first draft of his encyclopedic De occulta philosophia.

De occulta philosophia

The De occulta philosophia libri tres, first circulated in manuscript from 1510 onward and finally published in 1531 (Cologne, Soter), is the most comprehensive synthesis of Renaissance occult philosophy: a structured encyclopedia covering all three "worlds" of the Neoplatonic cosmos. Book I treats natural magic — the occult properties of things in the elemental world, the four elements, the harmony of the macrocosm and microcosm, the magical use of stones, plants, metals, animals, and numbers.
