These condemnations defined the institutional limits of scholastic enquiry into natural causation, celestial influence, and free will, directly shaping the context within which later medieval and Renaissance natural philosophers could discuss magical phenomena.

The Condemnations of 1270 and 1277

The 1270 condemnation targeted thirteen propositions associated with the "radical Aristotelianism" of Siger of Brabant and his associates, including the claim that the celestial intelligences (movers of the spheres) necessarily determine terrestrial events and that human will is subject to celestial causation. The 1277 condemnation, far broader at 219 theses, added propositions about the eternity of the world, the unity of the intellect, the knowability of future contingents through natural means, and numerous others.

For the history of magic, the most relevant condemned propositions are those concerning celestial determinism: the claim that the stars determine terrestrial events, including human choices and the course of history, is condemned. This condemnation did not eliminate astrological natural philosophy (which was too deeply embedded in medieval learned culture to be removed by episcopal decree) but it forced subsequent natural philosophers to be more careful in how they articulated the relationship between celestial influence and human free will. Since the theoretical basis of most image magic and astrological talismanic magic depended on some version of celestial determinism, the condemnations created pressure toward the naturalization of magical causation (explaining it through occult qualities rather than celestial determination).

Scholarship

The standard edition of the condemned theses is R. Hissette's Enquête sur les 219 articles condamnés à Paris le 7 mars 1277 (1977). For the implications for the history of magic, see Nicolas Weill-Parot's work on addressative image magic and the condemnations, and the relevant sections of Stuart Beaumont's Science and Religion in the Middle Ages (forthcoming). Luca Bianchi's Il vescovo e i filosofi (1990) provides the fullest analysis of the 1277 condemnation in context.
concepts.significance: University condemnation is an Analyst Term for institutional acts that classified, restricted, or prohibited suspect doctrines and practices, including astrology, image magic, and demonic arts.

concepts.label: Pastoral Care and Magic
concepts.definition_short: Pastoral care and magic names the confessional, preaching, and catechetical settings in which clergy identified charms, divination, and superstition as problems of Christian discipline.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Pastoral care and magic" designates the intersection between the institutional Church's programme of pastoral oversight — guiding lay Christians in proper religious practice — and the magical practices that pastoral handbooks, penitentials, and sermon literature consistently documented, condemned, and sometimes tacitly accommodated. The pastoral literature is one of the primary historical sources for knowledge of popular magical practice in medieval Europe, precisely because pastoral writers needed to know what practices existed in order to direct confessors to inquire about them and assign appropriate penances.

The Penitential Tradition

From the sixth century onward, penitential handbooks — guides for confessors listing sins and their appropriate penances — included sections on magical practices. Burchard of Worms's Decretum (c.1012), Book XIX (the Corrector sive Medicus), is the most comprehensive early medieval catalogue of popular magical practices for which penances were to be imposed: it covers charm-use, love magic, healing rituals, divination, weather-working, and many other practices, providing the most detailed window available into what popular magic actually consisted of in eleventh-century Germany. Similar material appears in Regino of Prüm's penitential (c.906) and in the penitentials of the insular tradition.

The later medieval tradition of sermon exempla — brief narratives used to illustrate moral points in preaching — provides another documentary layer: preachers recorded stories of magical practitioners (cunning folk, fortune-tellers, treasure-hunters) that give a sense of what their pastoral audiences knew and expected. Valerie Flint's The Rise of Magic in Early Medieval Europe (Princeton, 1991) analyses the pastoral literature's role in both condemning and accommodating popular magic. The essays in Don Bailey's and Catherine Rider's edited volumes extend this analysis to the later medieval period.
concepts.significance: Pastoral care and magic names the confessional, preaching, and catechetical settings in which clergy identified charms, divination, and superstition as problems of Christian discipline.

concepts.label: Pseudepigraphy
concepts.definition_short: Pseudepigraphy is an Analyst Term for attribution to authoritative figures such as Solomon, Honorius, Raziel, Aristotle, or Hermes; in grimoire studies it is a central mechanism of textual authority.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. Pseudepigraphy (from Greek pseudepigraphos, "falsely inscribed") designates the attribution of a text to an author who did not write it — a practice that, in the ancient and medieval worlds, served functions quite different from modern literary fraud. In the contexts most relevant to the history of magic, pseudepigraphic attribution to figures such as Solomon, Hermes Trismegistus, Aristotle (via the Secretum Secretorum), or Moses provided the attributed text with an authority it could not claim on its own merits: the antiquity, wisdom, royal power, or prophetic status of the named author transferred to the text and legitimated its contents.

Functions in the Magical Tradition

Solomonic pseudepigraphy is the most important instance in the history of the grimoire. Texts such as the Testament of Solomon, the Clavicula Salomonis, the Key of Solomon, the Lemegeton, and dozens of subsidiary texts claim to preserve the actual magical knowledge of the biblical king — the names and seals he used to bind demons in the construction of the Temple, the rings and pentacles with which he controlled spirits, the adjurations he taught to his sons or to Roboam. This attribution strategy accomplished several things simultaneously: it provided a pre-Christian, divinely sanctioned ancestry for procedures that might otherwise appear demonic; it anchored the text in biblical history, making its authority hard to dismiss without impugning Solomon himself; and it supplied the practitioner using the text with a vicarious identification with Solomon's royal, priestly authority.

Hermetic pseudepigraphy (attributing texts to Hermes Trismegistus) served parallel functions in the natural-philosophical magical tradition. The Corpus Hermeticum, the Asclepius, the Emerald Tablet, and the Picatrix all claim ancient Egyptian or Hermetic authority. The 1463 Ficinian translation of the Corpus Hermeticum launched a tradition that lasted until Casaubon's 1614 philological dating of the texts to the first three centuries CE.

Scholarship

Pablo Torijano's Solomon the Esoteric King (2002) is the primary analysis of Solomonic pseudepigraphy as a cross-cultural phenomenon. For Hermetic pseudepigraphy, Garth Fowden's The Egyptian Hermes (1986) and Brian Copenhaver's introduction to his Hermetica translation (1992) are foundational. John Monfasani has written on Aristotelian pseudepigraphy. For the broader phenomenon in late ancient and medieval literary culture, see Michael Stone, David Aune, and the entries in the standard encyclopedias of pseudepigraphy.
concepts.significance: Pseudepigraphy is an Analyst Term for attribution to authoritative figures such as Solomon, Honorius, Raziel, Aristotle, or Hermes; in grimoire studies it is a central mechanism of textual authority.

concepts.label: Ritual Diagrams
concepts.definition_short: Ritual diagrams are visual structures such as circles, notae, seals, tables, and figures that organize ritual knowledge and require attention to manuscript layout and copying.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. Ritual diagrams designate the visual-spatial components of learned magical practice: magic circles, geometric figures, planetary squares, spirit seals, and the elaborate composite images (the notae of the Ars Notoria, the pentacles of the Clavicula Salomonis) that constitute the visual dimension of the Solomonic and astrological magic traditions. Unlike the verbal components of magic (adjurations, divine names, prayers), ritual diagrams are spatial and graphical, existing on the boundary between text and image, between the language-like and the purely visual.

The Magic Circle

The magic circle — a drawn or marked circular space within which the practitioner stands during conjuration, inscribed with divine names, protective formulas, and/or spirit seals — is the most consistently required ritual diagram in the European learned magical tradition. It appears in the Munich Manual, the Clavicula Salomonis, the Heptameron, and virtually all practical demonic conjuration texts. The circle defines a protected space separated from the surrounding environment by its inscribed divine names; outside the circle, the conjured spirit must remain; within it, the practitioner is protected. The construction of the circle is typically elaborate and carefully prescribed.

The visual complexity of ritual diagrams varies enormously. The notae of the Ars Notoria are extremely intricate composite figures — surviving illustrated manuscripts show remarkable geometric complexity, with letter-forms, geometric patterns, and symbolic imagery combined in ways that require considerable draughtsmanship to reproduce. The pentacles of the Clavicula Salomonis are somewhat simpler but still require careful construction. Julien Véronèse's critical edition of the Ars Notoria (2007) includes analysis of the visual tradition; Sophie Page's work on magical manuscripts in institutional collections addresses the codicological significance of illustrated magical texts.
concepts.significance: Ritual diagrams are visual structures such as circles, notae, seals, tables, and figures that organize ritual knowledge and require attention to manuscript layout and copying.

concepts.label: Magical Alphabets
concepts.definition_short: Magical alphabets are nonordinary scripts and character systems used in ritual texts, amulets, and seals; they are visual technologies of secrecy, authority, and transmission.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. Magical alphabets are invented or adapted writing systems used in magical texts, either for writing divine names, spirit names, and magical words in a visually distinctive form, or for encrypting magical content so that it is not immediately legible to the uninitiated. The most famous examples associated with the Western learned magic tradition are the Theban script (attributed in late sources to Honorius of Thebes, though its actual origin is obscure), the Malachim script, the Passing of the River script, and the Enochian alphabet revealed to John Dee and Edward Kelley in 1583.

Function and Significance

Magical alphabets served multiple functions within the traditions that used them. First, they provided a visually distinctive form for divine and spirit names that emphasized their sacred or foreign character — using a non-standard script to write the name of an angel marks it as something other than ordinary language, imbuing it with the aura of esoteric knowledge. Second, they provided a degree of practical encryption: a text written in Theban or Malachim could not be read by someone who had not been taught the correspondence table, offering some protection from casual discovery.

Cornelius Agrippa's De occulta philosophia III includes tables of several magical alphabets with their Latin equivalents, presenting them as ancient or angelic scripts with intrinsic magical significance. The Enochian alphabet received by John Dee and Edward Kelley during their angel conversations (1583) was presented as the actual angelic language — the language in which God spoke to Adam before the Fall — and its letters carry specific phonological values and mystical associations documented in Dee's diaries. The subsequent ceremonial magic tradition (Golden Dawn, Thelema) has elaborated the Enochian system extensively, using the alphabet in ritual practice.
concepts.significance: Magical alphabets are nonordinary scripts and character systems used in ritual texts, amulets, and seals; they are visual technologies of secrecy, authority, and transmission.

concepts.label: Planetary Spirits
concepts.definition_short: Planetary spirits are named intelligences, angels, or demons associated with planets in ritual and astral texts, linking astrology to invocation and image practice.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Hybrid Term. Planetary spirits designate the intelligent beings — neither fully material nor fully divine — that Renaissance Neoplatonism and the astrological magic tradition posited as intermediaries between the celestial bodies (as physical objects) and their effects on terrestrial life. In the Neoplatonic hierarchy, each planet is governed by an intelligence (intelligentia) that moves it and by a spirit (spiritus) that conveys its influence to the sublunary world. The magic of Ficino, Agrippa, and the Picatrix tradition engages with these planetary spirits as potential partners in magical operation.

Theory

The doctrine of planetary spirits derives from the Neoplatonic account of the celestial hierarchy: Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus all discussed the daemons associated with the planets as intermediary beings between the divine intellect and material creation. In the Arabic astrological tradition, each planet was associated with an intelligence (a governing rational being) and a spirit (an executive power), whose cooperation could be secured through appropriate ritual — the right materials, timing, images, prayers, and fumigations specified by texts like the Picatrix and Thabit ibn Qurra's De imaginibus. Agrippa's De occulta philosophia II provides the standard Renaissance account, connecting the planetary intelligences to specific divine names and the planetary spirits to the camea (magic squares) of each planet.

The theological problem was the same as with all astrological magic: were the planetary spirits simply natural forces (and therefore exploitable within natural philosophy) or personal, rational agents (and therefore addressative magic that required explicit invocation and risked demonic cooperation)? Nicolas Weill-Parot's analysis of addressative magic identifies this question as the central contested point of scholastic astrological magic theory. The Renaissance resolution — treating planetary spirits as aspects of the natural celestial mechanism rather than as personal beings — was philosophically unstable but practically necessary for maintaining the claim to natural philosophy.
concepts.significance: Planetary spirits are named intelligences, angels, or demons associated with planets in ritual and astral texts, linking astrology to invocation and image practice.

concepts.label: Secret Names
concepts.definition_short: Secret names are divine, angelic, demonic, or voces magicae names whose ritual force is tied to secrecy, antiquity, revelation, or exact textual transmission.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. Secret names, in the context of medieval and Renaissance magic, designates the hidden or powerful names of God, angels, and demons that, when known and correctly pronounced or written, confer authority over the corresponding being or unlock specific magical powers. The concept is common to Jewish Kabbalah (the hidden names of God, the Tetragrammaton, the seventy-two names derived from Exodus 14), the Greek magical papyri (sequences of divine names including IAO, SABAOTH, ADONAI), and the Latin Solomonic tradition (the divine names inscribed on pentacles and spoken in conjuration formulas).

Theoretical Basis

The power of divine names in the magical tradition rests on several converging doctrines. In the Kabbalistic framework, the Hebrew letters of the Torah — especially the divine names — are not arbitrary signs but the actual creative words through which God made the world; knowing and manipulating them gives the adept access to creative power. In the Platonic tradition, names are not merely conventional but connected to the natures of things; the divine name participates in the divine nature it designates. In the Hermetic tradition, names are the handles by which the pneumatic world is manipulated; the magician who knows the true name of a spirit has power over it because names and natures are identical at the level of the world-soul.

The Solomonic grimoires exploit this doctrine systematically: each conjuration formula invokes a sequence of divine names (Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and invented) as compelling forces, and each spirit seal incorporates the spirit's name in a form that both identifies and binds it. The Enochian system received by Dee and Kelley represents the tradition's most elaborate development: an entire constructed language in which every word carries sacred power because the language itself is the original Adamic tongue in which God created. Agrippa's De occulta philosophia III, chapters on the sacred names, provides the most systematic Renaissance account.
concepts.significance: Secret names are divine, angelic, demonic, or voces magicae names whose ritual force is tied to secrecy, antiquity, revelation, or exact textual transmission.

concepts.label: Experimental Science
concepts.definition_short: Experimental science is an Analyst Term especially associated with older histories such as Thorndike's, where magic and experiment are studied as intertwined medieval attempts to test, command, or explain nature.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term (Roger Bacon's scientia experimentalis) and Analyst Term. Roger Bacon coined the term scientia experimentalis in the Opus maius (c.1267) to designate the highest branch of natural philosophy — the science that verifies the conclusions of the other sciences through direct experience and produces the most powerful practical effects from knowledge of nature's hidden causes. The relationship between Bacon's experimental science and magic is both close and contested: Bacon explicitly naturalized many phenomena that others attributed to magic, arguing that they resulted from natural processes accessible to careful investigation.

Bacon's Programme

Part VI of the Opus maius on scientia experimentalis identifies three prerogatives of experimental knowledge: it certifies the conclusions of the other sciences (only experience can confirm or refute theory); it adds new discoveries not available through syllogistic reasoning; and it produces marvellous arts that may seem magical to the uninitiated. This third prerogative — the production of wonders through natural knowledge — directly overlaps with natural magic: Bacon mentions the possibility of explosive powder (anticipating gunpowder), optical instruments that magnify distant objects, ships that move without oarsmen, and flying machines, all as products of experimental science rather than magic.

Bacon's stance on actual demonic magic was unambiguous: he condemned it as inferior to true natural knowledge because it depended on deceptive spiritual agents rather than genuine understanding of causes. But his naturalization of many apparently magical phenomena — through his theory of multiplication of species (the mechanism of celestial influence), his optics, and his account of the imagination's power — substantially expanded the domain of what natural philosophy could claim.

Historiographical Significance

Lynn Thorndike's History of Magic and Experimental Science (1923–1958) treated Bacon as a key figure in the gradual separation of experimental science from magic. David Lindberg's subsequent work on Bacon's optics and natural philosophy has provided a more nuanced account of his theoretical framework and its dependence on Arabic sources (Alhazen, al-Kindi). The relationship between Bacon's programme and early modern experimental science is debated: he had no direct institutional successors, and his practical programme was not realized until long after his death.
concepts.significance: Experimental science is an Analyst Term especially associated with older histories such as Thorndike's, where magic and experiment are studied as intertwined medieval attempts to test, command, or explain nature.

concepts.label: Natural Powers
concepts.definition_short: Natural powers names medieval attempts to explain unusual effects through created nature rather than demonic pact, a key boundary zone between natural philosophy and magic.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor and Analyst Term. "Natural powers" designates the hidden causal properties of things — primarily stones, plants, metals, and animals — that produce effects exceeding ordinary elemental analysis but operating through natural, not demonic, causation. The concept is central to the naturalistic defence of learned magic: if unusual effects can be attributed to occult natural properties, they do not require demonic assistance and are therefore potentially licit.

The Theory of Occult Properties

The Aristotelian tradition acknowledged "specific form" and "specific virtue" as causal properties of things that could not be reduced to the four elements and their qualities. Avicenna's medical philosophy elaborated a systematic account of occult properties in stones and plants, transmitted to Latin Europe through the twelfth-century translations of his Canon of Medicine. Albertus Magnus's De mineralibus (c.1262) applied this framework to the virtues of stones: a stone's occult property is impressed on it by the celestial body dominant at the moment of its formation, and this property persists and acts in ways analogous to a form, producing effects (healing, protection, influence) through purely natural causation.

Thomas Aquinas's short treatise De occultis operibus naturae (On the Occult Works of Nature), addressed to a soldier, argues against those who too hastily attribute unusual natural effects to demonic agency: many things in nature have properties that exceed ordinary explanation but operate through genuine natural causation. The magnet, the loadstone, the medicinal properties of specific herbs, the effects of celestial configurations on terrestrial generation — all are natural phenomena, however marvellous.

Magic and Natural Powers

The category of natural powers provided the primary resource for defenders of natural magic. If a talisman's effect can be attributed to the natural occult properties of its material combined with the natural influence of the planetary configuration under which it was made, it requires no demonic assistance and is therefore licit. This argument was deployed by the author of the Speculum astronomiae, by Ficino in De vita coelitus comparanda, and by della Porta in Magia naturalis, with varying degrees of philosophical sophistication and varying success in convincing theological critics.
concepts.significance: Natural powers names medieval attempts to explain unusual effects through created nature rather than demonic pact, a key boundary zone between natural philosophy and magic.

concepts.label: Prohibited Arts
concepts.definition_short: Prohibited arts is a hybrid category for practices forbidden by theological, legal, university, or pastoral authorities, including forms of divination, image magic, spirit invocation, and suspect astrology.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term (Latin: artes prohibitae; also artes vetitae, artes damnabiles, artes illicitae). The prohibited arts is the standard medieval category for magical, divinatory, and related practices condemned by canon law, theological teaching, and ecclesiastical authority. The category is defined negatively — by what the Church forbids — and its contents are relatively stable across the medieval period, derived primarily from Isidore of Seville's taxonomy in Etymologiae VIII.9 and codified in Gratian's Decretum.

Content of the Category

The prohibited arts typically include: necromancy (demonic conjuration); geomancy, pyromancy, hydromancy, and aeromancy (elemental divination); chiromancy (palmistry); augury and auspicy (divination from birds and natural signs); haruspicy (divination from entrails); astrology in its judicial form (predicting individual futures from horoscopes, as distinct from the legitimate natural science of astronomy); sortilege (divination by lot); and various forms of charm-use and image magic. The precise list varies between authorities — Isidore's taxonomy was the standard reference, but it was expanded and reorganized by subsequent writers including Rabanus Maurus, Johannes Hartlieb, and the authors of the late medieval magic classification treatises.

The boundary between the prohibited arts and legitimate natural philosophy was never definitively established. Natural magic — the use of occult natural properties without demonic assistance — occupied an ambiguous position: it was not straightforwardly included in the prohibited arts (since it claimed natural rather than demonic causation) but it was not clearly excluded either (since the claim to purely natural operation was philosophically contested). The negotiation of this boundary was the central intellectual task of scholastic magic theory from the twelfth century onward. Johannes Hartlieb's Buch aller verbotenen Kunst (c.1456) provides the most accessible vernacular account of the prohibited arts in their late medieval formulation.
concepts.significance: Prohibited arts is a hybrid category for practices forbidden by theological, legal, university, or pastoral authorities, including forms of divination, image magic, spirit invocation, and suspect astrology.

concepts.label: Mathematical Arts
concepts.definition_short: Mathematical arts refers to quadrivial and astral disciplines, especially astrology, whose learned status made their relation to divination and magic especially contested.
concepts.definition_long:
Mathematical Arts: Arithmetic, Geometry, and Their Occult Extensions

The mathematical arts—arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy, constituting the quadrivium of the medieval university curriculum—occupied an ambiguous position in discussions of magic and natural philosophy. On one hand, these disciplines represented the highest form of rational inquiry into natural order, foundational to both scholastic education and practical sciences such as surveying, medicine, and calendar calculation. On the other hand, the manipulation of number, figure, and proportion carried persistent associations with divination, astrological prediction, and the secret operations of nature that troubled ecclesiastical authorities and generated accusations of demonic involvement.

Arithmetic magic took several forms. Numerological speculation—the attribution of sacred or cosmic significance to specific numbers—pervaded both biblical commentary and practical magical texts. The divine names in Hebrew were subjected to gematria (letter-number equivalences), yielding numerical values thought to encode cosmic secrets. Magical squares (kamea), arrangements of numbers summing equally in all directions, were associated with planetary powers and inscribed on amulets. Geometry entered magical practice through the construction of ritual diagrams, circles, triangles, and pentagrams believed to bind or channel spiritual forces. The Ars Notoria's elaborate notae blended geometric form with sacred inscription, while the grimoire tradition prescribed precise geometrical configurations for spirit-summoning circles.

The condemnation of divinatory mathematics—geomancy, pyromancy, and related arts—by authorities from Isidore of Seville to Etienne Tempier's 1277 Paris condemnations reflected anxiety about the slippage between licit mathematical inquiry and illicit prophetic or demonic knowledge. Thinkers like Roger Bacon sought to rehabilitate mathematical sciences by grounding them in natural causation: the influence of celestial configurations on terrestrial matter was, in his account, a subject for natural philosophy rather than superstition. Nicole Oresme's critiques of astrology similarly attempted to police the boundary between legitimate mathematical astronomy and its astrological extensions. These debates established the contested epistemological terrain within which Renaissance figures like John Dee would pursue ambitious programs uniting mathematics, natural philosophy, and spiritual communication.
concepts.significance: Mathematical arts refers to quadrivial and astral disciplines, especially astrology, whose learned status made their relation to divination and magic especially contested.

concepts.label: Licit and Illicit Knowledge
concepts.definition_short: Licit and illicit knowledge is an Analyst Term for medieval debates over what could be known through nature, revelation, experiment, stars, demons, or ritual practice.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Licit and illicit knowledge" designates the boundary that medieval and early modern intellectual culture drew between forms of inquiry that were permissible within Christian orthodoxy and forms that were condemned as superstition, demonic magic, or presumptuous curiosity. The boundary was not fixed: it was actively contested by natural philosophers, theologians, practitioners, and inquisitors throughout the medieval period, and its shifting location is a major theme in the historiography of medieval magic and natural philosophy.

The Boundary in Theological Thought

The primary theological tool for drawing the boundary was Augustine's analysis of superstitio as giving to creatures what belongs to God, refined by Aquinas's systematic treatment in Summa theologiae II-II, qq. 92–96. Any inquiry that presupposed demonic assistance — whether explicitly (through conjuration) or implicitly (through using means that could only work through demonic power) — was illicit. Inquiry into natural causes, however hidden, was in principle licit: the philosopher who studied the occult properties of stones, the mechanism of celestial influence, or the hidden sympathies connecting distant things was pursuing legitimate knowledge, provided the operations he derived from that knowledge did not require demonic cooperation.

The practical negotiation of this boundary was complex and context-dependent. The same text (the Picatrix, for instance) could be read as natural philosophy (by a university-trained natural philosopher interested in celestial influence theory) or as demonic magic (by an inquisitor applying the condemnation of divination and spirit-working). The same operation (a talisman made under a specific planetary configuration) could be defended as natural magic or condemned as demonic image magic depending on whether it explicitly addressed planetary spirits as personal agents.

Scholarly Framework

Richard Kieckhefer's Magic in the Middle Ages (1989) provides the clearest account of how the boundary was negotiated in medieval learned culture. Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic (2013) traces how the boundary shifted across two centuries in the English manuscript tradition. Nicolas Weill-Parot's concept of addressative magic provides the most precise analytical tool for locating where specific operations fall relative to the licit/illicit boundary in the context of astrological image magic.
concepts.significance: Licit and illicit knowledge is an Analyst Term for medieval debates over what could be known through nature, revelation, experiment, stars, demons, or ritual practice.

concepts.label: Demonology
concepts.definition_short: Demonology is an Analyst Term for systematic learned discussion of demons, their powers, limitations, deception, and relation to divination, magic, superstition, and witchcraft.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Hybrid Term. Demonology designates both the historical study of demons conducted by theologians, philosophers, and learned magicians (actor-usage: the discipline of knowing demons) and the modern scholarly subdiscipline that studies such historical accounts (analyst-usage). In the medieval and early modern periods, demonology was a serious theological enterprise with practical stakes: if demons were real, what were their powers and limitations? Could they create genuine effects or only illusions? Could they be compelled by human art? These questions bore directly on the legal and theological assessment of magic, witchcraft, and popular protective ritual.

Historical Development

Christian demonology inherited a complex legacy from Jewish angelology, Neoplatonic daemon theory, and Pauline pneumatology. Augustine of Hippo's treatment of demons in De civitate Dei (VIII–X) and De divinatione daemonum established the foundational claims: demons are real, fallen angels with limited but genuine causal powers; they can appear to predict the future because they have better sensory equipment and faster movement than humans; they can cause apparent wonders but not true miracles; and all traffic with demons — even seemingly beneficial consultation — is illicit because it involves worship of beings other than God.

Medieval scholastic demonology elaborated this framework. Thomas Aquinas's Summa theologiae (especially the Treatise on Angels in the Prima Pars and the discussion of superstition in Secunda secundae qq. 92–96) provided the authoritative synthesis: demons are intellectual substances, created good but fallen through pride; their powers are real but limited by divine permission; they can affect material things (weather, disease, illusion) but cannot override free will or create genuine miracles. This framework licensed a highly specific taxonomy: natural effects (even extraordinary ones) remained within the domain of natural philosophy; genuinely miraculous effects belonged to God; demonic effects occupied a middle category of apparent wonder or praestigium.

The witch trials of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries generated a new genre of demonological treatise — from the Malleus Maleficarum (1486) through Bodin's Démonomanie des sorciers (1580), Remy's Demonolatreiae (1595), and del Rio's Disquisitionum magicarum (1599–1600) — that elaborated the concept of the demonic pact and the witches' sabbath as legal and theological categories. These texts are less concerned with the learned magical tradition (with which they overlap) than with the prosecution of popular magic understood as diabolical alliance.

Scholarly Resources

Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons: The Idea of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe (1997) provides the fullest analysis of early modern demonological thought as an intellectual system. Michael Bailey's Battling Demons (2003) traces the construction of the witch-sabbath concept in the fifteenth century. For the scholastic tradition, see Jan Machielsen (ed.), The Science of Demons: Early Modern Authors Facing Witchcraft and the Devil (2020). For ancient and Jewish demonology, Gideon Bohak and the relevant sections of Philip Alexander's work remain essential.
concepts.significance: Demonology is an Analyst Term for systematic learned discussion of demons, their powers, limitations, deception, and relation to divination, magic, superstition, and witchcraft.

concepts.label: Witchcraft
concepts.definition_short: Witchcraft is an Analyst Term for accusations, learned demonological categories, and late medieval constructions of harmful magic; it must be distinguished from ritual manuscripts and from broader categories of learned magic.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Hybrid Term. "Witchcraft" in scholarly usage designates both the historical belief — widely documented across cultures — that certain persons can cause harm (maleficium) through supernatural means, and the specific late medieval and early modern elaboration of that belief into the concept of the diabolical witch: a person who has made an explicit pact with the Devil, attends nocturnal sabbaths, engages in infanticide and cannibalism, and systematically inverts Christian religious practice. These two senses are related but distinct; conflating them distorts the history of both.

Maleficium and the Common Tradition

The older, more cross-culturally widespread belief involves maleficium (harmful magic): the attribution of disease, crop failure, livestock death, and other misfortune to the hostile magical action of a neighbour or enemy. This belief — documented in Roman law, early medieval canon law collections, and throughout medieval pastoral literature — constitutes the "common tradition" of popular magic in Kieckhefer's framework. The practitioner accused of maleficium need not be conceptualized as a Satanic witch; accusations of maleficium are structurally similar to accusations of witchcraft in non-Christian societies and do not inherently involve diabolism.

The Construction of the Diabolical Witch

The concept of the diabolical witch — the specific demonological construct that drove the major witch trials of the fifteenth through seventeenth centuries — was a learned, clerical construction. Michael Bailey's Battling Demons (2003) traces its emergence in the early fifteenth century from the confluence of three elements: the inquisitorial prosecution of heresy (which provided the concept of diabolical conspiracy), the pastoral concern with maleficium and popular magic, and the learned demonology of scholastic theology. The Malleus Maleficarum (1486) codified the construct: the witch explicitly renounces Christianity, makes a pact with the Devil, attends the sabbath, and performs maleficia through demonic power.

Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons (1997) analyses early modern demonological writing as an internally coherent intellectual system rather than as mere superstition. Richard Kieckhefer's work, Richard Gordon's studies, and the essays collected in Bengt Ankarloo and Stuart Clark (eds.), Witchcraft and Magic in Europe (6 vols., Athlone/Penn State, 1999–2002), provide comprehensive coverage.
concepts.significance: Witchcraft is an Analyst Term for accusations, learned demonological categories, and late medieval constructions of harmful magic; it must be distinguished from ritual manuscripts and from broader categories of learned magic.

concepts.label: Exorcism
concepts.definition_short: Exorcism names authorized Christian rites and adjacent ritual practices for expelling or commanding spirits, making it a boundary category between liturgy, pastoral care, and ritual magic.
concepts.definition_long:
Exorcism: Ecclesiastical Authority and the Expulsion of Evil Spirits

Exorcism—the formal expulsion of demonic presences from persons, places, or objects through authorized ritual speech and action—occupied a complex position in medieval religious and magical culture. As an official sacramental rite performed by ordained clergy, exorcism belonged squarely within the legitimate institutional apparatus of the Church. The minor order of exorcist existed as a formal clerical grade, and episcopal liturgical books provided standardized formulae for the expulsion of demons from catechumens, the blessing of water and salt, and the healing of possessed individuals. Yet the same conceptual framework that legitimized ecclesiastical exorcism also underwrote a vast popular and semi-learned tradition of protective and healing rituals that ecclesiastical authorities viewed with deep suspicion.

The theological rationale for exorcism rested on patristic and scriptural foundations: Christ's own expulsions of demons in the Gospels established both the reality of demonic possession and the efficacy of divine authority wielded through proper agents. Augustine's demonology, refined through centuries of scholastic commentary, held that demons were real spiritual entities subject to divine command but capable of harming humans through permitted affliction. Aquinas and his contemporaries elaborated sophisticated accounts of demonic psychology and the mechanisms by which adjuration, prayer, and the invocation of sacred names could compel compliance. This theoretical apparatus simultaneously supported official exorcism and provided conceptual resources for practitioners of learned magic who appropriated the same command-idiom in their conjuration texts.

The boundary between legitimate exorcism and illicit conjuration was perpetually contested. Critics like William of Auvergne and Jean Gerson drew attention to the structural similarity between the Church's own rites and the formulae in condemned magical texts: both employed divine names, commanded spirits in the name of Christ and the Trinity, and claimed angelic assistance. The grimoire tradition extensively borrowed ecclesiastical ritual forms—the Sworn Book of Honorius and the Munich Manual both drew on exorcistic prayer conventions—producing texts that their compilers may have regarded as extensions of legitimate clerical power rather than demonic trafficking. This ambiguity persisted into the early modern period, when debates over witchcraft, possession, and exorcistic authority became entangled with confessional conflicts between Protestants and Catholics.
concepts.significance: Exorcism names authorized Christian rites and adjacent ritual practices for expelling or commanding spirits, making it a boundary category between liturgy, pastoral care, and ritual magic.

concepts.label: Hydromancy
concepts.definition_short: Hydromancy is an Actor Term for divination by water, frequently named in medieval taxonomies of forbidden divination and often treated as suspect because of its association with spirit mediation.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. Hydromancy (from Greek hydor, water, and manteia, divination) is divination through water — reading visions or omens in a bowl, basin, pool, or other water surface. It is one of the four classical elemental divinations alongside geomancy, pyromancy, and aeromancy, appearing in standard medieval taxonomies of the prohibited arts. Historical forms of hydromantic practice ranged from catoptromancy (reading reflections in a polished surface) through scrying in water basins to divination by the behaviour of objects cast into water.

Medieval Examples

John of Salisbury's Policraticus (c.1159) provides a remarkable first-person account (I.11) of what appears to be a hydromantic or catoptromantic procedure: as a boy, John was used by a priest who attempted to see visions in a polished nail or water basin, seeking the appearance of demons or divine figures. John found the experience unproductive and disturbing, and his account provides unusually direct testimony from someone who participated in such a procedure. The Munich Manual contains procedures for divination through water and polished surfaces alongside its more explicit demonic conjuration material.

Scrying in crystals, polished stones, or water basins was closely related to hydromancy and was the basis of John Dee's angel communications: Edward Kelley gazed into a crystal "shewstone" to receive the Enochian messages. The practice of crystal-gazing (crystallomancy) was a direct descendant of the hydromantic tradition, and the crystal ball of modern popular imagination derives ultimately from this medieval and early modern practice of reflective surface scrying.
concepts.significance: Hydromancy is an Actor Term for divination by water, frequently named in medieval taxonomies of forbidden divination and often treated as suspect because of its association with spirit mediation.

concepts.label: Pyromancy
concepts.definition_short: Pyromancy is an Actor Term for divination by fire, appearing in medieval lists of mantic arts and classifications of illicit knowledge.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. Pyromancy (from Greek pyros, fire, and manteia, divination) is divination through fire or flame — reading omens in the movement, colour, and behaviour of flames, or casting objects into fire and interpreting the results. It is one of the classical four elemental divination types (alongside geomancy from earth, hydromancy from water, and aeromancy from air) that appear in standard medieval taxonomies of the forbidden arts, including Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae and Johannes Hartlieb's Buch aller verbotenen Kunst.

Historical Context

Pyromancy was consistently condemned in the canonical medieval taxonomy of the prohibited arts, though it is the rarest of the four elemental divinations in surviving practical magical texts. Fire-based divination in ancient practice ranged from reading the behaviour of sacrificial fires (a form of haruspicy) through casting laurel branches, beans, or other substances into flames and observing the results. In medieval contexts, pyromantic procedures appear occasionally in magical miscellanies — readings of candle-flames, interpretation of burning substances in ritual contexts — alongside other divinatory techniques.

Unlike geomancy, which developed a systematic and widely taught divinatory method in the medieval Islamic and Latin worlds, pyromancy does not appear to have generated an equivalent technical literature. Its appearance in the canonical lists of forbidden arts reflects its ancient reputation as a divinatory practice rather than its medieval vitality as a learned system. Johannes Hartlieb's brief treatment in the Buch aller verbotenen Kunst (c.1456) is typical: he mentions pyromancy as one of the seven forbidden arts without providing any practical details, suggesting he is following the traditional taxonomy rather than describing a living practice he has personally encountered.
concepts.significance: Pyromancy is an Actor Term for divination by fire, appearing in medieval lists of mantic arts and classifications of illicit knowledge.

concepts.label: Sortilege
concepts.definition_short: Sortilege is an Actor Term for divination by lots, books, or chance procedures, treated variously as superstition, clerical misuse, or illicit inquiry into hidden things.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term (from Latin sors, lot, and legere, to choose). Sortilege is divination by the casting of lots — the use of random or apparently random procedures (dice, marked sticks, cards, the random opening of a book) to generate an answer to a question or guidance for a decision. It is one of the oldest and most cross-culturally widespread divinatory practices, attested from ancient Mesopotamia (the casting of clay tablets) through the Roman sortes Vergilianae (divination from randomly opened passages of Virgil) and the medieval sortes sanctorum (divination from randomly opened Scripture or liturgical books).

Medieval Practice and Condemnation

Sortilege was consistently condemned in medieval canon law as a form of divination forbidden by Scripture (Acts 1:26, the casting of lots to choose Matthias, was treated as a one-time divinely sanctioned exception, not a model for general practice) and by the patristic tradition. Penitentials from the sixth century onward prescribed penances for various forms of sortilege. The canonical condemnation, transmitted through Gratian's Decretum, was clear. Nevertheless, the practice was widespread: lot-casting appeared in ecclesiastical contexts (choosing among candidates for office, dividing property), in medical contexts (determining lucky or unlucky days for treatment), and in popular magical contexts (answering questions about thieves, lost property, or future marriages).

The sortes sanctorum — divination by randomly opening Scripture — occupied a particularly ambiguous position: it used a sacred object (the Bible) and invoked divine providence rather than demonic assistance, making it hard to condemn straightforwardly. Some churchmen tolerated it as a pious appeal to God's guidance; others condemned it as presuming to direct divine power toward trivial ends. The theological debate over whether apparently random events could serve as vehicles for divine communication was never definitively resolved.

Scholarship

Michael Clanchy's work on medieval literacy and Don Skemer's Binding Words (2006) both touch on sortilege in the context of written and material divination. For the broader theological debate, see the relevant sections of Kieckhefer's Magic in the Middle Ages and Bailey's Magic and Superstition in Europe.
concepts.significance: Sortilege is an Actor Term for divination by lots, books, or chance procedures, treated variously as superstition, clerical misuse, or illicit inquiry into hidden things.

concepts.label: Notae
concepts.definition_short: Notae are the visual signs or figures central to Ars Notoria traditions of ritual learning, requiring attention to diagrammatic transmission as well as verbal prayer.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term (Latin plural, singular: nota). In the context of the Ars Notoria tradition, notae (notes or marks) designates the elaborate geometric and symbolic figures that serve as the visual components of the Notory Art's system of knowledge-acquisition. Each nota is a complex composite image — combining geometric shapes, letter-forms, and symbolic elements — that the practitioner contemplates while reciting the associated prayers (orationes) and that is believed, through divine grace and angelic mediation, to facilitate the infusion of specific knowledge (a particular liberal art, a language, a virtue).

Form and Function

The notae of the Ars Notoria vary considerably across manuscript traditions: the illustrated manuscripts show figures of remarkable complexity and visual interest, while many copies of the text were made without the figures (or with simplified schematic versions), suggesting that the practice could be adapted to different material conditions. The figures associated with the seven liberal arts are the most consistently represented; additional notae address practical knowledge, languages, theological understanding, and spiritual states.

The theoretical role of the notae is explained in various ways across the tradition. Some texts suggest they function as focal points for contemplation — looking at the figure while reciting the prayer concentrates the practitioner's attention. Others imply a more direct efficacy: the figure itself channels angelic or divine power. Thomas Aquinas's condemnation of the Ars Notoria (Summa theologiae II-II, q. 96, a. 1) turned partly on the notae and the Greek voces magicae in the prayers: because they bear no natural relationship to the knowledge they are supposed to produce, their claimed efficacy presupposes demonic rather than natural or divine causation. Julien Véronèse's critical edition of the Ars Notoria (2007) provides the most thorough analysis of the notae tradition; Claire Fanger's work on John of Morigny shows how one practitioner responded to and revised the figure-system under visionary guidance.
concepts.significance: Notae are the visual signs or figures central to Ars Notoria traditions of ritual learning, requiring attention to diagrammatic transmission as well as verbal prayer.

concepts.label: Confession
concepts.definition_short: Confession is a sacramental and pastoral context in which medieval clergy identified charms, divination, superstition, and illicit ritual practices as matters of correction.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term in a specific magical context. In the ritual magic tradition, "confession" (Latin: confessio) refers to the requirement — standard in most Solomonic grimoires — that the practitioner confess his sins to a priest and receive absolution before undertaking a major magical operation. This requirement is part of the broader ritual purity regime that Solomonic magic imposes on its practitioner: fasting, prayer, abstention from sexual activity, clean vestments, and sacramental confession are all prerequisites for the major conjurations of the Clavicula Salomonis, the Sworn Book of Honorius, and similar texts.

Theological Significance

The confession requirement is theologically anomalous: it incorporates a core sacramental practice of the Church into a magical procedure that the same Church condemned. This incorporation serves multiple functions. Practically, it aligns the magical operation with orthodox religious practice, making it harder to condemn as straightforwardly impious: a practitioner who has confessed and received absolution has satisfied the Church's standard requirements for receiving the sacraments. Theologically, it positions the conjuration within the framework of Christian devotion — the practitioner approaches the spirits as a purified Christian, not as a pagan or a demon-worshipper.

Frank Klaassen's analysis of how Solomonic magic aligned itself with Christian devotional categories — confession, prayer, fasting, Mass attendance — is the most thorough account of this strategy. The strategy was not merely cosmetic: practitioners seem to have genuinely understood their operations as extensions of legitimate Christian practice, operating within the divine order rather than against it. The spirits they conjured were bound by divine authority (invoked in the conjuration formulas), the procedures were conducted under divine oversight (the preparatory prayers), and the purposes were at least nominally legitimate (protecting the practitioner, acquiring knowledge, serving a patron). Whether the Church would have agreed is a different question.
concepts.significance: Confession is a sacramental and pastoral context in which medieval clergy identified charms, divination, superstition, and illicit ritual practices as matters of correction.

concepts.label: Secret of Secrets
concepts.definition_short: Secret of Secrets refers to the Secretum Secretorum tradition and its reception as a pseudo-Aristotelian vehicle for princely counsel, occult knowledge, physiognomy, astrology, and medicine.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. The "Secret of Secrets" tradition designates the influential pseudo-Aristotelian text (Secretum secretorum) and its derivative literature, comprising one of the most widely circulated genres of medieval learned writing at the intersection of natural philosophy, medicine, physiognomy, astrology, and practical wisdom. The original Arabic text (Sirr al-asrar or Kitab sirr al-asrar), probably composed in the ninth or tenth century, was translated into Latin in two recensions: a partial translation by John of Seville (c.1120) and a longer version by Philip of Tripoli (c.1220–1250). Over two hundred Latin manuscripts survive.

Contents and Magical Dimension

The text's framing as a letter from Aristotle to Alexander the Great gave its contents the authority of the most eminent philosopher addressing the most powerful ruler. Its advice ranged across: governance and statecraft; health maintenance through diet, exercise, and seasonal regimen; physiognomy (reading character from physical features); astrology (timing activities by planetary configurations); and the occult properties of stones, plants, and animals. The natural magic dimension — recipes using specific materials with specific properties, instructions for astrological timing of medical and practical operations — sits uneasily alongside the practical governance advice, suggesting that the text was assembled from multiple sources.

Roger Bacon's engagement with the Secretum secretorum — he edited it and wrote a commentary treating it as genuine Aristotle — illustrates how the text operated in the thirteenth-century natural philosophical context: it provided authoritative support for the naturalistic treatment of apparently magical phenomena (occult properties of things, astrological timing) within the Aristotelian framework that dominated university natural philosophy. Don Skemer's work on material amulets and Sophie Page's on magical manuscripts both document the Secretum secretorum's circulation alongside explicitly magical content.
concepts.significance: Secret of Secrets refers to the Secretum Secretorum tradition and its reception as a pseudo-Aristotelian vehicle for princely counsel, occult knowledge, physiognomy, astrology, and medicine.

concepts.label: Experimenta
concepts.definition_short: Experimenta is an Actor Term for trials, recipes, or procedures transmitted as experiential knowledge; in medieval magic studies it marks the overlap between practical experiment, secrets literature, medicine, and ritual operation.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term (Latin plural). Experimenta (experiments, singular: experimentum) is the standard medieval Latin term for individual practical magical procedures — the discrete recorded operations that constitute the practical content of magical handbooks. An experimentum specifies what to do (materials, words, actions), when to do it (timing by planetary hours, lunar phases, or calendar days), and what result to expect. The term is neutral with respect to the moral status of the operation: the same word covers medical recipes, natural philosophical observations, and demonic conjurations, reflecting the medieval understanding of magic as a form of practical technology rather than a categorically distinct enterprise.

The Experiment Literature

Frank Klaassen coined the term "experiment literature" to designate the body of texts that record experimenta, distinguishing this practical literature from the theoretical natural philosophy that provided its intellectual context. The experimenta tradition spans the full social range of medieval magical practice: from the simple vernacular charm ("take three hairs from a black cat and bury them at a crossroads") through the elaborate Latin conjuration of the Munich Manual, the same basic format — specified materials, actions, timing, and expected result — underlies the practical content.

The textual history of experimenta is characterized by extreme mobility: individual experiments circulated freely, were extracted from one compilation and incorporated into another, were translated between Latin and vernacular, and were modified in transmission in ways that make it very difficult to establish priority between related texts. This mobility is itself evidence for the practical orientation of the tradition: what mattered was whether the experimentum worked, not who composed it or what theoretical framework it presupposed. Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic (2013) and Sophie Page's Magic in the Cloister (2013) both engage extensively with the experimenta tradition.
concepts.significance: Experimenta is an Actor Term for trials, recipes, or procedures transmitted as experiential knowledge; in medieval magic studies it marks the overlap between practical experiment, secrets literature, medicine, and ritual operation.

concepts.label: Renaissance Magic
concepts.definition_short: Analyst term for the magical traditions of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Europe, characterized by the synthesis of Hermeticism, Neoplatonism, Kabbalah, and natural philosophy associated with figures including Ficino, Pico, Agrippa, Bruno, and Dee. The category has been contested since Frances Yates's foundational work of the 1960s-1970s: Yates argued for a sharp break from medieval magic toward a sanitized natural-Hermetic magic; Frank Klaassen's manuscript evidence shows strong continuity with medieval ritual magic traditions. The concept requires careful distinction from magia naturalis, occult philosophy, and demonic magic.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Renaissance magic" designates the complex of natural-philosophical, astrological, Neoplatonic, and Hermetic theories and practices concerning the manipulation of occult forces that flourished in Italian, German, French, and English learned culture between approximately 1460 and 1620. The term is primarily an analyst category: historical actors spoke of magia naturalis, philosophia occulta, or simply magia, understanding these not as unified movements but as overlapping approaches to a shared problem — how to account for, and exploit, the hidden sympathies, antipathies, and influences that connected the celestial and terrestrial worlds.

Major Currents

Ficinian Neoplatonism and magia naturalis. Marsilio Ficino's De vita coelitus comparanda (1489, Book III of the De vita trilogy) is the founding text of Renaissance learned magic. Building on Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus, Ficino proposed that the spiritus mundi — a subtle pneumatic medium pervading the cosmos — could be attracted and concentrated by materials (stones, plants, metals, foods, images) that resonated with specific planetary influences. The philosopher-physician could draw down solar or Jovian spiritus through talismans, music, and diet, thereby healing a melancholic temperament over-saturated with Saturnine influence. Ficino carefully insisted that his magic operated through purely natural causes, avoiding explicit demonic invocation; whether this insulation was philosophically coherent or merely prudential has been debated by D.P. Walker, Brian Copenhaver, and Wouter Hanegraaff.

Pico della Mirandola and Kabbalah. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's Conclusiones (1486) and Apologia added Christian Kabbalah to the Neoplatonic-Hermetic synthesis. Pico argued that Kabbalah — the Jewish mystical tradition of divine names and letter permutations — could confirm Christian theological claims and provide a superior technology of spirit-working that explicitly recruited angelic rather than merely stellar powers. His fusion of Kabbalah, Neoplatonism, and Hermeticism defined what later scholars call "the Florentine synthesis" and shaped Cornelius Agrippa's encyclopedic De occulta philosophia (published 1531).

Agrippa's synthesis and its reception. Cornelius Agrippa's De occulta philosophia libri tres collected and systematized the full range of Renaissance occult philosophy — natural magic (Book I), celestial or mathematical magic (Book II), and ceremonial or divine magic (Book III). The three-book structure corresponded to the three worlds of Renaissance Neoplatonism: the elemental, the celestial, and the intellectual. Agrippa's handbook became the most widely read compendium of learned magic in early modern Europe, shaping practitioners' self-understanding through to the eighteenth century.

Giordano Bruno and the limits of the tradition. Bruno's Hermetic writings of the 1580s — the Spaccio de la bestia trionfante, De magia, and the Italian dialogues — represent the tradition in its most philosophically adventurous form, also its most dangerous: Bruno's panpsychic universe, in which all things are animated by a world-soul, dissolved the boundary between natural magic and a kind of immanent theology. His execution in 1600 marked the end of the era in which learned magic could be openly promoted as a philosophically respectable programme.

Scholarly Frameworks

The foundational scholarly account is D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella (1958), which established the tension between natural and demonic interpretations of the same magical operations as the central problem of the field. Yates's Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964) placed the tradition within a grand narrative of the Scientific Revolution. Brian Copenhaver's work on Ficino and on the Hermetica (his 1992 translation remains standard) has provided the most careful textual analysis. Ioan Couliano's Eros and Magic in the Renaissance (1987) offered a semiotic interpretation. For the English tradition, Deborah Harkness's John Dee's Conversations with Angels (1999) and Glyn Parry's work on Dee in his court context provide the best coverage.
concepts.significance: Central to the historiography of the transition between medieval and early modern learned magic.

concepts.label: Hermeticism
concepts.definition_short: Hybrid term covering both an ancient body of Greek philosophical and magical texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus (a conflation of the Greek god Hermes and Egyptian Thoth), and the tradition of thought that drew on these texts from late antiquity through the Renaissance. As an actor term, Hermetic designated the Corpus Hermeticum and related Asclepius texts. As an analyst term, it was expanded by Frances Yates to describe a broader Renaissance synthesis including Neoplatonism, astral magic, and Kabbalah. The dating of the Hermetic texts to ancient Egypt was demolished by Isaac Casaubon's philological analysis (1614).
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term (primarily). "Hermeticism" designates the tradition of philosophical and religious thought associated with, or claiming derivation from, the Corpus Hermeticum and related texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus — the "thrice-greatest Hermes," a syncretic figure identified with the Egyptian god Thoth and presented in the texts as an ancient sage who received divine revelation about the nature of the cosmos, the human soul, and the path of spiritual ascent. The tradition encompasses philosophical Hermeticism (concerned with cosmology, soul, and gnosis) and practical Hermeticism (the application of Hermetic principles to astral magic, alchemy, and related arts).

The Corpus Hermeticum and Its Renaissance Recovery

The Corpus Hermeticum consists of seventeen Greek philosophical and religious dialogues, plus additional texts including the Asclepius (preserved in Latin) and the Definitions of Hermes Trismegistus. The dialogues address the nature of Mind (Nous), the constitution of the cosmos from divine emanation, the relationship between the human soul and the divine, and the possibility of spiritual regeneration or gnosis. The texts date, as Casaubon demonstrated in 1614, to the first three centuries CE — not, as Renaissance readers believed, to Egyptian antiquity contemporaneous with Moses.

Marsilio Ficino's Latin translation of fourteen dialogues (completed 1463, printed 1471) introduced the Corpus Hermeticum to Latin Europe and initiated what scholars have called the "Hermetic Renaissance." Ficino interpreted the texts as evidence of a prisca theologia (primordial theology) that anticipated Christian revelation; this reading made the Hermetica acceptable within a Christian framework and enormously influential.

Magic and Hermeticism

Philosophical Hermeticism provided the theoretical basis for Renaissance natural magic. The doctrine of the world-soul (anima mundi) as a single animating principle pervading the cosmos, the teaching that all things are connected through sympathetic bonds (the Hermetic "all is one"), and the vision of the sage as a magus capable of cooperating with cosmic forces — all these provided Ficino, Agrippa, Bruno, and their contemporaries with a justification for magical operations framed as natural philosophy. D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic (1958) and Brian Copenhaver's edition of the Hermetica (1992) remain the standard scholarly resources.
concepts.significance: Framework for the Yates thesis and key to debates about Renaissance magic's relationship to medieval learned traditions.

concepts.label: Prisca Theologia
concepts.definition_short: Latin actor term for the doctrine, articulated primarily by Marsilio Ficino, that a single ancient theology passed from Moses and Zoroaster through Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato to Christian truth. The term justified Ficino's engagement with pagan texts including the Corpus Hermeticum, Chaldean Oracles, and Orphic hymns as preparations for Christian revelation. Pico della Mirandola extended the chain to include the Kabbalistic tradition. The prisca theologia legitimated a speculative natural magic rooted in ancient wisdom. Its chronology was undermined when Casaubon dated the Hermetic texts to the Christian era.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. Prisca theologia (the primordial or ancient theology) designates the Renaissance doctrine that a single, divinely-revealed wisdom — anticipating and confirming Christian truth — was transmitted through a chain of ancient sages: Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, Pythagoras, Plato, and ultimately Moses. The doctrine was formulated systematically by Marsilio Ficino in the preface to his Theologia Platonica (1474) and in various other texts, and provided the legitimating framework for the Hermetic and Neoplatonic philosophy he promoted. If Hermes Trismegistus was as ancient as Moses and his wisdom anticipated Christian truth, then the Corpus Hermeticum carried divine authority.

Historical Basis and Collapse

The doctrine's historical basis was illusory. The belief that Hermes Trismegistus was an Egyptian sage of Mosaic antiquity was itself a product of late antique Hermetic propaganda, preserved in Lactantius and Augustine. Isaac Casaubon's philological analysis (De rebus sacris et ecclesiasticis exercitationes, 1614) demonstrated from linguistic evidence that the Corpus Hermeticum was composed in the first three centuries CE, not in Egyptian antiquity. This refutation, though immediately recognized as compelling, had limited immediate practical effect on the tradition: the prisca theologia continued to be invoked in occult and esoteric contexts well into the eighteenth century and beyond, and Yates argued that the belief in the texts' antiquity — not their actual date — was what historically mattered.

Magical Significance

For the history of magic, the prisca theologia doctrine was primarily a legitimating strategy. If Hermetic magic derived from ancient Egyptian divine revelation — more ancient than Plato, contemporary with Moses — it could not be dismissed as merely superstition or demonic innovation. The Solomonic tradition employed an analogous strategy: attributing magical knowledge to Solomon, the wisest and most divinely-favoured of biblical kings, gave it pre-Christian, Scriptural authority. In both cases, pseudepigraphic antiquity served as a defence against theological condemnation.
concepts.significance: Foundational doctrine for Ficinian magic and the Yates thesis.

concepts.label: Magia Naturalis
concepts.definition_short: Latin actor term for a branch of knowledge concerned with the hidden powers of natural objects and their manipulation through sympathy, antipathy, and occult correspondence. Distinguished from demonic magic (goetia) and ceremonial magic, magia naturalis claimed to operate through natural forces accessible to human knowledge rather than through demonic mediation. Elaborated by della Porta's Magia Naturalis (1558, 1589) and given philosophical depth by Ficino's spiritus theory, the category proved capacious: by the seventeenth century it absorbed alchemy, magnetism, optics, medicine, and experimental observation, blurring the boundary between natural philosophy and learned magic.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. Magia naturalis (natural magic) designates, in Renaissance and early modern usage, the study and application of the hidden powers of nature — the occult properties of things, the influences of the stars, the sympathies and antipathies linking all things through the world-soul — that produce marvellous effects without supernatural or demonic intervention. The term was used by Renaissance natural philosophers as a positive category distinguishing their enterprise from the condemned demonic magic of the grimoire tradition, and as a claim to scientific respectability: natural magic was, its proponents argued, simply the highest branch of natural philosophy, concerned with the hidden causes that superficial investigation missed.

Major Formulations

The classical Renaissance formulation of magia naturalis as a positive programme appears in Giovanni Battista della Porta's Magia naturalis (Naples, 1558; expanded to twenty books, 1589), which became one of the best-selling books of the sixteenth century. Della Porta defined natural magic as the practical application of natural philosophy, concerned with producing remarkable effects through knowledge of hidden natural causes. The work's range is characteristic: it covers sympathies and antipathies, the virtues of plants and animals, pyrotechnics, optical tricks (including early descriptions of the camera obscura), magnets, and alchemy, all framed as natural phenomena accessible to systematic investigation.

Earlier formulations include Ficino's De vita coelitus comparanda (1489), which frames astral medicine and talismanic magic as natural operations through the spiritus mundi; Agrippa's Book I of De occulta philosophia (1531), on the elemental world's occult properties; and Roger Bacon's concept of scientia experimentalis as the crown of natural philosophy, producing marvellous effects through knowledge of hidden causes.

Relationship to Science

The relationship between Renaissance magia naturalis and the emergence of early modern natural science is the central problem of the "Yates thesis" debate. Yates and her followers argued that the emphasis on operative, experimental knowledge in natural magic prepared the psychological ground for Baconian experimental science. Critics argued that the traditions were more opposed than convergent: Bacon himself rejected occult sympathies as unfit objects of natural philosophical enquiry. The current consensus treats magia naturalis and emerging experimental science as partially overlapping but ultimately divergent traditions, sharing a commitment to the investigation of hidden causes while differing on method and metaphysics.
concepts.significance: Central category for Renaissance naturalization of magical practice.

concepts.label: The Yates Thesis
concepts.definition_short: Analyst term for the historiographical argument advanced by Frances Yates in Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964) and related works: that Hermeticism and natural magic were central forces in Renaissance culture, that they drove a transformation of magic from medieval demonic practice to a naturalized astrological-mathematical philosophy, and that this Hermetic magic contributed causally to the Scientific Revolution. The thesis was challenged by Vickers (1979), Copenhaver, and Klaassen, whose manuscript evidence for strong continuity between medieval and Renaissance ritual magic contradicts Yates's narrative of a clean break.
concepts.definition_long:
Overview

The "Yates thesis" is the interpretive framework advanced by Dame Frances Amelia Yates (1899–1981) in her trilogy Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964), The Art of Memory (1966), and The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972). In its strongest form, the thesis holds that Renaissance Hermeticism — the recovery and promotion of the Corpus Hermeticum in Marsilio Ficino's 1463 Latin translation — was a decisive, generative force in the emergence of early modern natural philosophy, and that figures such as Giordano Bruno operated within a coherent "Hermetic tradition" whose emphasis on man as magus and on the active manipulation of natural and celestial forces provided the psychological and conceptual preconditions for the Scientific Revolution.

The Argument in Detail

Yates's reading of the Corpus Hermeticum and its Renaissance reception depended heavily on the assumption, widespread since the Renaissance itself, that the Hermetic writings were genuinely ancient — that Hermes Trismegistus was a real Egyptian sage, contemporary with or even prior to Moses, whose wisdom preserved a primordial philosophical theology (prisca theologia). This assumption was demolished by Isaac Casaubon in 1614, who dated the texts to the first three centuries CE on philological grounds. Yates, writing in the 1960s, knew Casaubon's refutation but argued that the belief in the texts' antiquity — regardless of their actual date — was what mattered historically. For Renaissance thinkers, the Hermetica carried the authority of Egyptian antiquity, and this authority structured the way Ficino, Pico della Mirandola, Cornelius Agrippa, and Bruno read them.

The central move in the Yates thesis is the claim that Hermetic magia — the technology of drawing down celestial influences through talismans, suffumigations, music, and ritual — constituted a specifically operative philosophy: an attempt to change the world, not merely understand it. Yates argued that this operativity prefigured, and in some sense enabled, the experimental orientation of seventeenth-century natural philosophy. Where scholastic Aristotelianism had counselled contemplative knowledge of fixed natural essences, the Hermetic magus sought to intervene in nature's processes. The magician and the scientist shared, Yates suggested, a will to power over the natural world.

Reception and Critique

The thesis was enormously influential through the 1970s and provoked sustained scholarly revision from the 1980s onward. Brian Vickers's edited volume Occult and Scientific Mentalities in the Renaissance (1984) collected essays challenging the continuity Yates posited between magical and scientific thought, arguing that figures like Francis Bacon explicitly rejected Hermetic magic even while absorbing some Hermetic rhetoric. Robert Westman and J.E. McGuire, in Hermeticism and the Scientific Revolution (1977), questioned whether the specific claims Yates made about Bruno's influence on Copernicus could be sustained.

Nicholas Campion, Wouter Hanegraaff, and Kocku von Stuckrad have assessed the thesis's reception within the historiography of Western esotericism more broadly. D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella (1958) — published before Yates's Bruno book — had already mapped the territory of Renaissance learned magic with greater caution about grand causal claims, and Walker's more measured approach has aged better than Yates's ambitious synthesis.

The contemporary consensus, represented by scholars such as Liana De Girolami Cheney, Wouter Hanegraaff, and Anthony Grafton, treats the Yates thesis as a productive exaggeration: it opened up the study of Renaissance magic and esotericism as legitimate historical subjects, established the Corpus Hermeticum's centrality to sixteenth-century intellectual life, and demonstrated that figures previously dismissed as cranks (Bruno, Agrippa, Dee) were engaged with serious philosophical problems — even if the direct causal link Yates drew between Hermeticism and the Scientific Revolution is no longer defended in its strong form.

Significance for the Study of Grimoire Tradition

For grimoire scholarship specifically, the Yates thesis matters because it established the learned magical tradition as a coherent intellectual phenomenon worthy of rigorous historical analysis, rather than as an embarrassing footnote to the history of ideas. Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic (2013) and Claire Fanger's edited volumes build on this legitimation while correcting Yates's tendency to flatten the distinction between Renaissance learned magic and the practical ritual books (experiment literature) that circulated alongside philosophical Hermeticism.
concepts.significance: Transformed Renaissance historiography; now substantially revised but still the organizing reference for debates about the period.

concepts.label: Occult Philosophy
