concepts.definition_short: Hybrid term used by Agrippa as the title of his major work (De Occulta Philosophia, 1531-1533) and by later writers to denote a systematic philosophy of hidden natural powers, astral influences, and ceremonial operations. As an actor term in the sixteenth century, it designated Agrippa's three-tiered synthesis of natural, celestial, and ceremonial magic. As an analyst term, it has been applied to the broader tradition of learned magic associated with Ficino, Pico, Agrippa, Dee, and related figures, and to the study of this tradition in works from Walker and Yates to the present.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor and Analyst Term. "Occult philosophy" (philosophia occulta in Latin; also magia, natural magic) designates the Renaissance and early modern intellectual enterprise of systematically accounting for phenomena that exceeded ordinary natural causation — the hidden properties of things, the influences of stars, the operations of spirit — within a unified philosophical framework. The term was popularized by Cornelius Agrippa's De occulta philosophia libri tres (1531) and came to designate the learned tradition of natural and ceremonial magic as a coherent discipline.

Historical Background

The concept draws on three main sources. First, the Aristotelian-scholastic tradition of "occult qualities" — properties of things (magnetic attraction, the healing power of certain stones and plants, the effect of the moon on the tides) that operate beyond the observable qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) and cannot be explained by elemental analysis. Second, the Neoplatonic tradition of sympathetic magic: the world-soul pervades all things, connecting like to like through bonds of sympathy and repulsion; the philosopher-magician exploits these bonds to produce effects at a distance. Third, the Hermetic tradition of the ancient Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus, recovered in Ficino's 1463 translation of the Corpus Hermeticum, which presented a theosophical account of the cosmos as animated by divine intelligence accessible to the wise.

Agrippa's synthesis of all three traditions in De occulta philosophia created the standard reference work for Renaissance learned magic. His three-book structure — natural (elemental), celestial (astral), ceremonial (divine) — provided a framework replicated or responded to throughout the sixteenth century, from Giovanni Battista della Porta's Magia naturalis (1558, 1589) through John Dee's intellectual projects.

Relation to Early Modern Science

The relationship between occult philosophy and the emergence of early modern natural science remains debated. Frances Yates argued in Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964) that Hermeticism provided crucial psychological preconditions for the Scientific Revolution. Brian Vickers, David Lindberg, and Robert Westman argued that the traditions were more opposed than parallel. The current consensus treats occult philosophy and early modern natural philosophy as overlapping but distinct traditions, sharing some methodological commitments (attention to effects, interest in hidden causes) while differing sharply on others (experimental method, mathematical quantification, repeatability).
concepts.significance: Links the philosophical claims of Renaissance learned magic to its manuscript and ritual practices.

concepts.label: Grimoire Printing History
concepts.definition_short: Analyst term for the history of grimoire transmission through print from the fifteenth century onward. The printing press dramatically changed the circulation of magical texts: works that had circulated in small numbers of manuscripts became available in multiple editions across Europe. Key events include the printing of Ficino's De Vita (1489), Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia (1531), the Arbatel and Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (c.1559), Trithemius's Steganographia (1606), and the French popular grimoire tradition (Grand Albert, Petit Albert, Grand Grimoire) in the eighteenth century. Owen Davies's Grimoires (2009) is the standard reference.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Grimoire printing history" designates the complex transitions by which the learned magical handbook tradition — previously existing primarily in expensive manuscript copies circulating among clerical, court, and university networks — was transformed by the hand press (from c.1450) and later offset and print-on-demand technologies into a widely available, commercially produced genre. The history is neither simply one of democratization nor of degradation, but of repeated negotiations between the social capital of rarity, the commercial logic of print, and the legal and theological risks of publication.

Manuscripts Before Print

Before Gutenberg, grimoires existed as expensive, laboriously produced codices whose cost of production limited circulation. The Picatrix, the Clavicula Salomonis, the Ars Notoria, and the Munich Manual all circulated in small numbers of manuscripts, often among university graduates, cathedral clergy, and court astrologers. Don Skemer's Binding Words: Textual Amulets in the Middle Ages (2006) and Claire Fanger's edited volumes document this manuscript culture. The relative rarity of copies did not make manuscripts safe from ecclesiastical attention — inquisitors seized and destroyed them — but scarcity provided a degree of practical protection.

The First Wave of Printed Magic, 1486–1600

The earliest printed magical texts appeared in contexts that minimized their transgressive content. Ficino's De vita (1489), including the controversial third book on astral magic, was published under Medici patronage in Florence. Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (1531) appeared openly in Cologne. Giovanni Battista della Porta's Magia naturalis first appeared in 1558 (four books) and was expanded to twenty books in 1589, becoming one of the best-selling books of the sixteenth century; della Porta consistently framed his magic as natural philosophy. The Heptameron of pseudo-Pietro d'Abano circulated as an appendix to Agrippa's fourth book.

The grimoires most resistant to print were those involving explicit demonic conjuration — the Munich Manual, the Sworn Book of Honorius, the Clavicula Salomonis — which circulated in manuscript long after other magical texts had been printed. The reason was legal and theological: explicit demonic pact had been criminalized by the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina (1532) in Germany and by various inquisitorial procedures elsewhere.

Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries: The Chapbook Grimoire

The decisive transformation came in the seventeenth and especially eighteenth century, when cheaper printing methods enabled the production of small, inexpensive pamphlet grimoires for a popular market. The Grand Albert, the Petit Albert, the Grimorium Verum, and the Grand Grimoire (also known as the Dragon Rouge) were printed, reprinted, and translated across France, Germany, and eventually England in editions designed for a market of literate craftsmen, village cunning folk, and urban fortune-tellers. Owen Davies's Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (2009) provides the most comprehensive account of this shift, tracing how magical texts moved from elite clerical culture to popular commercial publishing.

The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses, first printed in Germany c.1849 but drawing on older manuscript material, represents the endpoint of this trajectory: a grimoire produced explicitly for a mass market, with no pretence of elite origins, that spread through German immigrant communities into the American South and Caribbean, influencing hoodoo practice.

Nineteenth and Twentieth Century: Occult Revival Editions

The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn's manuscript-sharing culture in the 1880s–1900s was print culture's partial inverse: a movement of ritual magicians who deliberately withheld texts from publication, grading access by initiation level. Samuel Liddell Mathers's edition of the Key of Solomon (1889) and his translation of the Book of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin (1898) bridged manuscript scholarship and occult practice, appearing as commercial editions through Kegan Paul while retaining the air of recovered secrets. A. E. Waite's parallel editorial production served a similar market.

Joseph Peterson's Esoteric Archives (online from 1997) and his print editions through Ibis Press represent the contemporary digital-first equivalent: the exhaustive scholarly edition produced for practitioners and historians simultaneously, using digital technology to circulate texts previously known only to manuscript specialists.

Key Scholarly Resources

Owen Davies, Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (Oxford, 2009) is the essential overview. Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic (2013) covers the manuscript period. For chapbook grimoires in France, see Lawrence Principe and Lloyd DeWitt (eds.), Chymists and Chymistry. For print and magic more broadly, see the essays in Claire Fanger (ed.), Invoking Angels (2012) and the relevant sections of Richard Kieckhefer, Magic in the Middle Ages (1989).
concepts.significance: Key to understanding the transformation of medieval manuscript magic into modern print occultism.

concepts.label: Vernacular Grimoire Tradition
concepts.definition_short: Analyst term for the tradition of magical texts composed or transmitted in vernacular languages (English, French, German, Italian, Spanish) rather than Latin. While the high tradition of learned magic remained primarily Latin, vernacular grimoires emerged from the fifteenth century onward, often combining learned magical procedures with popular charms, medical recipes, and folk practices. Klaassen's Making Magic in Elizabethan England and The Magic of Rogues examine English vernacular magic manuscripts; Dan Harms and Joseph Peterson's Book of Oberon edition provides a major source text. The French Grand Albert and Petit Albert represent the popular side of the vernacular tradition.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. The "vernacular grimoire tradition" designates magical texts composed or compiled in vernacular languages — Middle English, Middle French, Middle High German, Italian, Spanish — rather than in the Latin that dominated learned magical writing through most of the medieval period. The emergence of vernacular grimoires reflects the broader expansion of vernacular literacy in the thirteenth through fifteenth centuries and the growing market for practical knowledge texts outside the clerical Latin-literate community.

Examples and Range

The vernacular tradition encompasses a wide range of texts and social contexts. At the learned end, vernacular translations and adaptations of Latin magical texts (the Clavicula Salomonis in French, Italian, and English; portions of the Picatrix in Castilian; astrological magic texts in German) brought sophisticated learned magic to readers with less Latin. At the popular end, the vernacular charm collections (the English "receipts," French "experiments," German Zauberbücher) address a lower social level, providing healing formulas, protective charms, and simple love or harm magic in accessible language.

The Book of Oberon (Folger Shakespeare Library MS V.b.26), edited by Harms, Clark, and Peterson (2015), exemplifies the Elizabethan vernacular tradition: a miscellany in English combining Solomonic conjuration (including the fairy spirit Oberon) with simpler practical magic in a single compilation, suggesting a practitioner who worked in both registers. Johannes Hartlieb's Buch aller verbotenen Kunst (c.1456) — written in German at the request of the Margrave of Brandenburg — provides a vernacular account of the seven prohibited arts (including chiromancy, geomancy, and nigromancy) that serves both as an encyclopedia of forbidden knowledge and as a warning against it.

Scholarship

Owen Davies's Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (2009) traces the vernacular tradition's development into the early modern chapbook grimoire market. Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic (2013) documents the manuscript context of vernacular magical texts in medieval England. The essays in Katelyn Mesler and others' work on vernacular encyclopedism provide broader context for the expansion of vernacular technical literature.
concepts.significance: Essential for understanding how Latin learned magic was adapted and democratized in the early modern period.

concepts.label: Neoplatonism and Magic
concepts.definition_short: Hybrid term for the relationship between Neoplatonist philosophy and magical practice from late antiquity through the Renaissance. Plotinus and Iamblichus theorized a hierarchy of being through which sympathetic operations (theurgy) could draw down divine powers. Ficino's translation of Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus alongside the Corpus Hermeticum gave Renaissance magic its philosophical framework of celestial hierarchies, spiritus mediation, and astral attraction. D.P. Walker and Frances Yates showed how Ficino's Neoplatonism provided an intellectual legitimation for astral magic operations. Klaassen has argued this legitimation was often more rhetorical than operational.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Neoplatonism and magic" designates the relationship between the philosophical tradition of Plotinus, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Pseudo-Dionysius and the magical practices — theurgy, ritual, talisman-making, spirit-working — that were embedded in some branches of that tradition and that shaped Renaissance learned magic through Ficino's recovery and promotion of Neoplatonic philosophy. The relationship is complex because Neoplatonism is not a single tradition: Plotinus himself was sceptical about ritual efficacy, while Iamblichus and Proclus endorsed theurgy (ritual operations aimed at union with the divine) as a higher form of philosophical practice than purely intellectual contemplation.

Plotinus and the Problem of Efficacy

Plotinus's Enneads acknowledge that magical operations can produce real effects — they exploit the natural sympathies that connect all things through the world-soul — but Plotinus himself was unimpressed by this. The wise man, he argued, would not use such techniques because they operate on the lower soul and distract from the intellectual ascent toward the One. The sage is "immune to magic" precisely because he has detached himself from the sympathetic network that makes magic possible.

Iamblichus, in his De mysteriis (a response to Porphyry's letter to Anebo questioning whether theurgy worked), defended ritual as essential to the philosopher's ascent: purely intellectual philosophy cannot achieve union with the divine because the divine transcends intellect; it is through theurgy — ritual acts that mirror the divine order and invoke divine response — that the philosopher completes his ascent. Iamblichus's defence of theurgy provided the philosophical grounding for practical magical ritual that Ficino and subsequent Renaissance magicians drew on.

Renaissance Reception

D.P. Walker's Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella (1958) identifies the tension between Plotinian naturalism and Iamblichan theurgy as the central philosophical problem for Renaissance Neoplatonism: Ficino needed Iamblichan theurgy to explain how his astral magic worked, but Iamblichan theurgy shaded into demonic magic as Christian theologians defined it. The resolution Ficino attempted — claiming natural (Plotinian) rather than theurgic (Iamblichan) efficacy for his procedures — was philosophically unstable but practically necessary. Brian Copenhaver's work on Ficino's sources and Wouter Hanegraaff's on Western esotericism provide the most recent accounts of this relationship.
concepts.significance: Defines the philosophical context of Ficinian and Agrippan magic.

concepts.label: Enochian System
concepts.definition_short: A system of angelic language, tables, and magical operations developed by John Dee and his scryer Edward Kelley through their angelic conferences of 1582-1589 and recorded in the Mysteriorum Libri Quinque and related diaries. The system comprises a non-natural language (Enochian) transmitted by angelic dictation, extensive tables of correspondences, and operatory procedures. Frank Klaassen has shown that the conference format and angelic invocation procedures are continuous with late medieval angelic magic traditions including the Sworn Book of Honorius and the Ars Notoria, rather than being a distinctly Hermetic or Renaissance innovation.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor and Analyst Term. The Enochian system designates the angelic language, cosmology, and ritual system revealed to John Dee and his scryer Edward Kelley during their angelic conversations of 1582–1589, and subsequently elaborated within the Western ceremonial magic tradition, most notably by the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn in the 1880s–1900s. In Dee's own usage, the system was not called "Enochian" — that designation was applied later; Dee and Kelley called the language received in their sessions the "Angelic Language" or the language of the angels, and connected it to the antediluvian patriarch Enoch.

The Communications

The angel conversations, conducted primarily at Dee's Mortlake house and then during the continental travels of 1583–1589, produced an elaborate angelic cosmology: forty-eight "Angelic Keys" or "Calls" in the angelic language (with English translations), tables of letters corresponding to angelic names and powers (the "Tabula Bonorum"), a system of angelic governors arranged in a complex cosmographic scheme, and extensive prophecy concerning the eschatological future of Europe. The communications were received through Edward Kelley's scrying in a crystal "shewstone," with Dee recording every utterance in his diaries.

Deborah Harkness's John Dee's Conversations with Angels (Cambridge, 1999) provides the most thorough analysis of the angel conversations in their historical context, arguing that Dee understood the system as a divinely-restored Adamic language and a programme for the reform of natural philosophy. The primary manuscript sources are BL Sloane 3188 and 3677; Meric Casaubon published a selection as A True and Faithful Relation in 1659.

Post-Dee Elaboration

The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn absorbed the Enochian material in the 1880s through the work of Samuel Liddell Mathers and William Wynn Westcott, incorporating the Enochian Calls into the Grade rituals and treating the system as a complete magical technology. Aleister Crowley's elaborations and the subsequent influence on twentieth-century ceremonial magic (the A∴A∴, Thelema, the Aurum Solis) have made "Enochian magic" one of the most widely practised systems in the modern Western magical tradition.
concepts.significance: Key example of Renaissance magical practice that claimed novelty while remaining within medieval ritual frameworks.

concepts.label: Print Culture and Magic
concepts.definition_short: Analyst term for the intersection of the history of print with the history of magical text circulation. The printing press from the 1450s onward transformed how magical texts reached audiences: works that survived in a handful of manuscripts could reach hundreds of readers in printed editions. This created new markets, new censorship pressures (Index Librorum Prohibitorum entries for many magical works), and new possibilities for the corruption and standardization of texts. Owen Davies's Grimoires (2009) is the standard account; Klaassen's work on sixteenth-century manuscript collections shows that manuscript transmission persisted alongside print throughout the early modern period.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Print culture and magic" designates the transformation of the magical tradition that resulted from the shift from manuscript to print as the primary medium of text production and distribution, a process beginning with the hand press in the 1450s and continuing through the nineteenth century's steam-powered mass printing. The introduction of print did not simply disseminate existing magical texts more widely; it changed what kinds of texts were produced, who could access them, how they were read, and what authority and social meaning they carried.

The First Wave: Learned Magic in Print

The earliest printed magical texts appeared in contexts that minimized their transgressive character. Ficino's De vita (1489) appeared under Medici patronage as a work of natural philosophy. Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (1531) was printed openly in Cologne. Giovanni Battista della Porta's Magia naturalis (1558, expanded 1589) became one of the century's best-sellers by framing natural magic as applied natural philosophy. The grimoires most resistant to print were those involving explicit demonic conjuration: the Clavicula Salomonis, the Lemegeton, the Munich Manual — these circulated in manuscript throughout the sixteenth century because their content risked legal and ecclesiastical prosecution.

The Chapbook Revolution

The decisive popular transformation came in the seventeenth and especially eighteenth century, when cheaper printing methods enabled a mass market for practical magic pamphlets. Owen Davies's Grimoires: A History of Magic Books (Oxford, 2009) provides the most comprehensive account: the French Grand Albert, Petit Albert, and Dragon Rouge; the German Sechste und Siebente Buch Mosis; and their English and American equivalents created a grimoire market aimed at literate artisans, tradespeople, and rural practitioners. The chapbook grimoire is not simply a diluted version of the learned tradition but a distinctively popular form adapted to different needs and social contexts.

Modern Occult Publishing

The Victorian occult revival — Mathers, Waite, Crowley, the Theosophical Society — created a new genre of scholarly-occult edition that bridged academic and practitioner audiences. The twentieth-century paperback occult market (Llewellyn, Weiser, Ibis Press) and the internet have extended this further. Joseph Peterson's Esoteric Archives (online from 1997) represents the digital equivalent: rigorous scholarly editions made freely available to a global audience of both historians and practitioners.
concepts.significance: Explains how medieval manuscript traditions became early modern print traditions.

concepts.label: Kabbalism in Renaissance Magic
concepts.definition_short: Hybrid term for the incorporation of Jewish Kabbalistic methods and cosmology into Renaissance Christian philosophical and magical systems. Pico della Mirandola was the first major Christian thinker to synthesize Kabbalah with Neoplatonism and magic in his 1486 Theses. Agrippa devoted substantial sections of De Occulta Philosophia to Kabbalistic letter magic, divine names, and numerical speculation. Frances Yates argued that Christian Kabbalah was central to the Hermetic tradition she traced through Bruno and Dee. Klaassen has noted that the Kabbalistic elements in actual practical magic manuscripts of the period are present but less dominant than the philosophical literature suggests.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Kabbalism and Renaissance magic" designates the synthesis of Jewish Kabbalah with Christian theology and Neoplatonic philosophy achieved by Pico della Mirandola, Johannes Reuchlin, and Cornelius Agrippa in the period 1486–1531, which produced "Christian Kabbalah" — an adaptation of Jewish mystical doctrines about divine names, sefirot, and letter-permutation serving as a technology of magical and theological knowledge. Christian Kabbalah provided the third element of the standard Renaissance occult synthesis: natural magic (elemental), astral magic (celestial), and Kabbalistic magic (divine or intellectual).

Pico and the Beginnings

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's 900 Conclusiones (Rome, 1486) included 72 Kabbalistic theses, among them the claim that no science demonstrates the divinity of Christ more effectively than Kabbalah. Pico learned Kabbalah from Jewish teachers — primarily the convert Samuel ben Nissim Abulfaraj (Flavius Mithridates) — and purchased a collection of Kabbalistic manuscripts. His Apologia (1487), written to defend the condemned theses, argued that Kabbalah was not demonic magic but a divinely revealed mystical tradition confirming Christian truth. His distinction between "practical Kabbalah" (the magical manipulation of divine names) and "speculative Kabbalah" (theological meditation) mapped onto the Christian distinction between licit and illicit enquiry, with Pico firmly placing his own interest in the speculative category.

Reuchlin and Agrippa

Johannes Reuchlin's De verbo mirifico (1494) and De arte cabalistica (1517) provided more systematic accounts of Christian Kabbalah for German humanist readers, focusing especially on the divine name (the Tetragrammaton) and its Christological interpretation. Cornelius Agrippa's De occulta philosophia III (1531) incorporated Kabbalistic materials systematically into the third level of his magical hierarchy — divine or ceremonial magic — arguing that the manipulation of Hebrew divine names could draw down angelic assistance and ultimately achieve direct divine communication.

Scholarship

François Secret's Les Kabbalistes chrétiens de la Renaissance (1964) is the foundational survey. Joseph Dan's work on Kabbalah and early modern Christianity, and Moshe Idel's comparative studies of Kabbalah and magic, provide the Jewish scholarly perspective. For Agrippa, see Charles Nauert's biography (1965) and V. Perrone Compagni's critical edition of De occulta philosophia (Brill, 1992).
concepts.significance: Links Renaissance philosophical magic to the Hebrew learned tradition and to debates about Yates's thesis.

concepts.label: Spiritual Magic
concepts.definition_short: A category developed by D.P. Walker in Spiritual and Demonic Magic (1958) to describe magical operations that work through the pneuma or spiritus, the subtle material medium between soul and body in Neoplatonist physiology, rather than through explicit demonic summons. Walker argued that Ficino's De Vita Coelitus Comparanda was a spiritual magic: operations on the spiritus through music, scent, diet, and talismans drew stellar influences without violating the natural order or summoning demons. Walker's distinction between spiritual and demonic magic parallels but is not identical to the Renaissance actor-term distinction between magia naturalis and goetia or nigromantia.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "Spiritual magic" is D.P. Walker's term, coined in Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella (Warburg Institute, 1958), for the type of Renaissance magical operation that works through the spiritus — the subtle pneumatic medium that Neoplatonic and medical philosophy posited as the link between the material body and the immaterial soul, and between the human organism and the world-soul of the cosmos. Spiritual magic is Walker's analytical category for operations that their practitioners claimed worked through purely natural causes (exploiting the spiritus's responsiveness to celestial influence) rather than through demonic cooperation.

Walker's Framework

Walker introduced the term to capture the specific philosophical territory occupied by Ficino's De vita coelitus comparanda and its successors: operations that used material means (foods, fumigations, music, talismans) to adjust the practitioner's pneumatic constitution by attracting or repelling specific planetary influences through the medium of the spiritus mundi. The key claim of spiritual magic is naturalistic: the spiritus is part of the natural world, subject to the same sympathies and influences as all other natural things, and operations that work through it are therefore natural philosophy rather than demonology.

Walker's analysis shows, however, that this naturalistic claim was philosophically unstable. The Neoplatonic framework that explained how spiritual magic worked — the doctrine of world-soul, daemonic intermediaries, and sympathetic resonance derived from Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus — was not entirely innocent of the personal, addressative spirit-working that Christian theology condemned as demonic magic. Ficino's insistence that his operations were purely natural (like medicine or music, not like necromancy) was a necessary claim for his own protection, but it could not be fully sustained within the Neoplatonic framework he actually used. Walker's concept thus identifies the central philosophical problem of Renaissance learned magic: the tension between the need for a naturalistic account and the dependence on a theoretical framework that could not be fully naturalized.
concepts.significance: Walker's framework for Ficinian magic remains the primary analytical tool for distinguishing categories within Renaissance occult philosophy.

concepts.label: Reformation and Magic
concepts.definition_short: Analyst term for the relationship between the Protestant and Catholic Reformations and the history of magical practice and belief in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The Reformation created new pressures on magical practice: Protestant theologians rejected Catholic sacramental and exorcistic rites as superstition while simultaneously enabling new forms of learned Protestant demonology. The Inquisition prosecuted magical practitioners in Catholic territories. The Arbatel (1575) shows Protestant inflections in its grimoire; the development of vernacular magic in England was shaped by the Reformation's disruption of monastic and clerical institutional contexts for manuscript transmission.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. "The Reformation and magic" designates the complex and contested relationship between the Protestant and Catholic reformations of the sixteenth century and the magical practices they inherited, tolerated, attacked, and transformed. The relationship is multidimensional: the Reformations attacked Catholic ritual as magic (the Mass as transubstantiation, indulgences, relic veneration); created new demarcations between acceptable religion and condemned superstition; intensified prosecution of witchcraft in some contexts while creating scepticism about it in others; and produced new forms of providentialist thinking that both condemned divination and generated prophetic cultures of their own.

Protestantism and Magic

Protestant reformers faced a distinctive problem: their dismantling of the Catholic sacramental and ritual system — exorcism, holy water, blessed candles, the sign of the cross as protection against demons — removed the institutional tools that had provided ordinary people with protection against maleficium. If holy water no longer worked against demons, what did? Protestant responses varied: some insisted that providentialist prayer and faith were the only legitimate protection; others tolerated or even promoted cunning folk and practical magic as filling the gap left by the abolished Catholic protective rituals. Keith Thomas's Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) argued that the Reformation's dismantling of Catholic magic created the demand for popular magic that cunning folk met. This thesis has been qualified by subsequent work showing that Catholic regions also had thriving popular magic cultures.

The Protestant witch-hunting of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries is a further dimension: if Protestant reformers were more aggressive in pursuing witchcraft prosecutions in some regions, this was not because they took magic more seriously than Catholics but because the institutional reconfiguration of the relationship between religion and magic created new anxieties and new legal frameworks. Brian Levack's The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe provides the standard overview. Stuart Clark's Thinking with Demons (1997) analyses Protestant and Catholic demonological writing as parallel intellectual systems.
concepts.significance: Contextualizes the social and institutional conditions of early modern magical practice.

concepts.label: Rosicrucian Movement
concepts.definition_short: Analyst term for the early seventeenth-century movement associated with three anonymous manifestos: the Fama Fraternitatis (1614), Confessio Fraternitatis (1615), and Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosenkreutz (1616). These texts claimed the existence of a secret brotherhood of Christian Rosenkreuz devoted to spiritual and magical reform of society. Frances Yates's Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972) argued that the movement represented a political and magical program connected to the Hermetic-Kabbalist tradition. The Rosicrucian synthesis drew on Paracelsian natural philosophy, alchemy, and the occult philosophy of Agrippa and Dee to produce a distinctive early modern magical-religious worldview.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. The Rosicrucian movement designates the early seventeenth-century cultural phenomenon initiated by the anonymous publication of three manifestos — Fama Fraternitatis (1614), Confessio Fraternitatis (1615), and Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosencreutz anno 1459 (Chemical Wedding, 1616) — purporting to announce the existence of a secret fraternity of learned brothers (Fratres Rosae Crucis) founded by the legendary "Christian Rosenkreuz" who had gained wisdom from Arabic and Eastern sources in the fifteenth century. The manifestos called for a universal reformation of arts, sciences, and religion, combining Hermetic, Paracelsian, and Protestant themes.

The Manifestos and Their Context

The Fama Fraternitatis narrated the life and posthumous discovery of Christian Rosenkreuz: born in 1378, he travelled to Morocco, Damascus, and Fez, absorbing Arabic wisdom; returning to Europe, he founded a fraternity of eight brothers dedicated to healing the sick freely and preparing for a general reformation. His tomb, discovered 120 years after his death in perfect preservation, contained books, instruments, and a preserved body — the symbolism of hidden wisdom waiting for the right moment to be disclosed. The manifestos provoked an enormous response: over two hundred pamphlets were published between 1614 and 1620 by writers seeking to contact or join the fraternity.

Frances Yates's The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972) linked the manifestos to the Palatine court of Frederick V and Elizabeth Stuart and to a network of Hermetic reformers including Michael Maier, Robert Fludd, and Johann Valentin Andreae (the likely author of the Chemical Wedding). Yates argued that the Rosicrucian movement was a coherent political and intellectual programme connecting Hermetic magic, early modern science (Francis Bacon), and Protestant utopianism. This reading has been contested: subsequent scholars have found the Rosicrucian connection to Bacon and early science much looser than Yates claimed, and the fraternity itself may never have had more than imaginary existence.

Legacy

The Rosicrucian tradition persisted through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in various forms, contributing to Freemasonry and the broader tradition of secret society esotericism. By the late nineteenth century, formal Rosicrucian orders existed in Europe and North America. The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn's degree structure drew on Rosicrucian symbolism. Christopher McIntosh's The Rosicrucians: The History, Mythology and Rituals of an Esoteric Order (Weiser, 1997) provides the most accessible scholarly overview.
concepts.significance: Marks the culmination of Renaissance magical synthesis into an early seventeenth-century reform movement.

concepts.label: Adjuration
concepts.definition_short: Actor Term (from Latin adjurare, to swear by). The ritual speech act by which a practitioner compels a spirit, demon, or angel to act, typically by invoking divine names, Solomonic authority, or binding formulas. Adjuration is the central ritual mode of the Solomonic grimoire tradition, distinguishing this literature from prayer (petitionary) and from simple invocation.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term (from Latin adjurare, to swear by, to compel by oath). The adjuration is the ritual speech act by which a practitioner compels a spirit — demon, angel, or ambiguous intermediate being — to appear, obey, or depart, typically by invoking divine names, Solomonic authority, or binding oaths sworn in God's name. It differs from prayer (oratio), which petitions; from invocation, which calls; and from suffumigation or physical rite, which acts materially. The adjuration is the central operative verbal mode of the Solomonic grimoire tradition.

Structure and Examples

A typical adjuration follows a recognizable pattern: address to the spirit by name and title; statement of the divine authority by which the practitioner speaks ("I adjure you by the living God, by the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, by the seal of Solomon..."); specification of what the spirit is commanded to do; and often a threat of what angel or divine name will punish the spirit's non-compliance. The spirit catalogues of the Testament of Solomon, the Clavicula Salomonis, and the Lemegeton organize their material around adjuration formulas keyed to specific spirits.

Jewish adjuration (Hebrew hashba'ah) appears in the Sepher ha-Razim, the magical papyri, and Geonic-period amulet texts analysed by Gideon Bohak (Ancient Jewish Magic, 2008). The Arabic tradition of Solomonic adjuration is preserved in texts studied by Pablo Torijano (Solomon the Esoteric King, 2002). The Latin tradition, from the Clavicula Salomonis through the Munich Manual's conjuration rituals (Kieckhefer, Forbidden Rites, 1997), represents the medieval crystallization of this tradition.

Theological Status

The adjuration of spirits was theologically contested: the adjuration of demons was universally condemned as an implicit demonic pact; the adjuration of angels was more ambiguous. The Ars Notoria addresses prayers to God and angels in ways that blend petition and adjuration; its condemnation by Thomas Aquinas turned partly on the question of whether the formulas addressed divine power or presupposed demonic assistance. Richard Kieckhefer's analysis of the Munich Manual distinguishes levels of coerciveness in the conjuration formulas as evidence for the spectrum of relations with spirits that practitioners imagined.
concepts.significance: Primary ritual speech act of the Solomonic and demonic conjuration tradition

concepts.label: Ring of Solomon
concepts.definition_short: Actor Term. The signet ring with which Solomon was said to bind, seal, and control demons, appearing in the Testament of Solomon and pervasive in Islamic, Jewish, and Christian magical literature. The ring functions as a symbol of divine authority over the demonic hierarchy and as the architectural concept underlying seals and pentacles in the Solomonic grimoire tradition.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Actor Term. The Ring of Solomon is the signet ring given by the archangel Michael to King Solomon (according to the Testament of Solomon), inscribed with a pentagram or divine name, that granted Solomon power to summon, interrogate, and bind demons, compelling them to serve him in the construction of the Temple in Jerusalem. The ring is the foundational magical instrument of the Solomonic tradition: all subsequent Solomonic authority — the seals, pentacles, and conjuration formulas of the grimoire corpus — derives symbolically and narratively from this originary instrument of demonic binding.

Sources

The Testament of Solomon (probably second to fifth century CE) provides the fullest account: the ring is described as bearing a five-pointed seal (pentagrammon) and is given by Michael in response to Solomon's prayer. Josephus (Antiquities 8.2.5) mentions Solomon's knowledge of exorcistic arts and roots, but not the ring specifically. The ring's power to bind Asmodeus — the demon who had been plaguing Solomon's servant — and all subsequent demons makes it the architectural concept underlying the entire spirit-binding tradition.

In Islamic tradition, the "seal of Solomon" (khatam Sulayman) is even more central: Sulayman's ring (given by God) is described in Qurʾanic commentary and hadith literature as bearing God's greatest name and as enabling his rule over jinn, animals, and winds. The visual motif of the hexagram — the six-pointed Star of David / Seal of Solomon — became associated with Solomonic power across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic magical traditions, appearing on amulets and magical seals throughout the medieval and early modern periods. Pablo Torijano's Solomon the Esoteric King (2002) and Gideon Bohak's Ancient Jewish Magic (2008) provide the fullest scholarly analyses.
concepts.significance: Central symbol of Solomonic magical authority and demonic binding

concepts.label: Solomonic Authority
concepts.definition_short: Analyst Term. The legitimating strategy by which magical texts attribute their contents to Solomon, thereby claiming royal, divinely-granted, and pre-Christian authority for their procedures. Solomonic authority is a form of pseudepigraphy that confers prestige and apparent safety on texts that might otherwise be condemned as demonic. Torijano (2002) and Klaassen (2013) both analyze Solomonic attribution as a dynamic textual strategy.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. Solomonic authority designates the legitimating strategy by which magical texts attribute their content to King Solomon — claiming that the procedures, spirit names, seals, and adjurations they contain were originally revealed to, compiled by, or passed down from the biblical king who was the wisest man in history and who built the Temple of God with demonic labour. The attribution accomplishes several things simultaneously: it gives the text a pre-Christian, Scriptural pedigree; it associates magical knowledge with royal power and divine favour; and it frames potentially condemned operations as part of a divinely sanctioned historical project (building the Temple).

The Attribution Strategy

Solomonic attribution is not a single fixed claim but a repertoire of framing devices deployed with varying specificity across the tradition. Some texts (the Testament of Solomon) narrate Solomonic magic as a historical event. Others (the Clavicula Salomonis) present themselves as the actual book Solomon compiled from his magical knowledge. Others still invoke "the wisdom of Solomon," "the seal of Solomon," or "the pentacle of Solomon" as authorizing concepts without claiming direct textual transmission. In Islamic tradition, Sulaymanic authority functions in parallel ways across a different set of textual and cultural resources.

Frank Klaassen's The Transformations of Magic (2013) analyses Solomonic attribution as a dynamic textual strategy that changes across the medieval period: earlier texts tend to frame Solomonic magic within a broadly Christian ritual framework (Solomon as proto-Christian king, the demonic work as God-ordained); later texts sometimes adopt the attribution more mechanically, as a conventional marker of the grimoire genre rather than a substantive theological claim. Pablo Torijano's Solomon the Esoteric King (2002) provides the deepest analysis of the attribution across Jewish, Christian, and Islamic sources.
concepts.significance: Key mechanism of legitimation in the learned magical grimoire tradition

concepts.label: Spirit Catalogue
concepts.definition_short: Analyst Term. A structured list or hierarchy of named demons, angels, or spirits with their ranks, attributes, seals, and functions, constituting a major organizational feature of the Solomonic grimoire tradition. Spirit catalogues appear in the Testament of Solomon, the Ars Goetia (Lemegeton book 1), and numerous medieval Latin and vernacular compilations. Kieckhefer (1997) treats them as evidence of a learned clerical engagement with demonological classification.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Analyst Term. A spirit catalogue is a structured list or hierarchy of named demons, angels, or spirits with their individual attributes — ranks, seals or sigils, powers, associated celestial bodies, and sometimes the means of binding or dismissing them — constituting a major organizational feature of the Solomonic grimoire tradition. Spirit catalogues represent one of the most distinctive features of the learned magical tradition, distinguishing it from popular protective magic (which typically addresses spirits generically rather than by name) and from philosophical demonology (which classifies demons theoretically rather than enumerating them operatively).

Historical Development

The earliest and most influential spirit catalogue is in the Testament of Solomon (probably second to fifth century CE): thirty-six or more demons are summoned by Solomon, each revealing its name, the affliction it causes, the angel that can thwart it, and (in some recensions) its physical appearance. This pattern — named spirit, function, counteracting angel — is the template replicated across two millennia. The Ars Goetia (part of the seventeenth-century Lemegeton) catalogues seventy-two demons with names, ranks (king, duke, marquis, count, etc.), seals, and powers, derived from an earlier catalogue appended to Johann Weyer's De praestigiis daemonum (1563). The Sepher ha-Razim catalogues the angelic inhabitants of the seven heavens with their periods of activity and adjuration formulas.

Richard Kieckhefer's analysis in Forbidden Rites (1997) treats spirit catalogues as evidence of a learned clerical engagement with demonological classification: the detailed enumeration of spirits by name, rank, and function reflects the same scholastic impulse toward systematic taxonomy visible in natural philosophy and theology. The operative function — using the name to summon the spirit — may be primary, but the classificatory structure reflects learned culture's organizing habits.
concepts.significance: Structural feature distinguishing learned grimoire from popular charm tradition

concepts.label: Pentacles and Magical Figures
concepts.definition_short: Hybrid Term. In the Solomonic grimoire tradition, pentacles (also called lamens, sigils, or seals) are geometric or symbolic figures drawn on paper, parchment, or metal and attributed with power over specific spirits or for specific operations. The term has both actor usage (practitioners made and used pentacles) and analyst function (scholars classify them as material artefacts of ritual practice). The Clavicula Salomonis devotes major sections to pentacle construction and consecration.
concepts.definition_long:
Definition

Hybrid Term. In the Solomonic grimoire tradition, "pentacles" (pentacula, also called lamens, sigils, or pentagrammata) are geometric or symbolic figures — typically circles containing divine names, astrological symbols, planetary characters, and/or spirit seals — inscribed on parchment, paper, or metal and attributed with power over specific spirits or for specific magical operations. The term combines actor usage (practitioners made and used pentacles as material ritual objects) and analyst function (scholars classify them as distinctive artefacts of the Solomonic tradition).

The Clavicula Salomonis Pentacles

The Clavicula Salomonis (Key of Solomon) devotes major sections of its second book to the pentacles: forty-four pentacles keyed to the seven planets, each with a specific figure, a set of divine and spirit names inscribed within it, and a brief account of its use and efficacy. The figures are circular, typically divided into segments containing names in Hebrew and Latin, astrological symbols, and geometric patterns. Each planetary set (seven pentacles of Saturn, seven of Jupiter, etc.) addresses a specific range of operations appropriate to that planet. The pentacle is not merely symbolic but operative: the practitioner holds or displays it during conjuration, and its possession is understood to give authority over the spirits within the relevant planetary domain.

Joseph Peterson's edition of the Key of Solomon (Weiser, 2004) documents the manuscript variation in the pentacle figures, showing that different manuscript families reproduce substantially different figures under the same names — suggesting that the figures were copied and modified without access to a stable original, and that their specific content was less important than their ritual function as material signatures of Solomonic authority.

Relationship to Seals and Characters

Pentacles overlap with "seals" (spirit-specific sigils attributed to individual named demons or angels, as in the Lemegeton Ars Goetia) and "characters" (the generic term for magical graphic signs). The broader category of magical figure-work — including magic circles, geometric diagrams, and ritual drawings — is treated by Frank Klaassen in The Transformations of Magic (2013) as a key feature distinguishing the learned grimoire tradition from popular magical practice, which generally used simpler verbal formulas rather than elaborate graphic systems.
concepts.significance: Material ritual object central to Solomonic grimoire practice
